Title: chordoma dedifferentiation after proton beam therapy: a case report and review of the literature.
Authors: Frankl J;Grotepas C;Stea B;Lemole GM;Chiu A;Khan R
Institution: university of arizona college of medicine
Family History: no family history of skin cancer except for skin cancer in her grandfather
Medical/Surgical History: NA
Signs and Symptoms: she complained of 4 weeks of pressure-like headaches, mostly in the posterior occipital area, and intermittent nausea with several episodes of emesis in june of 2012; 2.5 years later after the surgical resection, she experienced acute cranial nerve 6 palsy
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: physical examination (significant for decreased sensation to light touch over the right side of her face and her right upper extremity); magnetic resonance imaging of brian (revealed a large heterogenous emanating intracranially from the base of her clivus and extending throgh the foramen magnum to c1-c2; a small portion was anterior to c1-c2 in her nasopharyngeal soft tissues with extension through her left hypoglossal canal; posteriorly, the lesion displaced her pons and medulla; multiple cranial nerves were not well seen and were either displaced or encased by the mass as it filled the right cerebromedullary angle; the lesionw as t1 isointense to muscle and only mildly enhanced in portions; the lesion had a predominantly very bright t2 signal; there was restricted diffusion with bright diffusion-weighted imaging and dark apparent diffusion coefficient signals, indicating hypercellularity); mri 2.5 years later (showd a 3x1.5x4 cm mass in the resection cavity with signal change suspicious for dedifferentiation; the recurrent tumor was centered at the rightward aspect of her clivus and extended superiorly to the dorsum sella and inferiorly to the level of the occipital condyle; the signal intensity of this mass was intermediate to dark, isointense to gray matter on t2-weighted images in contrast to the very t2 hyperintense signal like cerebral spinal fluid as seen on the initial presentation; in addition, on follow-up the lesion was avidly enhancing post-contrast on t1-weighted imaging as compared to the initial lesion where there was only mild enhancement.)
Diagnosis: chordoma that dedifferentiated to sarcoma after proton beam therapy
Laboratory Values: NA
Pathology: the biopsy from the initial lesion showed classic chordoma histology with physaliphorous cells with multivacuolated cytoplasm mixed with epithelioid cells arranged in anastomosing cords, clusters, and chains. there was a myxoid matrix and occasional fibrous septa. no immunohistochemical stains were performed as histology provided a definitive diagnosis. hematoxylin and eosin staining of the recurrent tumor obtained during our patient’s second surgery, however, showed a high-grade anaplastic spindle cell neoplasm. there were areas of geographical necrosis with no particular architectural pattern visible at low magnification. in the higher power images, the cells were very pleomorphic with epithelioid and spindle shapes, and there were mitotic figures present. myofibroblastic tumor and fibrosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma were ruled out with immunohistochemistry. vimentin was positive, consistent with sarcoma in general. ki-67, a proliferation index that is normally very low in a chordoma, was scored at 80 %, indicating rapid cellular division. epithelial membrane antigen (ema), cytokeratin, and brachyury were negative, indicating full dedifferentiation
Pharmacological Therapy: she was referred to a proton facility where she received fractionated proton and photon beam therapy: 77.4 gy total, 59.4 gy (cobalt gray equivalent) in 33 fractions with protons and 18 gy in 10 fractions with photons. after the recurrence of the cancer, she completed 17 cycles of ifosfamide and etoposide alternating with vincristine, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide with the last round in april 2016. she began maintenance capecitabine on 26 april 2016
Interventional Therapy: endonasal surgical resection occurred; the resection of the chordoma left residual tumor in her lateral skull base at the hypoglossal canal and jugular foramen; after the second mri was taken, she had a second surgery
Patient Outcome Assessment: the most recent mri, 14 months after her second surgery, showed a mild interval decrease in tumor size
Funding Source: no outside funding was used to support this research
Disclosures: the authors declare that they have no competing interests

Title: alternaria infectoria brain abscess in a child with chronic granulomatous disease.
Authors: Hipolito E;Faria E;Alves AF;de Hoog GS;Anjos J;Gonçalves T;Morais PV;Estevão H
Journal: european journal of microbiology & infectious diseases
Institution: hospital pediátrico de coimbra, portugal.hospital pediátrico de coimbra, portugal

Comorbidities: brain abscess due to a melanised; catalase-positive fungus; a. infectoria
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: admitted to the hospital after a short-time focal seizure involving the right upper limb; the patient was clinically well, except for sinusitis; a computed tomography (ct) scan revealed a cerebral abscess in the left parietal dorsally frontal cortex, with a vasogenic oedema ; after the seizure, the clinical examination was normal, except for a giant lymphadenopathy at the left axilla; this lymphadenopathy had first been observed at the age of 6 months, when it had the same volume, and it was never drained on the assumption that a reaction to bcg was concerned, as is known for other cgd patients [7]; the ct scan also revealed a sinusitis, confirming the clinical observation; microbiological parameters included blood culture, culture of cerebrospinal fluid (csf) and blood aspergillosis serology (precipitin test); the microbiological analysis yielded a negative result; on hospital day 3, a brain magnetic resonance imaging (mri) scan confirmed the previous diagnosis and showed a left brain lesion with a focal region surrounded by a vasogenic oedema ; one month later, the purulent material of the brain abscess was aspirated and sent to the microbiology laboratory; culture from this material revealed a dark pigmented fungus, exhibiting sterile hyphae only; at that time, it was impossible to identify the fungus, but judging from the melanised character, a recurrence of invasive aspergillosis was excluded; this result prompted a change in therapy; several attempts were made to identify the dematiaceous fungus on the basis of classical morphological features; this approach was unsuccessful, since, in our routine setting, it was not possible to optimise the conditions for sporulation, and, hence, morphological key features for identification remained absent; amplification of the rdna its region was performed using the primers its1 5?-tcc gtaggtgaacctgcgg-3? and its4 5?-tcctccgctt attgatatgc-3?; the fragment obtained was sequenced in an abi prism 310; using comparable sequences available in genbank and a dedicated database maintained at cbs, the fungus was identified as a; infectoria; following this identification, the fungus was grown in 12-h alternating light–dark incubation on corn meal agar, and scarce conidia, characteristic of a; infectoria, were obtained ; the fungus also proved to be catalase-positive
Diagnosis: chronic granulomatous disease (cgd); brain abscess due to a melanised, catalase-positive fungus, a. infectoria
Laboratory Values: microbiological parameters included blood culture, culture of cerebrospinal fluid (csf) and blood aspergillosis serology (precipitin test). the microbiological analysis yielded a negative result; one month later, the purulent material of the brain abscess was aspirated and sent to the microbiology laboratory. culture from this material revealed a dark pigmented fungus, exhibiting sterile hyphae only; amplification of the rdna its region was performed using the primers its1 5?-tcc gtaggtgaacctgcgg-3? and its4 5?-tcctccgctt attgatatgc-3?. the fragment obtained was sequenced in an abi prism 310. using comparable sequences available in genbank and a dedicated database maintained at cbs, the fungus was identified as a. infectoria. following this identification, the fungus was grown in 12-h alternating light–dark incubation on corn meal agar, and scarce conidia, characteristic of a. infectoria, were obtained (fig. 3). the fungus also proved to be catalase-positive
Pathology: NA
Pharmacological Therapy: therapy was started with liposomal amphotericin b, 3 mg/kg, intravenously every day, interferon gamma (ifn?; 10 subcutaneous administrations; 75 ?g/m2 /day, three times a week), methylprednisolone (day 26, 1.5 mg/kg/day) and intravenously administered antibiotics (vancomycin, 50 mg/kg/day, twice a day; ceftazidime, 100 mg/kg/day, every 8 h); amphotericin b and antibiotics were replaced by voriconazole (8 mg/kg, intravenously, twice a day) and caspofungin (50 mg per day); therapy with intrathecal 5 mg of caspofungin was started on a daily basis
Interventional Therapy: upon the diagnosis of a hydrocephaly, a ventricular reservoir was placed, and some liquid was removed daily, in order to decrease the intracranial pressure
Patient Outcome Assessment: however, the child became critically ill and died after 144 days of voriconazole, 124 days of caspofungin, 60 days of ifn-? and 12 days of intrathecal caspofungin

Title: beneficial effect of sodium dichloroacetate in muscle cytochrome c oxidase deficiency.
Authors: Burlina AB;Milanesi O;Biban P;Bordugo A;Garavaglia B;Zacchello F;DiMauro S
Institution: neurological institute, columbia-presbyterian medical center, new york, usa
Family History: the patient was born at term to non-consanguineous healthy parents
Medical/Surgical History: here, we report the successful treatment of severe lactic acidosis associated with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in a patient with muscle cytochrome c oxidase (cox) deficiency; the patient was born at term to non-consanguineous healthy parents (birth weight 2700g; apgar scores 9 and 10 at 1 and 5 rain); at the age of 1 month was admitted to a local hospital because of rapid respiration, feeding difficulty, weakness, and lack of ocular fixation; the liver was 5 cm below the costal margin and had severe metabolic acidosis with elevated blood lactate (5.5 mmol/1); ecg showed signs of ischaemia and echocardiography showed marked hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; was transferred to our department in a critical condition (polypnoic and dyspnoic) and a repeat ecg showed marked hypertrophy of the left ventricular posterior wall (diastolic thickness 8.5 mm, normal value 4-6 mm), reduced diastolic left ventricular function and mild pericardial effusion; blood chemistry showed normoglycaemia and severe metabolic acidosis (ph7.18, hco3 8; lactate 15retool/i, reference value <2 mmol/1; pyruvate 0.35 mmol/1, reference value < 0.16 mmol/1; lactate/pyruvate molar ratio 42; 3-hydroxybutyrate 0.55 mmol/ 1, reference value < 0.06; acetoacetate 0.12 mmol/1, reference value < 0.02; 3-hydroxybutyrate/acetoacetate molar ratio 4.58); urinary organic acid screening revealed increased excretion of lactic acid (4800 mmol/mol creatinine, reference < 200), 2-hydroxybutyric acid (55 mmol/mol creatinine, reference < 2), 3-hydroxybutyric acid (212 mmol/mol creatinine, reference <2), fumaric 134mmol/mol creatinine, reference <5), malic (74mmol/mol creatinine, reference <5), ct-ketoglutaric (165 mmol/mol creatinine, reference <10), and citric acid (325 mmol/mol creatinine, reference <20); serum total and free carnitine concentration were 56 and 44gmol/1, respectively; total cpk was 216u/1 (normal < 290) with normal ck-mb fraction; he received large doses of carnitine and sodium bicarbonate without clinical benefit; because of increasing lactate levels (18 mmol/1) and clinical worsening, dca (tokyo kasey, japan) was administrated orally in three doses (150rag per day); after 3, 6, 9, 12 and 24h, blood lactate levels were 18 and decreased to 12, 10, 6 and 1.8retool/i, respectively, and pyruvate from 0.37 to 0.14retool/i, then remained within the normal range although the dose of dca was gradually decreased to 25 ng/kg 15er day within 7 days; on the 2nd day of dca therapy a muscle biopsy was performed and revealed reduced activity in cox (18.9 nmol/mird mg; control 63 + 29) and normal succinate cytochrome c reductase, citrate synthase, nadh dehydrogenase, succinate dehydrogenase and pyruvate dehydrogenase; after 16 days of oral administration of dca, the drug was discontinued because of the improved clinical condition; 12 h later, however, the lactate level again increased to 15 mmol/1 and remained between 14 and 18 mmol/1 until dca administration was resumed; after 9 months of therapy, there has been a dramatic reduction of heart size: echocardiography showed a normal heart, with normal wall thickness (5 mm; controls 4-6 ram) and left ventricular function (ejection fraction 76%, systolic fraction 43%) and low blood lactate values ranging from 1.6 to 3.1mmol/1; because it is thought that dca is metabolised to oxalate and glyoxalate in liver we measured plasma oxalate which was normal (5 gmol/1; controls < 7); the child is developing normally, both physically and mentally; eeg and auditory and somatosensory evoked potentials are normal; although experience with dca therapy is still limited to few cases, this is the first patient with muscle cox deficiency who appears to have responded to this therapy

Title: biventricular pacing in a patient with severe congestive heart failure.

Institution: department of thoracic and cardiovascular surgery, tokyo medical and dental university

Signs and Symptoms: 1993: chest oppression on exercise; 1996: shortness of breath in light daily exercise; now: he was admitted for biventricular pacing in medically refractory chronic heart failure
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: 1993: coronary angiography (showed 75% stenosis of the left anterior descending artery); 1996: ecg (showed complete left bundle branch block (qrs=240 ms)); now: echocardiography (showed diffuse severe hypokinesis of the lv wall (lvdd/s = 96/87 mm, la = 62 mm, lvef = 19%); showed moderately severe mitral regurgitation); cardiothoracic ratio - 61%; intracardiac pressure obtained at the previous hospital showed 85/60 (71) in the aorta, and 30/18 (22 mmhg) in the main pulmonary artery; mean pulmonary artery capillary wedge pressure was 19 mmhg
Diagnosis: severe congestive heart failure
Laboratory Values: NA
Pathology: NA
Pharmacological Therapy: 1996: he received full medical treatment with betablockers, maximum doses of diuretics, and ace inhibitors
Interventional Therapy: 1993: successfully treated with percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty; 1996: an intravenous implantation of a left-ventricular lead via the coronary sinus for bvp was attempted; bvp did not succesed because the lead could not be threaded into the coronary sinus; now: one day before surgery, right atrial and ventricular bipolar endocardial leads were inserted successfully into the right atrium (ra) and right ventricle (rv), and proximal ends of leads were hidden in a subcutaneous pocket formed in the left subclavicular region of the chest; surgery was conducted under general anesthesia and intravenous dopamine infusion; we approached the left pleural cavity through a small left lateral thoracotomy; adhesion between the pericardium and epicardial surface associated with previous open heart surgery was dissected and a screw-in epicardial lead inserted on the lateral surface of the lv 3 cm from the atrioventricular groove; the proximal end of the lv lead was tunneled subcutaneously to the previously formed subclavicular pocket; in the pocket, lv and rv leads were connected to a y-shaped adapter (lv to ?, rv to +); both the ra lead and the single lead from the y-adapter were connected to a pacemaker generator; the thresholds of the lv, rv, and ra leads at lead implantation were 0.5 v, 1.75 v, and 1.0 v, all at a pulse-width of 0.4 ms; pacing was begun in ddd mode (hr 60, ventricular amplitude = 5.0 v at 0.4 ms, atrial amplitude = 3.5 v at 0.4 ms, a-v delay = 120 ms); after bvp, systolic blood pressure immediately increased from 100 mmhg to 126 mm hg; surgery was completed without complications
Patient Outcome Assessment: now: a hemodynamic study by swan-ganz catheter done in the icu 3 days after bvp implantation showed an approximately 20% increase in systolic blood pressure and cardiac output (table i); predischarge echocardiography showed reduced mitral regurgitation and la chamber size (from 64 mm to 56 mm); the patient’s symptoms and exercise tolerance dramatically improved

Title: mitochondrial encephalomyopathy due to a novel mutation in the trnaglu of mitochondrial dna.
Authors: Pancrudo J;Shanske S;Bonilla E;Daras M;Akman HO;Krishna S;Malkin E;DiMauro S
Institution: h. houston merritt clinical research center for muscular dystrophy and related diseases, department of neurology, 4-420 college of physicians and surgeons, columbia university medical center, 630 w. 168th street, new york, ny 10032, usa
Family History: family history is notable for a brother, age 12 years with autistic features, possibly asperger syndrome; he is somewhat clumsy, has decreased muscle tone, and has mild proximal arm weakness; his serum creatine kinase is normal; the mother and 10-year-old sister are normal and have normal serum creatine kinase levels; similar analysis of accessible tissues from the patient’s mother and siblings showed that the mutation was detectable in the mother, but not in either sibling; analysis of accessible tissues from the proband’s rela- tives showed some interesting features (figure 3); in the proband, the mutant load was highest in both urine sedi- ment and cheek mucosa and lowest in blood; this pattern is similar to that of the common a3243g mutation associ- ated with the melas (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes) syndrome.5 in the proband’s mother, the mutation was barely detectable in blood, whereas it was clearly present in urinary sedi- ment cells and in buccal smears; analysis of the mother’s tissues confirmed another feature of the a3243g mutation, namely, that individual hair follicles have widely different mutant loads; surprisingly, we could not detect the muta- tion in any accessible tissues from either of the patient’s siblings; this finding was particularly unexpected for the brother, who had low muscle tone, proximal weakness, and autistic features; it is still possible that, although unde- tectable in accessible tissues, the mutation might be present in muscle or brain
Medical/Surgical History: NA
Signs and Symptoms: a 14-year-old boy developed persistent fatigue, weakness, difficulty breathing, headache, and unsteady gait after 3 days of hiking on the mountains; neurological examination showed facial weakness, constant facial grimaces, proximal limb weakness, unsteady gait with positive romberg sign, dysmetria, ataxic tandem gait, and inability to hop; laboratory investigations showed elevated serum creatine kinase (2600, normal <238; muscle and brain fraction 126, normal <3.9), lactic acid (22.3, nor- mal 3–12), but normal pyruvate and complete blood count; urinary amino acids, plasma amino acids, and very long chain fatty acids were normal; the electrocardiogram was remarkable for a pr interval >0.02; brain computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging (mri) were normal
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: the electrocardiogram was remarkable for a pr interval >0.02; brain computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging (mri) were normal
Diagnosis: cytochrome-c oxidase deficiency
Laboratory Values: laboratory investigations showed elevated serum creatine kinase (2600, normal <238; muscle and brain fraction 126, normal <3.9), lactic acid (22.3, nor- mal 3–12), but normal pyruvate and complete blood count. urinary amino acids, plasma amino acids, and very long chain fatty acids were normal
Pathology: histochemical study of muscle using 8-?m-thick frozen sections was carried out as described. biochemical analysis was performed in 10% muscle homogenates as previously described; histochemical analysis of the muscle biopsy showed fre- quent ragged-red fibers and cytochrome c oxidase–deficient fibers (figure 1). in keeping with the mitochondrial pro- liferation, biochemical analysis revealed increased activi- ties of citrate synthase and succinate dehydrogenase, which are both synthesized entirely by nuclear dna. when normalized to citrate synthase, activities of com- plexes i, iii, and iv were all reduced (table 1). the presence of ragged-red fibers and cytochrome c oxidase–negative fibers and the reduced activities of respira- tory chain enzymes containing mtdna-encoded subunits suggested a mutation in mtdna. in fact, sequencing of the 22 mtdna trna genes revealed a novel mutation in the trna for glutamic acid (trnaglu). the change was a c-to-a at nucleotide position 14680 (figure 2a). polymerase chain reaction and restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis of the patient’s tissues showed mutant loads of 98% in muscle, 96% in urinary sediment, >99% in cheek mucosa, and 83% in blood (figure 2b)
Patient Outcome Assessment: NA
Funding Source: national institutes of health; muscular dystrophy association; marriott mitochondrial disorders clinical research fund
Disclosures: this work has been supported by nih grant hd32062, a grant from the muscular dystrophy association, and the marriott mitochondrial disorders clinical research fund (mmd- crf)

Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: imaging studies that were performed during that hospitalization included chest radiography and computed tomographic (ct) angiography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis; these studies revealed basilar atelectasis, changes consistent with mild congestive heart failure, and a new subpleural nodular opacity (1.3 cm in diameter) in the right middle lobe (figure 1a); there was also bilateral mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy with coarse calcifications, a finding that was unchanged from imaging studies that had been obtained 2 years earlier; ct of the chest, performed without the administration of contrast material, revealed multiple small pulmonary nodules, many of which were subpleural (figure 1c); the nodules were unchanged from imaging studies obtained 2 years earlier, and the new nodule in the right middle lobe that had been seen on the previous study had resolved; ct of the abdomen and pelvis, performed without the administration of contrast material, revealed a right renal cyst (2.9 cm in diameter) and an enlarged prostate; a bone scan showed no evidence of bone metastases; thyroid ultrasonography revealed bilateral colloid cysts but no extrathyroid nodules; a skeletal survey showed diffuse osteopenia, with lucent lesions in the calvarium and possibly the mandible, as well as subtle, indeterminate lucent lesions in the legs that raised concerns about multiple myeloma or metastatic cancer; a chest radiograph revealed a tortuous calcified aorta, evidence of aortic-valve replacement, and no evidence of pneumonia or effusion; electrocardiography (ecg) showed sinus rhythm at a rate of 50 beats per minute; the results were otherwise unchanged from earlier tracings; 18f-fluorodeoxyglucose (fdg) positron-emission tomography (pet) revealed marked fdg avidity in the mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy (figure 1d)
Diagnosis: sarcoidosis
Laboratory Values: urinalysis showed no evidence of blood; the platelet count and red-cell indexes were normal, as were blood levels of glucose, total protein, albumin, globulin, total and direct bilirubin, aspartate aminotransferase, and alanine aminotransferase; other laboratory test results are shown in table 1. urinalysis revealed clear yellow urine, with a specific gravity of 1.009, a ph of 5.5, and trace albumin by dipstick, and was otherwise normal. after the test results were known, the patient was advised to go the emergency department of this hospital; cytologic examination and culture of the urine were negative; blood levels of lactate dehydrogenase and vitamin a were normal, and testing was negative for hepatitis b virus surface antibodies and antigen and hepatitis c virus antibodies; additional laboratory test results are shown in table 1. repeat urinalysis revealed 1+ occult blood and albumin by dipstick; examination of the urinary sediment revealed 0 to 2 red cells and white cells, few bacteria, and few squamous cells per high-power field. the urinary sodium level was 55 mmol per liter, the creatinine level was 0.44 mg per milliliter (3890 ?mol per liter), and the osmolality was 329 mosm per kilogram of wate; levels of complement (c3 and c4) were normal, and testing was negative for antibodies to double-stranded dna, ssa (ro), ssb (la), sm, and rnp
Pathology: pathological examination of a bone marrow–biopsy specimen showed 7% plasma cells and an increased number of monoclonal plasma cells with kappa light chains; pathological examination of the renal-biopsy specimen revealed two glomeruli with global sclerosis (out of the six examined), interstitial fibrosis, and tubular atrophy affecting 30% of the cortex. the principal finding was a focal but dense infiltrate of mononuclear cells that was composed predominantly of lymphocytes, with some histiocytes and plasma cells and without eosinophils. there were foci of tubulitis that was characterized by disruption of basement membrane by the inflammatory cells (figure 2a). interstitial fibrosis resulted in tubular atrophy (figure 2b). these findings indicate chronic active tubulointerstitial nephritis. in addition, localized collections of histiocytes were present. the epithelioid character of the histiocytes, as well as their circumscription, can be described as granulomatous or as poorly formed granulomas (figure 2c).1 the glomeruli that were observed in the renal-biopsy specimen were normal apart from the global sclerosis in areas of inflammation (figure 2d); a biopsy of a paratracheal lymph node. on histopathological examination, the node was subtotally replaced by compact, confluent, non-necrotizing granulomas with microfocal necrosis. a discrete granuloma impinged on a lymphatic vessel in the node (figure 3b). these findings were consistent with sarcoidosis. the degree of necrosis was within the range that is commonly encountered in sarcoidosis, and stains and cultures for organisms were negative. lymph node biopsy, whether of an enlarged peripheral lymph node12 or an enlarged mediastinal lymph node,13 remains a standard procedure for the definitive diagnosis of sarcoidosis
Pharmacological Therapy: donepezil hydrochloride, citalopram, tamsulosin, ranitidine, quetiapine, aspirin, psyllium, and a multivitamin. bicarbonate, isoniazid, rifampin , oral glucocorticoids
Patient Outcome Assessment: approximately 2 years ago, the glucocorticoids were discontinued; hypercalcemia has not recurred, the results of serum protein electrophoresis are unchanged, and the patient has not required any additional therapies

striking contrast to the normal myelination of the peripheral nerves beginning at the extra-axial cranial and spinal nerve roots. rarely, single subcortical arcuate fibres or other myelinated axons connecting fibres and internal capsule were totally demyelinated and gliotic. the width of the cortical band was normal. large numbers of residual axons remained throughout the demyelinated areas, although the overall volume of the axonal mass was decreased. basal ganglia - the neuronal population of the caudate and putamen was normal, as was the ratio of large to small neurons. the claustrum was normal. the globus pallidus contained many pigment-filled glial cells and a normal complement of neurons. the anterior limb of the internal capsule was markedly atrophic. the posterior limb was gliotic, as were the myelinated bundles of the striatum. status marmoratus was not present. some residual myelinated fibres remained in the ansa lenticularis. the substantia nigra contained decreased numbers of neurons and extruded pigment, free within the parenchyma and in regional macrophages. many of the remaining neurons contained normal amounts of melanin. there were no inclusion bodies. diencephalon - the lateral thalamus was extremely gliotic with marked loss of neurons; the medial thalamus was less affected. lipofuscin was present in some thalamic neurons and in regional macrophages. the posterior thalamus showed a moderate neuronal loss with increased astrocytes, microglia and macrophages. the subthalamic nucleus contained a normal neuronal population. the hypothalamus was normal. hippocampus - the dentate fascia and hilus were normal. sectors cab ca2, and caa all contained a normal neuronal population; specifically, there was no abnormality in sommer's sector. on the other hand, the alveus, fimbria, fornix and cingulum were totally demyelinated. cerebellum.-the dentate nucleus had a normal number of neurons; purkinje cells were decreased, bergmann's layer was thickened. there was a diffuse gliosis of the molecular layer; the granular cell layer was well populated. no myelin remained in the afferent or efferent cerebellar connexions. brain-stem - the superior cerebellar peduncle contained a small amount of residual myelin and there was an occasional tuft of myelin in basis pontis. the neurons of the basis pontis were normal; no neurofibrillary tangles were encountered in tegmental neurons. the locus caeruleus neurons were normaliy pigmented. in the midbrain the medial and lateral lemnisci retained small amounts of myelin, as did the spinal and mesencephalic tracts of the fifth nerve and one central tegmental tract. the peduncles were totaliy unmyelinated. the medial longitudinal fasciculi were not visible in myelin stain. in general, the cranial nerves retained some myelin in their infranuclear portions, and this increased as they neared their exit from the brain-stem. the peripheral portions of the cranial nerves were well myelinated. spinal cord.-the cross section of the spinal cord was triangular in outline as a result of loss of bulk in the lateral and dorsal funiculi. both of these regions were demyelinated with more marked loss in fasciculus gracilis than in cuneatus. anterior horn cells were present in normal numbers and contained much lipofuscin. in the widely demyelinated regions there was a marked reduction of oligodendrogliacytes. throughout the white matter a marked fibrillary gliosis was present. the myelin deficit and dense fibrillary gliosis extended throughout the central nervous system from telencephalon to spinal cord and included the cerebellum. there was no evidence of inflammation. small numbers of macro phages, both parenchymal and perivascular in location, were found in hemispheral white matter; and, to a lesser extent, in cerebellar white matter, but not in brain-stem, optic nerves, tracts or spinal cord. two varieties of these cells were present. the first was a typical macrophage with a vesicular, vacuolated cytoplasm and a nucleus of normal size. the second appeared to contain a more homogeneous cytoplasm or small masses of homogeneous material within the cytoplasm. both varieties were found in parenchyma, as well as in perivascular spaces. the staining characteristics were quite different. chloroform-methanol extractable material in the first variety (vacuolar) stained well with oil red 0, sudan black b, and periodic acid schiff (pas), and was black in osmium tetroxide et-naphthylamine in frozen sections of formalin-fixed brain. the material in the second (homogeneous) variety was not stainable by any of these methods but appeared to be well demonstrated in cajal gold sublimate preparations. hortega silver carbonate method for microgliacytes readily demonstrated several stages in the evolution of the microgliacyte to the vacuolated macrophage; the homogeneous macrophage was not recognized in this preparation. two additional points of interest were that (a) the material in the vacuolar macrophage could not be demonstrated when the macrophage lay in parenchyma, but was readily demonstrated when the macrophage lay in a perivascular space, and (b) the macrophages bore no obvious relationship to the few residual tufts of myelinated axons. the largest tuft in the basis pontis had no macrophages near by. myelin in the residual tufts was pas negative, in contrast to the pas-positive material in macrophages and in the normal peripheral myelin. optic system - the entire right eye and the posterior pole of the left eye were available within normal limits. the lens was normal. in the posterior segment there was a marked reduction in the number of ganglion cells, particularly in sections passing through the peri macular area. there was also a reduction in the number ofaxons in the retina and optic nerve, especially evident at the margin of the optic disc. there was no myelin in the optic nerve which should be myelinated at this age; a gross increase in interfascicular connective tissue was present. there was no evidence of pigmentary proliferation in the retina, and the retinal pigment epithelium appeared intact. sections of the posterior pole of the left eye showed that the number of retinal ganglion cells was also reduced in this eye; it seems probable that the pathological process was identical in the two eyes. the lateral geniculate bodies showed diffuse and marked loss of neurons and disruption of laminar pattern. the parvocellular portions were almost completely depopulated with some preservation of neurons in the magnocellular portion. the optic radiations showed slight retention of myelin but were markedly atrophic. the calcarine cortex retained a distinctly laminated pattern of neurons. a very pale Authors: Rosé CD;Doyle TM;McIlvain-Simpson G;Coffman JE;Rosenbaum JT;Davey MP;Martin TM
Institution: thomas jefferson university, dupont children's hospital, wilmington, delaware, usa
Family History: 2 nonconsanguineous parents and his younger brother have remained healthy, with no evidence of any rheumatic or ocular disease despite 20 years of followup; a sister died at age 1 year of complications of cystic fibrosis

Signs and Symptoms: initial evaluation at our center at the age of 39 months revealed a well appearing young boy tracking at the 25th percentile for weight and height, who was normotensive and afebrile; he had a typical tan-colored erythematous scaly rash mainly on his legs, shoulders, and trunk; he had a moderate cushingoid appearance and his cardiopulmonary, abdominal, neurological, and peripheral vascular examinations were normal; he had limitation of neck motion, boggy synovial thickening of both wrists with 130° range of motion, remarkable swelling of all pip joints of both hands and swelling and limitation of both elbows, slight hip limitation, bilateral ankle boggy synovitis, and tenderness over 1st to 4th metatarsal phalangeal (mtp) joints bilaterally; his chest radiographs were normal and the skeletal radiographs showed periarticular osteopenia at the affected locations as well as prominent soft tissue swelling; the articular course was characterized by corticosteroid dependency with unremitting polyarthritis; deformities, however, were limited to contracture of the pip joints and distal radioulnar subluxation; his uveitis after 20 years of disease has remained active; at age 10 he was noted to have normal lenses and pressures and some vitreal involvement, with no evidence of retinitis; at age 13 his vision was 20/40 on the right and 20/50 on the left; currently his uncorrected vision is 20/30 on the right and 20/60 on the left; there was no evidence of anterior chamber inflammation at his most recent evaluation; secondary cataract

genomic dna was extracted from cheek cells using the puregene dna purification kit according to manufacturer’s instructions (gentra systems, minneapolis, mn, usa); polymerase chain reaction (pcr) was performed to amplify a region of exon 4 from card15 using faststart taq dna polymerase with gc-rich solution (roche diagnostics, mannheim, germany) and a touchdown pcr strategy; since the yield and purity of genomic dna did not allow a robust pcr amplification, a secondary pcr amplification of the first reaction product was performed using an internal primer set; the resultant pcr product was excised from an agarose gel, purified using zymoclean gel dna recovery kit (zymo research, orange, ca, usa), then subjected to direct dna sequencing in both directions on an abi377 automated fluorescence dna sequencer (applied biosystems, foster city, ca, usa) by the portland va medical center molecular biology core laboratory; results; the majority of card15 exon 4 (i.e., corresponding to mrna nucleotides 752–2407) was sequenced in both directions from the secondary pcr amplification product; sequencing revealed a c to t mutation at position 1105, a mutation reported previously in blau syndrome families; the mutation causes a substitution of tryptophan for arginine at amino acid position 334 (r334w); in addition to this mutation, we detected the presence of 3 other polymorphisms in exon 4: one corresponds to an amino acid substitution of proline to serine at position 268 (p268s) and the other 2 are silent mutations, encoding arginine at position 459 (r459r) and arginine at position 587 (r587r); Institution: department of cardiology, hospital de la santa creu i sant pau, barcelona, spain
Medical/Surgical History: no history of rheumatic fever, alcohol intake, chest pain, recent fever or infection was noted; had lost 15 kg in weight over several months
Signs and Symptoms: he was admitted for acute arterial occlusion of the right leg and congestive heart failure; on admission, he complained of dyspnoea and pain in the right inferior extremity
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: physical examination (showed a cold and mildly pale right leg with absent distal pulses; cardiopulmonary physical findings included a vigorous apical heart beat, the auscultation of a systolic murmur in mitral and tricuspid areas and basal pulmonary rales; neck veins were distended and the liver mildly enlarged; an exophthalmos was noted.); electrocardiogram (showed atrial fibrillation and diffuse t-wave abnromalities but no q waves); chest x-ray (revealed moderate cardiomegaly and signs of pulmonary oedema); echocardiogram (showed mild left ventricular enlargement (57 mm end-diastolic diameter) and a reduction in the left ventricular ejection fraction of 49%); femoral artery angiography (revealed an embolus at the level of hte right common femoral artery)
Diagnosis: hyperthyroidism leading to myocardial damage
Laboratory Values: elevated plasma free t4 concentrations and undetectable thyroid-stimulating hormone titres were found indicating the presence of hyperthyroidism. a monoclonal antimyosin study was performed, which indicated intense myocardial uptake of monoclonal antimyosin antibodies (heart-to-lung ratio: 1:89)
Pathology: NA
Pharmacological Therapy: appropriate treatment for heart failure was instituted. treatment for hyperthyroidism was strated with carbimazole (35 mg per day)
Patient Outcome Assessment: five months later, the thyroid was functioning normally after treatment with carbimazole (35 mg per day); a progressive decline in free t, concentration, paralleled by a decrease in antimyosin uptake, was noted; at 18 months, the antimyosin study was normal, and the echocardiogram disclosed a left ventricular chamber of normal size (51 mm end-diastolic diameter) and left ventricular ejection fraction (62%)

Title: cranial nerve-vi palsy as the main clinical manifestation of neurosarcoidosis.
Authors: Al-Qudah ZA;Yacoub HA;Souayah N
Institution: associated specialists inc., united hospital center, bridgeport, wv center for advanced health care, lehigh valley health network, allentown, pa ‡neurological institute of new jersey, rutgers, the state university of new jersey, newark, nj
Medical/Surgical History: had no history of seizures or head trauma
Signs and Symptoms: painless bulging of the left eye of 3 months duration but no feeling of pulsation; symptoms were associated with diplopia, which was worsened on left horizontal gaze; he denied any facial droop, weakness, paresthesia, or unsteady gait; the patient had a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure preceded by a feeling of lightheadedness but no nausea, sweating, or palpitations; on examination, he was found to have left cn-vi palsy; diplopia resolved when the right eye was covered; pupils were round and reactive to light and accommodation; no facial weakness was appreciated and facial sensation was intact; motor, sensory, coordination, and gait examination was unremarkable
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: lumbar puncture: cerebrospinal fluid (csf) analysis revealed clear fluid appearance with protein of 40 mg/dl, glucose of 64 mg/dl, and white blood cell count of 9 cells/µl (92% were lymphocytes and 8% monocytes); csf analysis revealed no malignant cells or oligoclonal bands with normal igg index and was negative for cryptoccocus neoformans antigens; an electroencephalogram was normal; brain magnetic resonance imaging (mri) with and without gadolinium revealed diffuse thickening and enhancement of the dura involving the left cavernous sinus, mild mass effect on the left temporal lobe, and soft tissue enhancement extending anteriorly through the foramen rotundum and left orbital apex; a computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with and without contrast was unremarkable for any granulomatous disease, lymphadenopathy, or malignancy; left cavernous sinus dural biopsy
Diagnosis: neurosarcoidosis; cranial nerve-vi pals
Laboratory Values: laboratory studies were significant only for mild leukopenia and erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 17 mm/h. concentration of angiotensin-converting enzyme was 49 u/l (normal, 12 to 68 u/l). renal, liver, and thyroid functions were within normal limits. antibodies for human immunodeficiency virus and lyme disease were negative. reactive reagent protein was negative. cerebrospinal fluid (csf) analysis revealed clear fluid appearance with protein of 40 mg/dl, glucose of 64 mg/dl, and white blood cell count of 9 cells/µl (92% were lymphocytes and 8% monocytes). csf analysis revealed no malignant cells or oligoclonal bands with normal igg index and was negative for cryptoccocus neoformans antigens
Pathology: a left cavernous sinus dural biopsy revealed extensive chronic inflammation containing non-necrotizing granulomas, consistent with neurosarcoidosis. there were no toxoplasma gondii, histoplasmosis, or cryptococcus organisms identified on giemsa or hematoxylin and eosin stains. there was no sequestration of lymphocytes in and near blood vessels to suggest vasculitis
Pharmacological Therapy: intravenous methylprednisolone, 1000 mg daily, for 5 days; discharged on oral prednisone, 60 mg daily, followed by a taper over a 2-month period
Patient Outcome Assessment: neurological evaluation 18 months after discharge revealed resolution of the cn-vi palsy; no recurrent seizures were reported

Title: clitoral priapism: a rare condition presenting as a cause of vulvar pain.
Authors: Medina CA
Institution: department of obstetrics and gynecology, division of gynecology, university of miami school of medicine, jackson memorial hospital, miami, florida, usa
Medical/Surgical History: para 1; 3 year history of recurrent vulvar and clitoral pain initiating in 1994 with a burning sensation lasting up to 3 minutes, followed by clitoral sweling and pain, and episodes progressed in duration from 3 to 8 hours although inconsistent, and recurred every 4 to 6 weeks; swollen and tender clitoris; hospitalization due to automobile accident and treated with nightly trazodone hydrochloride to treat ongoing depression; migraine headaches and anxiety disorders (treated with sumatriptan and lorazepam, respectively); asthma; seizure disorder due to drug reaction; not sexually active
Signs and Symptoms: clitoral priapism episodes; swollen and tender clitoris
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: physical examination (no vulvar or other pelvic abnormalities); wet smear and cervical and vaginal cultures (all normal)
Diagnosis: clitoral priapism due to trazodone medicatioin
Laboratory Values: NA
Pathology: dilatation, pathologic
Pharmacological Therapy: imipramine hydrochloride (25 mg, twice a day) to prevent episodes of priapism; discontinuation of trazodone (established as an etiologic factor for clitoral priapism); imipramine was discontinued 4 weeks later
Patient Outcome Assessment: there were no recurrences of clitoral priapism at 8 weeks after the discontinuation of trazodone; a telephone query approximately 42 months after the discontinuation of trazodone revealed the patient as having had only three episodes of priapism during this time, the last one nearly a year from the interview date

Title: newly diagnosed chronic granulomatous disease in a 53-year-old woman with crohn disease.

Institution: department of internal medicine, indiana university school of medicine, indianapolis, indiana 46202-5289, usa

Diagnosis: chronic granulomatous disease

Pathology: NA
Interventional Therapy: 14-day course of intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole at home
Patient Outcome Assessment: the patient continues to do well 12 months after hospital discharge

Title: lung transplantation in gaucher disease: a learning lesson in trying to avoid both scylla and charybdis.
Authors: de Boer GM;van Dussen L;van den Toorn LM;den Bakker MA;Hoek RA;Hesselink DA;Hollak CE;van Hal PT
Institution: departments of respiratory medicine and internal medicine, erasmus mc, university medical center, rotterdam, the netherlands; department of endocrinology and metabolism, academic medical center, amsterdam, the netherlands; and department of clinical pathology, maasstad hospital, rotterdam, the netherlands
Medical/Surgical History: gaucher's disease was diagnosed in the patient when was 5 years old; at 14 years of age, she underwent a splenectomy; at age 25, she experienced osteomyelitis, and 4 years later, she developed avascular necrosis of the left femoral head; during a pregnancy at the age of 32 years, nephrotic-range proteinuria developed (4-5 g/24 h).results of a renal biopsy found several sclerosed glomeruli, interstitial fibrosis, and tubular atrophy, as well as interstitial infiltration with cd68-positive gaucher cells; electron microscopic studies showed foamy gaucher cells containing inclusion bodies; ert with aglucerase, later followed by imiglucerase (cerezyme, genzyme corporation), became available for the treatment of gd in the early 1990s, and the patient started ert at age 34 years in 1994; she responded favorably to this therapy, with a reduction in liver volume and improvement in chitotriosidase levels, the most sensitive gaucher cell marker; pulmonary hypertension was diagnosed in the patient at age 37; at that time, there were no signs of interstitial lung disease; epoprostenol dose was reduced because of adverse effects, and bosentan treatment was initiated; the ph proved to be refractory to therapy, the patient was therefore referred for lung transplantation
Signs and Symptoms: the patient was referred for a lung transplantation screening; after the patient's lutx, the patient's renal function deteriorated further, necessitating kidney transplantation
Comorbidities: gaucher's disease was diagnosed in the patient when she was 5 years old; at 14 years of age; she underwent a splenectomy; at age 25; she experienced osteomyelitis; 4 years later; she developed avascular necrosis of the left femoral head
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: the patient was screened for lutx, with special attention paid to the extrapulmonary complications of gd1, including renal insufficiency, osteonecrosis, and an increased risk of infections secondary to splenectomy; right-sided heart catheterization revealed pulmonary arterial pressures of 92/41/60 mmhg; the decreased left ventricular function seemed to be secondary to the severe ph and was expected to improve after transplantation
Diagnosis: pulmonary hypertension secondary to gaucher's disease
Laboratory Values: her hematologic and visceral response to imiglucerase were satisfactory, although there was a high residual burden of gd, as evidenced by a stable, elevated chitotriosidase activity (6829 nmol/ml/h). despite the dose reduction of imiglucerase, no increase in chitotriosidase levels was observed, suggesting stabilized, low residual disease burden. in the pretransplantation period, the patient’s estimated glomerular filtration rate (gfr) slowly decreased to 21 ml/min/1.73 m2 with proteinuria levels in the nephrotic range on the day of transplantation. biochemical follow-up after transplantation revealed a sharp decrease in chitotriosidase activity (from 6,829 to 1,910 nmol/ml/h). posttransplantation, the patient's gfr initially improved to 54 ml/min/1.73 m2. this finding may be related to renal hypoperfusion resulting from severe ph before lutx and the improved cardiac output after lutx. this initial improvement was followed by a gradual decrease in gfr. after the kidney transplantation and reduction of tacrolimus dose, the patient's renal function stabilized. her estimated gfr is 42 ml/min/1.73 m2. there were no abnormalities on microscopic examination of her urine and limited proteinuria only (<0.5 g/d)
Pathology: in the explanted lungs, sparse gaucher cells were present as small aggregates in the interstitial connective tissue. a few gaucher cells were found in the alveolar air spaces, the alveolar septa, and subendothelial locations. no gaucher cells were identified within the capillary lumen. histologic stigmata of ph were seen, including plexogenic arteriopathy (plexiform and angiomatous lesions), intimal fibrosis, and medial hypertrophy with focal fibrinoid changes in the pulmonary arteries. because of a progressive decline in estimated gfr (from 75 to 45 ml/min/1.73 m2), a kidney transplantation biopsy was performed 18 months after kidney transplantation. the biopsy specimen showed no evidence of acute rejection, transplant glomerulopathy, recurrent iga nephropathy, diabetic nephropathy, tubulointerstitial nephritis, bk virus-associated nephropathy, or infiltration with gaucher cells
Pharmacological Therapy: upon referral for lung transplantation, she was treated with epoprostenol (1,000 u/24 h), bosentan (250 mg/d), and sildenafil (100 mg/d). in addition to imiglucerase (30 u/kg every 14 days), she used digoxin (0.25 mg/d), spironolactone (50 mg/d), furosemide (40 mg bid), acenocoumarol, and nitroglycerin (0.4 mg as needed). because of a worldwide shortage of imiglucerase, the patient's dosage was decreased by half. her immunosuppressive regimen consisted of tacrolimus (initial trough concentration between 12 and 15 ng/ml), mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisolone. prednisolone has been reported to reduce chitotriosidase activity. tacrolimus was replaced by sirolimus 13 months after transplantation due to gradual decrease of gfr. after kidney transplantation and a diagnosis of calcineurin inhibitor-associated nephrotoxicity was made, the patient's tacrolimus dose was reduced
Interventional Therapy: the patient was accepted for a bilateral lutx in 2004; her who status was 4 at the time of listing; in may 2009, she underwent a bilateral lutx; the patient was extubated on day 1, and 5 days later she was transferred to the pulmonary ward; in 2011, twenty-one months after lutx, a living unrelated donor kidney transplantation; this transplantation was complicated by several urinary tract infectiosn and bk polyomavirus infection; a kidney transplantation biopsy was performed 18 m onths after kidney transplantation
Patient Outcome Assessment: currently, 6 years after the lutx, the patient is doing well, with a vital capacity and fev1 of 2.17 l (72%) and 1.54 l (62%) respectively, compared with her pretransplantation values of 1.98 l (64%) and 0.87 l (33%) and values 13 months’ posttransplantation of 2.12 l (68%) and 1.71 l (66%)

Title: left ventricular systolic dysfunction in a cardiac transplant recipient treated with carvedilol.
Authors: Gardner RS;McGowan J;McDonagh TA
Institution: the scottish cardiopulmonary transplant unit, royal infirmary, glasgow, uk
Keywords: cardiac transplantation;heart failure;left ventricular systolic dysfunction;beta-blocker
Medical/Surgical History: he underwent orthotopic cardiac transplantation in 1995 for valvular heart disease; the heart was from a donor that was 39 years old; he did not have a history of rejection
Signs and Symptoms: five and a half years post-transplantation, he became progressively more breathless on exertion (nyha class iii) and required admission to his local hospital with acute heart failure

Laboratory Values: viral titres were negative, including cmv (igm, specific mrna, and direct detection), ebv, hsv and varicella zoster

Patient Outcome Assessment: he improved symptomatically (nyha class iii to ii)and a repeat rnvg at 8 months showed that his lvefhad dramatically increased to 30%; in response to the change in his anti-failure medication, he had an asymp-tomatic decrease in his heart rate to 48 per min and fallin his blood pressure to 104y68

Title: delayed postpartum hemorrhage--a rare clinical presentation of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura-hemolytic uremic syndrome: a case report.
Authors: Chen YC;Chen HS;Shen CJ;Chang HM;Tsai EM
Journal: the kaohsiung journal of medical sciences
Institution: department of obstetrics and gynecology, kaohsiung medical university chung-ho memorial hospital, kaohsiung; medical university, kaohsiung, taiwan department of obstetrics and gynecology, college of medicine, kaohsiung medical university, kaohsiung, taiwan
Keywords: delayed postpartum hemorrhage;thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura;hemolytic uremic syndrome
Medical/Surgical History: gravida 2, para 1; uncomplicated cesearean section at 38 weeks' gestation at a local clinic under the indication of a previous cesarean section; prenatal and medical histories were unremarkable
Signs and Symptoms: ten days after surgery, the first episode of delayed postpartum hemorrhage occurred; the second and third episodes of postpartum hemorrhage were on the 26th and 37th days postpartum; the fourth episode of postpartum hemorrhage happened on the 42nd day postpartum; no fever, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, or right upper quadrant or epigastric pain were reported; at our hospital, icteric sclera was the first noted sign; vital signs included a temperature of 37.5 'c, pulse of 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 20/minute, and blood pressure of 130/78 mmhg; a few hours after admission, she developed a fever of more than 38 $c with rapidly progressive jaundice; oligouria and a small amount of tea-colored urine were also noted

Title: primary carnitine deficiency dilated cardiomyopathy: 28 years follow-up.

Family History: no family history of heart anomalies
Medical/Surgical History: a 3-and-a-half-year-old girl was admitted to our hospital in february 1984 due to severe congestive heart failure; delivery, birth weight and perinatal period were normal; there was no family history of heart anomalies; on initial examination on admission in our pediatric cardiology unit, the patient presented with generalized hypotonia (normal deep tendon reflexes), fatigue and marked pallor; chest x-ray revealed significant cardiomegaly along with signs of pulmonary vascular congestion; the echocardiogram showed enlargement of the left atrium and ventricle and a dilated mitral valve ring, very thin left ventricular walls (fig; 1a) and extremely low left ventricle ejection fraction , with abnormal septal and posterior wall motion (fig; 1b); laboratory test showed very low level of plasma carnitine (17.2 ?mol/l); a muscle biopsy was obtained in order to assess carnitine levels and complete the diagnostic course; test results showed lipid storage and low carnitine levels, confirming the suspicion of dilated cardiomyopathy due to carnitine deficit (fig; 1c); the patient underwent treatment with l-carnitine supplements, initially at 3 g/day, and after 6 months at 2 g/day, showing rapid signs of improvement with a progressive increase in muscular strength and cardiac function; during the 28-year follow-up our patient maintained a normal heart size on chest x-ray, and normal ecg and echocardiographic parameters (fig; 2), except in one occasion, at the age of 12 years, when the patient decided to suspend treatmentwith l-carnitine because of its side effects (fishy body odor); this suspension of therapy resulted in signs and symptoms of recurrence (muscular weakness, fatigue, cardiac enlargement, low cardiac function); upon re-introduction of the treatment an improvement was soon noticed; at present, our patient is 31 years old, leads a normal life, works as a teacher and performs regular physical activity in fitness room; long-chain fatty acids are an important energy substrate for the myocardium and other muscle tissue; primary carnitine deficiency syndrome (pcds) is due to a defect in the high affinity carnitine transporter octn2; the gene responsible for this defect, slc22a5, has been cloned [2,3]; pcds can present as metabolic encephalopathy, hypoglycemia, lipid storage myopathy or cardiomyopathy; dilated cardiomyopathy is frequently encountered in patients with pcds; continued therapy with l-carnitine supplements leads to dramatic resolution of severe congestive heart failure within a short period, altering the natural history of the disease, and reducing or eliminating the signs of cardiomyopathy, as described in the literature [1,4–6] and demonstrated in our case; furthermore, our case shows that suspension of treatment leads to the recurrence of signs and symptoms; very few cases of dcm due to primary systemic carnitine deficiency with long-term follow-up have been reported in the literature, and to our knowledge, no case has undergone 28 years of treatment and observation; kishimoto et al; [5] refer to a follow-up of 30 years, but in a case with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; in patients with cardiomyopathy due to primary systemic carnitine deficiency, supplementation therapy permits the resolution of cardiac dysfunction, allowing the patient to lead a normal life; our experience demonstrates that therapy should never be suspended

Title: sideroblastic anaemia and primary adrenal insufficiency due to a mitochondrial respiratory chain disorder in the absence of mtdna deletion.
Authors: O'Grady MJ;Monavari AA;Cotter M;Murphy NP
Institution: department of paediatrics, midland regional hospital, mullingar, ireland.\
Medical/Surgical History: was born at term weighing 4 kg to non-consanguineous parents and attained normal early developmental milestones; height and weight were on the 10th and 50th centiles, respectively; preliminary examination was remarkable only for hepatomegaly extending 3.5 cm below the right costal margin

Life Style: although his developmental milestones were nor­mal, he had been below average in his primary school records. at the age of 13, he began having attacks of vomiting after hard exercise. from the age of 16, he vomited more frequently, lost much of his appetite, and had cramps and swelling in his calves while walking
Family History: family and past histories were noncontributory

physical examination revealed no abnormalities in the chest or abdomen; from the neurological examination, was determined to be mentally normal except for a moderately decreased intelligence; his verbal iq score was 61; performance iq score was below 60, and estimated full-scale iq score was 51, according to the wechsler adult intelligence scale; the cranial nerves were all normal including ocular movements, auditory sense and eye grounds; there were slight weakness (4/5) and atrophy of the musculature in his hands and feet; his deep tendon reflexes were moderately low and no pathological reflexes were elicited; there were no cerebellar disturbances, ataxia, sensory disturbances or involuntary muscular contractions; the ck activity in the blood was markedly high (1,270 iu/1); his creatine level was increased in the urine (198.9 mg/day) but not in the blood; myoglobin was occasionally found in the blood and urine; the blood content of lactate was 20.1 mg/dl (normal range 4-16) and pyruvate was 1.17 mg/dl (normal range 0.3-0.9); the thyroid function, glucose tolerance test and arterial blood gas analysis were within normal limits; cerebrospinal fluid (csf) examination revealed increased lactate (35.9 mg/dl; normal range 11-27) and pyruvate (1.17 mg/dl; normal range < 1.02), but the cell count, pro­tein, sugar and electrolytes were within normal limits; a forearm ischemic exercise test showed normal elevation of lactate and pyruvate levels; an aerobic exercise test using an ergometer at 15 w for 15 min produced marked increases in the lactate and pyruvate lev­els, causing metabolic acidosis (fig; 1); these findings indicated the presence of a mitochondrial disorder; a brain computed-tomographic scan revealed diffuse cerebral atrophy with no abnormal density areas; an electroencephalogram showed alpha rhythm pre­ dominantly in the bilateral occipital areas with occasional 7-hz theta waves, which appeared more frequently during hyperventilation, in the bilateral frontal and central areas; his electrocardiogram was normal; electromyography (emg) and electronurography were performed using conventional methods with a dantec emg 1500 sys­ tem; the motor nerve conduction velocities, f wave conduction velocities, sensory nerve conduction velocities (scv) in the arms and legs were all within normal limits except for slightly low scv of the sural nerve (40.2 m/s), but the action potential was of normal amplitude (4 pv) and shape; a concentric-needle emg showed that high-amplitude motor unit action potentials (muaps) of 6-10 mv appeared frequently in the bilateral thenar, forearm, anterior tibial and femoral quadriceps muscles, although their duration and phase were within the normal range of 6-10 and 3-4 ms, respectively, using a delay line method; the interference pattern consisted of high-amplitude muaps and normal-shaped muaps were markedly reduced at the maximal force of the muscles (fig; 2); in these muscles, however, normal muaps with a full interference pattern were also recorded in some parts; short-duration waves were dominant in the deltoid muscles; there were no spontaneous activities in these muscles; a muscle biopsy from the right anterior tibial muscle revealed ragged-red fibers with modified gomori's trichrome stain, fiber type grouping and type i fiber predominance with atpase stain (fig; 3); there was a scattering of a few small angulated fibers, but no grouped atrophy was observed; an electron-microscopic study revealed subsarcolemmal aggregation of enlarged and deformed mito­chondria associated with many glycogen granules; mitochondria containing paracrystalline inclusions were occasionally seen among the myofibrils (fig; 4); an enzymatic study of isolated mitochondria from the biopsied muscle was performed by the method described elsewhere [10], which revealed low cco activity (table 1); subunit analysis of the complexes in the oxidative phosphorylation system using an immunochemical method [ii] demonstrated that, in the complex iv, the amounts of the subunits 2, 6 and 7 were markedly low but those of the subunits of complex i, iii and v were not low as compared with the control (fig; 5); a sural nerve biopsy was not performed because of no apparent neuropathic findings; coenzyme qio (coq) medication (300mg/day orally) was started on october 3, 1986, with the patient's and his parents' informed consent; after discharge, however, he stopped taking the medication following his mother's judgement in july 1987; after that time, he began to vomit frequently, and his limb muscles under­ went progressive wasting; when coq was restarted on the second admission of september 16, 1987, the elevated lactate, pyruvate and ck levels in the blood gradually decreased almost to their normal ranges and he began to recover from the symptoms including the muscle atrophy; coq (150 mg/day) therapy also moderately reduced the amounts of lactate and pyruvate in the csf and their increases during the aerobic exercise test were almost half those of the premedicated values (fig; 6); he has still been doing well on this medica­tion at the outpatient clinic

Title: proliferative myositis in a child.
Authors: Mulier S;Stas M;Delabie J;Lateur L;Gysen M;Dal Cin P;Robberecht C;De Wever I
Institution: department of surgical oncology, university hospital gasthuisberg, herestraat 49, b-3000 leuven, belgium; department of pathology, university hospital gasthuisberg, leuven, belgium; department of radiology, university hospital gasthuisberg, leuven, belgium; department of nuclear medicine, university hospital gasthuisberg, leuven, belgium; center for human genetics, university hospital gasthuisberg, leuven, belgium

Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: physical examination (extreme antalgic scoliosis; the left dorsolumbar paraspinal region was very tender on palpation and moderately swollen; there was no skin discoloration nor local warmth; no other abnormalities were noted on physical examination); radiograph of the lumbar vertebral column (showed a confined area of homogenous calcification on the left side of l3); ultrasound (showed an inhomogenous mass with calcifications); ct scan (revealed a heterogenous hypodense mass with contrast enhancement); t1 weighted mr images (a markedly contrast-enhanced nodular lesion of 4 cm in the left sacrospinalis muscle was found, surrounded by a moderately contrast-enhanced in homogenous infiltration of the quadratus lumborum muscle as well as of the left psoas muscle); methylene diphosphonate bone scan (a focal area of intense radiotracer accumulation was seen adjacent to the left part of the third lumbar vetebra; a second focal area of radiotracer accumulation was seen on the dorsal part of the seventh rib and was attributed to an old fracture.); whole-body fluorine-18 deoxyglucose pet scan (showed an intense hot spot lateral to the lumbar spine); biopsy
Diagnosis: proliferative myositis in the lumbar paraspinal muscles
Laboratory Values: the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (esr) was 31 mm in 1 h, and c-reactive protein as well as leukocyte count were normal. tumor markers carcino embryonal antigen (cea), alpha-fetoprotein (?fp), beta human chorionic gonadotropin (?hcg) and neuron-specific enolase (nse) were normal
Pathology: an incisional biopsy (2 cm3) of the nodular lesion at the edge of the dorsolumbar spine was performed 3 weeks after the onset of the pain. macroscopically, the lesion was gray and friable, with no distinct edge to the surrounding pale and edematous muscle fibers. histological examination revealed a proliferation composed of two cell populations: a minor population of small spindle cells with an elongated nucleus and a major population of ganglion-like giant cells with a large nucleus, a prominent nucleolus, and a fair amount of basophilic cytoplasm. no obvious cellular pleomorphism was present. mitoses were frequent but not atypical. a typical checker-board pattern was formed by the proliferation of cells with marked edema between the perimysial septa. focal necrosis of muscle fibers at the periphery of the lesion was seen. few lymphocytes were seen in the lesion. polymorphonuclear cells were notably absent. there was no evidence of cartilage or osteoid formation. immunohistochemical analysis revealed vimentin and alpha smooth muscle actin by the ganglion-like cells. these cells did not express desmin or myosin. because of the typical morphological and immunophenotypic findings, the diagnosis of proliferative myositis (pm) was made. cytogenetic analysis, after short-term culture of part of the specimen, revealed a normal chromosomal pattern46, xy
Interventional Therapy: physical therapy and exercise were discouraged
Patient Outcome Assessment: seven weeks after the onset of the pain, the patient was seen in the outpatient clinic; pain control was good, the antalgic scoliosis had almost disappeared, and the local swelling had decreased, although there was still some induration under the scar; three months after the onset of the pain, the swelling was gone and pain was only occasionally felt on physical exercise; a new pet scan showed that the paraspinal area of activity had disappeared

Title: chondroid chordoma of the l5 spinous process and lamina: a case report.

Institution: department of orthopedics, ucms and gtb hospital, new delhi, india
Keywords: chordoma;physaliphorous cells;lumbar spine;bone tumors;vertebrae spinous process
Medical/Surgical History: he presented with a history of intermittent, dull, poorly localized back pain for 1 year; the patient had received symptomatic treatment elsewhere with no relief
Signs and Symptoms: a history of intermittent, dull, poorly localized back pain for 1 year; there was no history of weakness, numbness or incontinence; there was no history of any constitutional symptoms such as fever, cough, haemoptysis, anorexia, weight loss, malena etc
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: physical examination (the spinous process of l5 was prominent but no localized spinal tenderness was elicited); neurological examination (confirmed no deficit); readiological evaluation (revealed an expansile osteolytic lesion of l5 spinous process and lamina); computed tomogram of the affected vertebrae (confirmed the finding of the osteolytic lesion with he confines of tumor limited to the posterior elements of l5 and no obvious pathological fracture)
Diagnosis: chondroid chordoma of the l5 spinous process and lamina
Laboratory Values: routine laboratory tests including hematological, blood biochemical and urine analysis were all normal
Pathology: ct-guided fine needle aspiration cytology was attempted but was inconclusive. postoperative histology sections revealed the lesion to be a chordoma with cartilage cells. surgical margins after resection were reported free of tumor. histologically, the tumor showed lobules separated by fibrous bands. cells were arranged in syncytial nests and cords lying in pink mucinous stroma. typical physaliphorous cells were seen. nuclear pleomorphism was minimal. few multinucleated tumor cells were present. no areas of soft tissue infiltration were seen. in areas of cartilaginous differentiation, the tumor cells were located in lacunae separated from each other by abundant hyaline substance. these chondroid areas merged imperceptibly with the typical chordoid areas. he tumor tested positive with s-100 staining. however, staining for ck and ema was focal and mild
Interventional Therapy: the patient was taken up for enbloc excision to prevent contamination by spillage; the posterior elements involved with the tumor were removed enbloc, and the excised specimen sent for histopathology; since facets joints were left intact, no fusion or instrumentation was performed
Patient Outcome Assessment: when last seen at 21 months postoperatively, the patient was painfree and there were no clinical or radiological signs suggestive of recurrence or instability

echocardiography (a left ventricular ejection fraction (lvef) of 25% and moderate pericardial effusion were observed); after receiving support therapy, the patient's cardiac function improved to an lvef of 59%, and he was discharged on the 16th hospital day; 2009: echocardiography (showed an lvef of 58% and lv end-diastolic dimension of 46 mm); january 2013: chest x-ray (revealed mild cardiomegaly with a cardiothoracic ratio of 53% and further enlargement); electrocardiography (showed low-voltage in the limb leads and st-segment elevation in the precordial leads which had not been observed on the electrocardiogram obtained six months before admission); echocardiography (showed dilatation of the lv with an end-diastolic dimension of 52 mm and diffuse lv dysfunction with an lvef of 28%; echocardiogram 2 weeks after discharge (the postsystolic ventricular shortening improved)
Diagnosis: repetitive fulminant influenza myocarditis
Laboratory Values: february 1997: there was a significant elevation in the serum titer of influenza b virus from ×32 to ×256. march 2001: laboratory studies showed a white blood cell (wbc) count of 8,390/?l, a hemoglobin level of 16.7 g/dl, a platelet count of 11.6×104/?l and a c-reactive protein (crp) level of 0.5 mg/dl. a cardiac troponin test was positive. the level of serum ck was within the normal limits at the time of admission (226 u/l); however, it rose to 1,103 u/l on the fourth hospital day. january 2013: laboratory studies showed a wbc count of 1,020/?l, a hemoglobin level of 15.7 g/dl, a platelet count of 14.8×104/?l, a c-reactive protein concentration of 5.76 mg/dl and a crp level of 0.12 mg/dl. the total and mb fractions of ck were 753 u/l and 76 u/l, respectively, and the level of cardiac troponin was 0.815 ng/ml (normal range, 0.014 ng/ml), indicating the presence of myocardial damage. the serum level of brain natriuretic peptide (bnp) was elevated to 1,485 pg/ml. a cardiac troponin test was positive. on admission, the following titers of antibodies against suspected viruses were measured: influenza a (h1n1), ×20; influenza a (h3n2), ×80; parainfluenza 2, ×10; and parainfluenza 3, ×320. the titers of antibodies against the following species were negative: influenza b, adenovirus, echovirus 3, echovirus 11, coxsackie virus a9, coxsackie virus b3 and parainfluenza 1. the serum titer of influenza a virus (h3n2) was significantly elevated from ×80 to ×1,280, consistent with a diagnosis of fulminant myocarditis associated with influenza a virus infection. the viral titers against influenza a (h1n1), influenza b, echoviruses, coxsackie viruses and parainfluenza viruses were not significantly elevated (data not shown). the bnp level remained within the normal range (49.2 pg/ml)
Pathology: NA
Pharmacological Therapy: january 2013: the patient was diagnosed with influenza a infection at a nearby clinic and started on oral oseltamivir. to support cardiac function, a neuraminidase inhibitor, peramivir hydrate, was administered intravenously. neither corticosteroids nor immunosuppressants were administered
Interventional Therapy: february 1997: he underwent tracheal intubation, insertion of percutaneous cardiopulmonary support (pcps) and intra-aortic balloon pumping (iabp) devices with catecholamine infusion; weaning from the pcps and iabp was performed seven and nine days, respectively, after the insertion of these mechanical support devices; january 2013: his blood pressure had decreased and his hemodynamic condition was decompensating; as a result, the insertion of an iabp and infusion of catecholamines were ultimately required to maintain the patient’s peripheral circulation

figure 2. the longest portion was 17.5 cm long after fixation in 10% formalin. there was an attached cuff of stomach, measuring 2.0 cm in width. no external or mucosal lesion was seen except for a minute focus of mucosal erosion adjacent to the proximal line of the first resected portion of the esophagus. no luminal construction, thickening or induration of the esophageal wall were seen. the examination: after fixation the esophagus was divided into 61 blocks for subserial microscopic examination. the distribution of the carcinoma in situ, severe dysplasia, slight to moderate dysplasia (fig. 5, 7) and esophageal gland involvement by carcinoma in situ or severe dysplasia is shown in figure 2. dysplasia was categorized as mild, moderate or severe depending on the degree of cellular alteration between normal and carcinoma in situ. almost all the mucosal surface of the resected specimen was involved by dysplasia or squamous cell carcinoma in situ, leaving only small islands of normal mucosa. the abnormal squamous epithelium appeared to be generally thinner than normal. measurements of the thickness of the normal epithelium with a micrometer eyepiece in the microscope gave a range from 150 to 230,. the areas of carcinoma in situ varied from 37 to 156 p, severe dysplasia from 62 to 144 p and the mild dysplasia from 97 to 156 p. many esophageal glands and their ducts were involved by degrees of dysplasia and by carcinoma in situ (fig. 2, 6) most frequently noted in the middle third and often associated with carcinoma in situ and moderate to severe dysplasia. carcinoma in situ was more common in the upper one half than in the lower one half and was always accompanied by dysplasia. a severe chronic inflammatory reaction composed of lymphocytes, plasma cells and a few histiocytes was universally present in the submucosa. occasional ganglia of the myenteric plexus were involved by inflammatory cells (fig. 8). although the constant constriction of the upper esophagus was present on the radiological examination, there was no anatomical evidence of constriction. the constriction may have been a functional abnormality secondary to diffuse submucosal chronic Title: a novel mutation in the sco2 gene in a neonate with early-onset cardioencephalomyopathy.

Institution: tallinn children's hospital, tallinn, estonia

family history was complicated; both parents had mild mental retardation; they had met in a school for disabled children; the mother studied first in a standard school, but since the fourth grade she had not been able to pass; it can be hypothesized, therefore, that the sco2 gene may be involved in the etiology of mother’s mental retardation; the fact that the patient’s fibroblasts had relatively higher enzyme activity than muscle tissue suggests that there could be differences in different tissues of his mother, as well; nonetheless, the enzymatic activity in fibroblasts in this family is consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance, and the results do not confirm biochemical evidence between genotype and the mild phenotype of the parents; there is no information in the literature on clinical problems of heterozygotic carriers.
Medical/Surgical History: a boy was born after uneventful pregnancy at 38 weeks gestation; because of fetal cardiac problems and failure to progress, the child was delivered by cesarean section; birth weight was 3040 g ( 1 s.d.), length 47 cm ( 1.3 s.d.).
