Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: heart ultrasound evaluation indicated hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; cranial magnetic resonance imaging investigation revealed bilateral hyperintensity in the putamen region with t2 signals, consistent with leigh syndrome (fig 1); electromyographic investigation revealed fibrillations in muscles of upper and lower limbs; no response was registered on evaluation of motor and sensory nerves
Diagnosis: cytochrome c oxidase deficiency
Laboratory Values: lactate in serum and cerebrospinal fluid was elevated up to 4.2 mmol/l and 3.8 mmol/l, respectively (reference <2.9 mmol/l). serum amino acid profile (including alanine) was normal. urinary organic acid analysis (gas chromatography-mass spectrometry) revealed elevated excretion of mitochondrial metabolites: pyruvate, malate, 2-hydroxyglutaric acid, ketoglutaric acid, and citric acid. these metabolites were not quantified, but their excretion is normally very low
Pathology: the parents refused autopsy; routine histologic examination of muscle biopsies of this patient revealed variation in muscle fibers (fig 2a). muscle enzyme histochemistry indicated normal checkerboard staining for reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (nadh), but there was no detectable cytochrome c oxidase activity at all (fig 2b). ragged red fibers were not found. electron-microscopic evaluation revealed enlarged and irregularly shaped mitochondria with electron-dense matrix, as well as hypertrophic mitochondria with pale matrix and granular deposits (figs 2c and 2d). respiratory chain enzyme activities were measured in muscle and in fibroblasts of the patient (table 1). the studies indicated severely reduced cytochrome c oxidase activity and mildly reduced activity for complex i in the muscle and reduced cytochrome c oxidase activity in fibroblasts of this patient. because both parents had mild mental retardation, respiratory chain enzyme activity measurements were performed in them as well, and normal results were observed (table 1); during molecular genetic studies, four genes (surf1, sco1, sco2, and cox10) associated with cytochrome c oxidase deficiency were sequenced in the patient. a hetero- zygous mutation c.418g > a (leading to a p.e140k) in exon 2 and heterozygous insertion of 19 the present at po- sition 17 (c.17ins19bp, leading to a truncated protein) was detected in the coding region of the sco2 gene by se- quence analysis. the father was found to be a heterozygous carrier of the c.418g > a mutation and the mother was a het- erozygous carrier of the c.17ins19bp mutation in this gene. no mutation was found in coding regions of the other inves- tigated genes by sequence analysis. no mutations were dis- covered in the mitochondrial genome using sequence analysis of the whole mitochondrial dna
Pharmacological Therapy: treatment to support mitochondrial energy production (ubiquinone 5 mg/kg/day; thiamine 150 mg/day; l-carnitine 50 mg/kg/day) was initiated at the age of 6 weeks. despite treatment, the child’s condition worsened rapidly: stridorous breathing was observed from the age of 8 weeks, and the muscular hypotonia and feeding difficulties worsened. the patient died at the age of 13 weeks because of respiratory insufficiency

Title: desmoplastic melanoma of the lower lip: a case report.
Authors: Godoy GP;de Castro Gomes DQ;Pereira JV;de Queiroz Figueiredo RL;Nonaka CF;da Costa Miguel MC
Journal: oral surgery oral medicine oral pathology oral radiology and endodontology
Institution: oral pathology, state university of paraíba, campina grande, pb, brazil
Social History: the patient reported frequent sun exposure because of his work on a farm
Medical/Surgical History: his medical history was not contributory
Signs and Symptoms: presented for evaluation of a painful swelling in the lower lip, which had been identified 7 months earlier; physical examination showed a poorly demarcated, indurated swelling in the lower lip, measuring approximately 3 cm in diameter; the surface of the lesion presented ulceration extending from the labial mucosa to the vermilion border, scattered crusts, and white patches
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: incisional biopsy
Diagnosis: desmoplastic melanoma (dm)
Laboratory Values: NA
Pathology: histological examination showed proliferation of round to spindle-shaped cells, which were arranged in nests along the epithelial-connective tissue junction and in the lamina propria, and in parallel bundles in the submucosa. the tumor cells exhibited pleomorphism, intense hyperchromatism, an altered nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio, and typical and atypical mitoses. occasional multinucleated cells with hyperchromatic nuclei were identified in areas of the specimen. the cells were embedded in a predominantly desmoplastic stroma presenting myxoid foci, and exhibited marked neurotropism, accompanied by extensive perineural and endoneural infiltration. many scattered lymphoid aggregates and areas of solar elastosis were also observed. the tumor cells were negative for cytokeratin 14, and positive for s-100 protein and hmb-45, suggesting a melanocytic origin despite the absence of pigmentation; histopathological analysis revealed a metastatic tumor in the right cervical lymph node
Interventional Therapy: wide surgical excision of the tumor and dissection of cervical lymph nodes were performed; the patient received adjuvant radiotherapy (25 gy in 25 fractions) in the neck region
Patient Outcome Assessment: continues to be under careful follow-up

Pathology: the histologic appearance of the tumor from the 1977 and 1978 specimens revealed a chordoma characterized by compact masses and elongated cords of clear cells with a regular cytologic appearance. the cells contained large characteristic intracytoplasmic vacuoles. these were separated by fibrous bands of connective tissue proffering a lobular pattern to the tissue. in march 1979, the tumor once again consisted of chordoma. special stains revealed abundant intracellular glycogen, an extracellular pas-negative, alcian blue-positive mucin, and a fine reticulin network surrounding individual cells. the fibrous connective tissue component, however, had become more cellular and taken on a more spindle shaped appearance with a subtle tendency to whorl. occasional cells contained glycogen. a dense reticulin network was present in these areas. the specimen from 1983 revealed a striking intermingling of chordoma elements merging imperceptibly with spindle-shaped elements most pronounced in the reticulin stain. both components retained similar staining characteristics to earlier biopsy specimens. several spindlecelled areas were noted to have numerous mitoses the tumor from the january 1984 biopsy specimen was composed of a triad of chordoma, intense spindle cell proliferation without mitoses, as well as frank malignant fibrous histiocytoma (mfh). the latter's plump and densely cellular component was arranged in a storiform pattern with whorls. keratin stains demonstrated strong positivity in the chordoma cells. to our surprise, several adjacent spindle-shaped cells showed keratin positivity. the majority of spindle cells do not exhibit this phenomenon, and these unique cells were interpreted as transitional cells between the chordomatous cell line and that of the malignant fibrous histiocytoma. in addition, a large group of keratin-negative spindle cells contained abundant intracellular glycogen. in july 1984, no evidence could be found for chordoma. the specimen consisted entirely of mfh as described above. no keratin- or glycogen-positive cells were present in this tumor

proximal segment of the left anterior descending artery. obstructive platelet thrombi also were observed in the diagonal, septal perforating, and small intramural branches of the left anterior descending artery. in some instances, acute thrombotic lesions occurred on the older intimal proliferative lesions (fig 3). neither the intimal proliferative lesions nor the platelet thrombotic lesions were observed in other organs, and there was no evidence of active or healed arteritis. chronic myocardial lesions included micro focal areas of fibrosis or granulation tissue (fig 4). because carcinoma/mantle cell lymphoma, respectively. the previous bipsy specimens of conjunctival nodules and cervical lymph nodes were reviewed and showed similar features of mantle cell lymphoma. after surgery, histological examination of the resected specimen confirmed the presence of squamous cell carcinoma and residual mantle cell lymphoma. the initial, fresh oesophageal endoscopic biopsy specimen was submitted for examination. half of the specimen was frozen for subsequent immunohistochemical studies and the other half was promptly fixed in 10% neutral formalin and embedded in paraffin wax. sections, 3 gim thick, were cut and stained with haematoxylin and eosin, gordon and sweets' silver, periodic acid schiff, and methyl green pyronin stains. immunohistochemistry was carried out on the frozen tissue using the streptavidin-biotin complex technique for cd5 (dako, glostrup, denmark), cd23 (dako), immunoglobulins (igd from dako, igg from biotest diagnostic, and igm from biotest diagnostic), k and x light chains (becton dickinson), and a panel of b (cd 19 from becton dickinson and cd22 from dako) and t cell markers (cd3 from becton dickinson). the oesophagectomy specimen was also processed similarly after representative blocks were sampled from the fresh tissue. macroscopically, the oesophageal tumour was an ulcerative growth, situated 6.5 cm proximal to the gastro-oesophageal junction, measuring 9 cm at its widest point. histological examination of the endoscopic biopsy revealed several tiny fragments of oesophageal mucosa with severe dysplasia of the surface squamous epithelium with focal suggestion of stromal invasion. in one of the tissue fragments, several clusters of lymphoid aggregates, composed mainly of a monotonous population of small lymphoid cells, were present. the cells had irregular nuclear membrane and scanty cytoplasm. the cytological features were similar to those of the previous conjunctival and cervical lymph node biopsy specimens. immunohistochemical studies showed that these lymphoid cells were positive for cd5, cd19 and cd22, but negative for cd3 and cd23. surface igd and igm, as well as k light chain restriction, oesophagectomy specimen. the excised specimen showed a moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus with transmural infiltration. keratin pearl formation was frequently found. Pharmacological Therapy: investigational treatment with glucocerebrocidase was chosen as the option wtih lower risk. hematologic improvement obviating the need for splenectomy was selected as the therapeutic endpoint. human placental glucocerebrosidase was isolated, and the oligosaccharide units were sequentially deglycosylated to yield a mannose-terminated preparation as described. the final preparation was formulated in 4% human serum albumin/155 mm sodium chloride/20 mm sodium dihydrogen phosphate adjusted to ph 5.0 with 0.3 m citric acid. each preparation was rigorously tested for and found to be free of pyrogens and bacterial contamination. mannose-terminated glucocerebrosidase was administered on a weekly basis by i.v. infusion at a dosage of 10,000,000 units (167 international units). for each infusion, the enzyme solution was injected over -5 min in a total volume of 5-10 ml. one unit of enzymatic activity hydrolyzes 1 nmol of glucocerebroside per hr. expressed in international units, this amount corresponds to 1.67 x 10-5 ,mol per min. enzyme infusions were begun at age 4 yr and 1 mo. fourteen infusions were administered during the first 26 weeks of the treatment protocol due to limited availability of modified enzyme. thereafter, infusions were administered without interruption until week 105 (age 4 yr and 7 mo to 6 yr and 1 mo). subsequently, inusions were withheld until week 130 (age 6 yr and 1 mo to 6 yr and 7 mo) to determine whether the observed responses reverted to the baseline state. the complete blood count was monitored weekly during the period of active treatment and every 2 weeks afterwards. routine serum chemistry values, acid phosphatase and prothrombin levels, and partial thromboplastin time were monitored every 3-6 mo, and liver/spleen scans and plain films of the long bones were monitored every 6-12 mo during the study period

thereafter, epistaxis ceased and the enzyme infusions were given without interruption between weeks 26 and 105; a gradual and progressive increase in hemoglobin from severely depressed to near normal values was seen; the response became clearly evident between weeks 26 and 45; upon withdrawal of the enzyme infusions between weeks 105 and 130, hemoglobin declined from a plateau of 10.2 ± 0.4 g/dl (±1 sd) to pretreatment values of 6.9 ± 0.8 g/dl (± 1 sd); this reduction occurred in the absence of blood loss; a rise in platelet count from a pretreatment value of 30,000 + 7.000/mm3 (±1 sd) to 54,000 ± 11,000/mm3 (±1 sd) was also seen during enzyme supplementation; although less striking than the hemoglobin response, this change is significant at the 99% level of confidence; in concert with the hematological response, the patient appeared much more vigorous; the abdomen was less protuberant, and splenic size appeared to decrease on physical examination after several months of enzyme supplementation; the phagocytic activity of spleen decreased significantly during enzyme supplementation, as demonstrated by comparing the relative uptake oftechnetium sulfur colloid by liver and spleen; the pattern of colloid uptake reverted to the pretreatment state upon cessation of the enzyme infusions; subtle evidence of improvement in the skeleton was also seen but was slower to develop; plain films of the long bones revealed increased mineralization, decreased endosteal scalloping, and a finer trabecular pattern after 18 mo of enzyme supplementation; the enzyme infusions were well tolerated throughout the entire treatment protocol; no untoward reactions of any type were seen; no significant changes were observed in routine serum chemistry values or serum acid phosphatase activity during the study

Institution: department of biotechnological and applied clinical sciences, university of l’aquila, italy
Medical/Surgical History: NA
Signs and Symptoms: progressive photophobia and diplopia; sudden-onset headaches, vomiting, dizziness and tinnitus; a neurological examination revealed binocular multidirectional diplopia, convergence-retraction nystagmus and mild photophobia; an eye examination showed normal focus range, fundus and hess–lancaster test
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: a computed tomography (ct) scan of the brain showed a well-circumscribed pineal region expansive process measuring 25 mm; it was well delineated, with spontaneous high density, and there was patchy calcification in the central part of the tumour, as well as mild hydrocephalus; electroencephalography (eeg) demonstrated mild abnormalities more prominent in the left posterior sites; brainstem auditory evoked potentials (baep) evidenced impaired hearing on the left side; motor evoked potentials were normal; routine blood investigations were within normal limits; magnetic resonance imaging (mri) was performed using t1- and t2-weighted standard spin echo sequences, fluid attenuating inversion recovery and diffusion-weighted images/apparent diffusion coefficient sequences; post-contrast t1- weighted images were also obtained on the axial, sagittal and coronal planes; mri examination revealed a lesion in the pineal region which compressed the tectal plate and cerebral aqueduct; the mass appeared heterogeneously hypointense on the t1-weighted images; on t2-weighted images, the mass was heterogeneously iso- to hyperintense to the cortex (figure 1(b)); a homogeneously enhanced mass was observed after administration of contrast medium (figure 1(c)); on diffusion-weighted imaging, the mass was markedly hyperintense with hypointense signal on corresponding apparent diffusion coefficient maps; proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy of the lesion identified a relatively increased n-acetylaspartate (naa) peak and an increased choline (cho) peak; a slight increase of glutamate/glutamine (glx) peak was also observed; a brain mri performed three months later showed spontaneous regression of the tumour and resolution of the hydrocephalus (figure 3(a))
Diagnosis: pineal mass
Laboratory Values: blood and cerebrospinal fluid markers of germinal tumours were negative. however, lymphoid elements (97% t cd3þ, 3% b cd20þ) were detected
Pathology: NA

Title: cervical mullerian adenosarcoma with heterologous sarcomatous overgrowth: a fourth case and review of literature.
Authors: Patrelli TS;Gizzo S;Di Gangi S;Guidi G;Rondinelli M;Nardelli GB
Institution: department of gynecological and human reproduction sciences, university of padua, via giustiniani 3, 35128 padua, italy
Medical/Surgical History: para 2012, in menopause from the age of 51 years, who had never taken hormone replacement therapy (hrt),
Signs and Symptoms: metrorrhagia from about 20 days; pelvic examination revealed an elongated fleshy polyp, protruding through the cervical ostium, probably from endocervix
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: transvaginal ultrasonography revealed a polypoid mass subverting completely the uterine echostructure, with a thin residual posterior margin of intact myometrium; abdominal computed tomography contrast medium that shows a solid lesion with axial diameter of about 6 cm, with inhomogeneous densitometry, assuming contrast medium, surrounded by a thicker rim, containing gas bubbles, present in the pelvic, in continuity with the uterus, extending to the cranio-caudal about 9 cm; cystoscopic examination revealed an urethra displaced upwards, bladder trigone raised significantly compared to standard as ab-extrinseco compression, but covered with mucosa of normal appearance
Diagnosis: mullerian adenosarcoma with sarcomatous overgrowth (maso)
Laboratory Values: the serum concentrations of cancer markers cea, afp, ca 19-9, ca 125, he4, ca 15-3 are within the norm
Pathology: biopsy of the polypoid mass: macroscopically, the lesion was measured as 3 × 1, 5 × 1, 5 cm. microscopically, it was composed of a mucus-blood material encompassing lymphocytes, histiocytes and atypical elements of neoplastic nature. there were markedly anaplastic focal areas composed of pleomorphic spindle cell proliferation. about the immunophenotype, vimentin was positive and desmin was positive in focal areas, but keratin (mnf116) was negative. on gross examination, a friable and polypoid lesion arised from uterine cervix and involved the cervical-isthmic mucosa and the endometrium. a focal chronic ulceration of the head of the polyp was noted. the cut surface of the tumor was fleshy and gelatinous. there was focal myometrial invasion. on microscopic examination, the tumor was characterized by intimate admixture of epithelial component and sarcomatous stromal component. the epithelial component was minimal and mostly without epithelial atypia; while the sarcomatous component was clearly predominant (pure sarcoma: 70%), of high grade, with a high mitotic rate (10 mfs/10 hpfs). in addition, heterologous pure sarcomatous areas were noted comprising of rhabdomyosarcoma. there was no lymph node metastasis or lymphatic vascular space invasion, but a non-neoplastic focal thrombosis of small blood vessels in the head of the polyp was noted. omentum and appendix were negative for tumor localization. the cytoplasm of the stromal cells showed a strong positive reaction for vimentin and desmin, but was negative for smooth muscle actin. also, tumor cells were negative for ?-hcg, estrogen and progesterone receptors. only the focal areas of stromal tissue were positive for myf 4 and also glands and rare isolated cells were positive for keratin (mnf116)
Interventional Therapy: total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, systematic pelvic lymph node dissection, omental biopsy and appendectomy adjuvant whole-pelvis radiation (45 gy)
Patient Outcome Assessment: after three month of follow up, the patient was free of tumor
Disclosures: the authors declare that they have no competing interests

Title: primary uterine osteosarcoma presenting synchronously with bilateral breast carcinomas.
Authors: Powell G;Barth L;Todd R;Ganesan R
Institution: department of histopathology, royal shrewsbury hospital, shrewsbury, uk; department of gynaecology, university hospital of north staffordshire, stoke-on-trent, staffordshire, uk; department of histopathology, birmingham women's hospital, birmingham, west midlands, uk
Medical/Surgical History: NA
Signs and Symptoms: postmenopausal bleeding
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: staging ct imaging prior to mastectomy showed a 12 cm pelvic mass which on initial impression was thought to be a fibroid uterus; pelvic ultrasound, hysteroscopy and biopsy; ct imaging showed the development of multiple peritoneal and pulmonary deposits, confirmed on biopsy to be metastatic osteosarcoma
Diagnosis: primary uterine osteosarcoma; bilateral breast carcinomas
Laboratory Values: NA
Pathology: the biopsy showed undifferentiated sarcoma, unclassifiable with immunohistochemistry; histological examination of the resection specimen showed a partially necrotic tumour with a discrete outline located within and extending throughout the myometrium. the tumour was composed of malignant spindle cells (figure 1a), with an intermittent component of pleomorphic cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. plentiful osteoclast-like giant cells were present (figure 1b). mitoses were numerous and structurally abnormal forms were common. neoplastic cells were surrounded by hyaline osteoid matrix and foci of coarse neoplastic woven bone (figure 1c). generous sampling of the tumour showed no admixed neoplastic epithelial elements, thus ruling out the more common carcinosarcoma (malignant mixed müllerian tumour); tumour cells showed immunohistochemical expression for vimentin, smooth muscle actin (sma), desmin (focally) and cd99. epithelial markers were not expressed. the morphological and immunohistochemical appearances were in keeping with primary uterine osteoblastic variant of osteosarcoma
Patient Outcome Assessment: the patient received palliative chemotherapy and died several months later

Title: a rare cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: primary pericardial mesothelioma masquerading as pericardial constriction.
Authors: Fernandes R;Nosib S;Thomson D;Baniak N
Institution: department of internal medicine, unviersity of saskatchewan, saskatoon, canada
Life Style: had used illicit drugs before, but not in the last 5-6 years
Medical/Surgical History: past history of hiv (diagnosed in may 2010 and been on antiretroviral therapy) and hepatitis c; 4 month history of gradual but progressive swelling of her lower limbs and abdomen
Signs and Symptoms: 4 month history of gradual but progressive swelling of her lower limbs and abdomen; no chest pain, dyspnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: stable vitals; cardiovascular examination (elevated jugual venous pressure of about 12 cm with a pronounced 'y' descent, prominent pericardial knock sound heart over the praecordium, no pericardial rub or murmur; lungs were clear to auscultation, markedly oedematous from the abdomen to the lower limbs); blood tests (ruled out renal and hepatic diseases); peritoneal fluid was negative for malignancy; echocardiogram (thickened bright pericardium adjacent to the right heart border with parallel separation between epicardial and pericardial echoes, septal bounce, lack of pericardial slide, left ventricular ejection fraction was 64% and the right ventricle was normal in size and function); tissue doppler (annulus paradoxus demonstrated, constrictive physiology was shown in mitral and triscuspid inflows, marked dilation of inferior vena cava with no change during inspiration or expiration); ct of the chest (thickening of the pericardium with no evidence of calcification; no lung nodules; bilateral pleural effusions, interstitial thickening present in the lung bases); mri (presence of a diffusely thickened pericardium at 5 mm, inferior vena cava and hepatic veins appeared plethoric, rapid early diastolic filling); right and left heart chaterisation (confirmed constrictive physiology); haemodynamics (mean right atrial pressure was markedly elevated at 28 mm hg; right ventricular pressure was 43/19 mm hg with a mean of 28; pulmonary artery pressure was 38/25 mm hg with a mean of 32 mm hg; mean pulmonary capillary wedge pressure was markedly elevated at 29 mm hg (figure 5); diastolic equalisation of pressures, the haemodynamic hallmark of constrictive physiology, was demonstrated; there was prominent ‘y’ descent noted in the arterial wave form; discordance between right ventricular and left ventricular pressures during inspiration and expiration was noted; interventricular dependence was demonstrated after 500 ml of saline challenge.)
Diagnosis: malignant pericardial mesothelioma
Laboratory Values: blood tests ruled out renal and heaptic diseases
Pathology: peritoneal fluid was negative for malignancy. four pieces of rubbery, tan pericardial tissue, the largest of which was 10.2×5.2×0.6 cm, were sent for histopathological studies. on cut section, the centre of the tissues was white and firm with an irregular border expanding centrifugally low-power microscopy of h&e staining showed a proliferation of epithelioid-like cells with ample cytoplasm and pleomorphic nuclei very deep within the pericardial tissue, suggesting a mesothelial origin. in few sections, there was evidence that the cells lined up in a single file, suggesting a possible metastatic lobular carcinoma of the breast. they did appear to be lining an anatomical structure, but it was not discernable whether this was a vessel or some other structures. no significant inflammatory cells were noted in the tissue background.the epithelioid-like cells in question stained positively for vimentin, d240 and calretinin, highlighting them as mesothelial cells. given the depth of infiltration of the mesothelial cells into the pericardium, some irregular cytological features, and no obvious background inflammatory reaction to account for this change, a tetative diagnosis of atypical mesotehlial proliferaiton was considered. the fact that these cells were also producing their own mucoid stroma confirmed their malignant potential. this ominous histological feature combined with the depth of the mesothelial aggregates into the pericardium, favoured a diagnosis of malignant pericardial mesothelioma. the diagnosis was confirmed by molecular fluoresence in situ hybridization which showed that 38% of the proliferating mesothelial cells had a homozygous deletioin for p16, putting them in the malignant range
Pharmacological Therapy: received diuretics and inotropes after resuscitation
Interventional Therapy: pericardiectomy (the pericardium was very firm, taut and appeared to be calcified; the visceral and parietal surfaces were heavily involved and only a limited pericardiectomy was achieved as the visceral layer could not be completely released; fibrocartilaginous changes were found to involve the visceral and parietal pericardial layers as well as parts of the myocardium; there was a marked venous bleeding secondary to elevated venous pressure, but estimated blood loss was minimal; postoperatively, she was transferred to the coronary care unit because of hypotension and oliguria requiring pressor support and haemodynamic monitoring.)
Patient Outcome Assessment: the patient's condition deriorated in the hospital; eventually, she coded on pulseless electrical activity; she was successfully resuscitated and started on inotropes for haemodynamic support; but, her condition continued to deteriorate, and she was recommended for compassionate terminal care; the patient was kept comfortable and died in the coronary care unit

Title: rapid improvement of glucagonoma-related necrolytic migratory erythema with octreotide.
Authors: Kimbara S;Fujiwara Y;Toyoda M;Chayahara N;Imamura Y;Kiyota N;Mukohara T;Fukunaga A;Oka M;Nishigori C;Minami H
Institution: department of clinical oncology, osaka city general hospital, osaka, japan
Family History: no family history or complication for the pituitary or parathyroid glands
Medical/Surgical History: NA
Signs and Symptoms: fingernail deformity and fragility 2 years prior to admission; erythematous erosive lesions appeared on her face, neck, trunk, and extremities, particularly in the interdigital spaces of the feet; he erythema and papules fused into red plaques with clear outlines and covered with scars; exudates or scabs were present on the erosive surfaces; the eruptions expanded outward, leaving a bronze or dark brown pigmented deposition, and the affected areas were often pruritic and painful; skin lesions recurred with remissions and exacerbations, and were unaffected by treatment with antibiotics or corticosteroids; at the same time, she also lost 15 kg in weight over 6 months, and developed proximal muscle weakness and gastrointestinal symptoms, including anorexia and vomiting; performance status was 2
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: ultrasonography and contrast-enhanced dynamic computed tomography (ct) of the abdomen revealed the presence of multiple tumors in the pancreatic tail and liver; these tumors were enhanced during the early arterial phase (fig; 2a) and washed out during the delayed phase
Diagnosis: pancreatic glucagonoma; necrolytic migratory erythema (nme)
Laboratory Values: routine blood biochemistry tests on admission showed normochromic and normocytic anemia, normal liver and renal function; further endocrine testing showed a serum glucagon concentration of 8,400 pg/ml (normal range 70–160). serum insulin, c-peptide, hba1c, and glycoalbumin revealed mild abnormality in glucose tolerance. serum zinc level was decreased to 56 ?g/ml (normal range 65–110); her serum glucagon concentration decreased from 8,400 to 3,500 pg/ml for 5 months

Pharmacological Therapy: short-acting octreotide 100 ?g subcutaneously twice daily for 4 weeks; octreotide long-acting release (lar)
Patient Outcome Assessment: octreotide lar achieved tumor shrinkage for 6 months, and durable stable disease for 16 months from diagnosis

Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: an mri was performed, which showed no difference between the ischiofemoral spaces and no abnormality of quadratus femoris a further mri now showed selective narrowing of the right ischiofemoral space when compared to the left (28.3 mm vs; 34.2 mm on the left) and quadratus femoris space (21.3 mm vs; 24.0 mm on the left), the ischiofemoral space being defined as the smallest distance between the lateral cortex of the ischial tuberosity and medial cortex of the lesser trochanter and the quadratus femoris space as the smallest space for the passage of the quadratus femoris muscle delimited by the superolateral surface of the hamstrings tendons and the posteromedial surface of the iliopsoas tendon or lesser trochanter; a diffuse edema-like signal was observed near the origin of quadratus femoris on the right ischial tuberosity and minor linear fluid-like signal seen related to the muscle more laterally; a dynamic ultrasound was performed that showed no cause for the snapping hip from the psoas tendon or iliotibial tract; mri performed 23 months following the injury revealed further narrowing of the right ischiofemoral space (14.6 mm vs; 22.2 mm on the left) and quadratus femoris space (10.5 mm vs; 16.0 mm on the left).there was diffuse edema seen within the right quadratus femoris at the narrowest point of the ischiofe-moral space; t1-weighted fat-suppression images following iv gadolinium showed some minor diffuse enhancement within the muscle at the site of the edema and a thin layer of enhancing tissue along the lateral border of the hamstring tendons ; to illustrate the progressive narrowing of the ischiofemoral space, axial slices through the lesser trochanter from the three mri scans are presented side by side; post-operative radiograph showed adequate decompression of the ischiofe-moral space
Diagnosis: ischiofemoral impingement
Laboratory Values: NA
Pathology: NA
Interventional Therapy: a iliotibial band z-plasty was performed; ct-guided steroid and local anesthetic injection around the quadratus femoris provided relief of her pain but not the clunking, for 24 h; surgery :at surgery, the iliotibial band was divided to gain good exposure of the posterior aspect of the hip; there was no obvious mass lesion in the external rotators or obturator externus, and it became clear that when she extended (in a neutral position of her hip) the lesser trochanter impinged directly on the posterior ischium; there was a considerable amount of thickened bursal type tissue in the area of the impingement; quadratus femoris was mobilized off the ischium allowing exposure of all the bursal tissue around the lesser trochanter, which was then excised; a subperiosteal release of psoas was then performed to expose the lesser trochanter which was removed, and in the neutral position of the hip in extension there was subsequently no impingement; psoas was reattached back to the femur and quadratus femoris reattached back onto the ischium

sanger sequencing of several cox assembly genes and structural components did not identify causative variants, prompting whole exome sequencing. prioritisation of candidate disease genes was performed essentially as reported previously,27 with our analysis focussing on nonsynonymous variants. based on the rare disease phenotype we expected disease-causal variants to have a low frequency in the general population, and hence we excluded detected variants present in 3600 control exomes and public databases. assuming an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance, we searched for genes carrying predicted compound heterozygous or homozygous variants; this filter left 38 genes. two genes, namely myh14 (mim*608568) and anks6 (mim*615370), have been previously linked to human disease. variants in both were excluded as likely candidates because of different clinical presentations, reportedly autosomal dominant mode of inheritance in the case of myh14, and the fact that both heterozygous anks6 variants were confirmed to be in cis on the same allele. only one gene, pet100 (nm_001171155.1), carried two predicted loss-of-function alleles. the patient was homozygous, for a truncating pet100 variant (c.[142c>t][142c>t], p.[(gln48*)][(gln48*)] clinvar reference id: mdi-3317) that resides in the fourth coding exon and predicts a truncated protein in which the last 26 amino acids are lost (33% of the full-length protein). concordant with a disease-causal role of the homozygous (c.142c>t, p.(gln48*)) variant, confirmatory sanger sequencing revealed that both healthy parents were heterozygous carriers

Title: successful left trisegmentectomy for ruptured hepatoblastoma using intraoperative transarterial embolization.

Institution: first department of surgery, shinshu university school of medicine, matsumoto, japan

Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: real-time ultrasound showed a large heterogeneous mass occupying almost the entire abdomen; a computed tomographic (ct) scan showed a multinodular low-density mass (10 cm in diameter) occupying almost the entire liver and compressing the thin posterior segment of the right lobe (fig 1); angiography was performed, and a large tumor was noted, displacing the right and left hepatic arteries (fig 2a); pharmacological arterial portography showed a patent but compressed right portal vein (fig 2b); however, a catheter for arterial embolization could not be inserted into the proper hepatic artery; , an emergency ct scan showed rapid growth of the mass, and appearance of fluid in the abdominal and thoracic cavities (fig 3), which had not heen noted during the previous examination; , intraoperative ultrasonography showed that the tumor involved the left medial and right anterior segments
Diagnosis: hepatoblastoma
Laboratory Values: the patient was anemic, with a hemoglobin level of 7.5 g/dl and an elevated platelet count (666,000/mm3). hepatic function tests showed a serum total bilirubin value of 2.4 mg/dl, aspartate aminotransferase level of 83 u/l, lactate dehydrogenase level of 1233 u/l, and negativity for hepatitis b antigen and antihepatitis c antibody
Pathology: histological examination of the tumor showed a hepatoblastoma of the mixed mesenchymal type. most of the tumor was composed of necrotic and degenerated tissue

Interventional Therapy: emergency laparotomy was performed; six hundred twenty milliliters of blood was aspirated from the abdominal cavity; the rupture sites of the hepatoblastoma were found to be on the left medial segment, just to the right of the cranial end of the falciform ligament, and on the left medial side of the stalk of the tumor, which bulged toward the caudal side and reached the level of the pubic bone; the rupture site was packed with gauze and compressed gently, but a considerable amount of bleeding continued; the left and middle hepatic arteries were dissected and taped; after ligation of the proximal side of these arteries, iotae was performed, using an 18-gauge teflon catheter; , three intrahepatic metastases were found in the left lateral segment, which was extremely atrophic; the left hepatic duct and the left portal vein were dissected and divided; at this stage, the tumor size had diminished gradually, and no further bleeding was observed from the sites of rupture; , transection of the liver was begun from the caudal side along the right hepatic vein, using pringle’s maneuver; the line of resection was free of tumor, and no residual, tumor was seen in the right posterior segment; residual pieces of tumor were removed meticulously from the abdominal cavity, which was irrigated subsequently; , the total volume of aspirated blood and ascites was 3,950 ml, and the total operation time was 8 hours, 50 minutes; the tumor weight was 1,350 g, which represented 13.5% of the patient’s body weight; the postoperative course was uneventful
Patient Outcome Assessment: the patient was discharged from the hospital 1 month after bmt, but she died of reye’s syndrome 30 months after surgery; before her death, liver function test results and the serum afp value were normal, with no sign of tumor recurrence, and she had normal physical and social development; an autopsy was not performed

Laboratory Values: NA
Pathology: gross findings: the corpus uterus and cervix weighed 80 g. the bivalved uterus revealed a tan-yellow 7.0 cm x 4.5 cm x 4.0 cm polypoid endometrial mass with focal hemorrhage attached to the posterior uterine wall. bilateral ovaries and fallopian tubes were unremarkable; light microscopic findings: sections from the formalin-fixed endometrial biopsy showed a malignant epithelial element with cribriform and glandular patterns admixed with sarcomatous areas composed of spindle shaped cells with a high mitotic rate (up to 7 per hpf). several fragments of necrotic tissue were also present. neither heterologous features nor rhabdoid components were seen. sections from the tumor in the resected uterus were quite different from the biopsy specimen. although a small area showed malignant epithelial cells that were similar to the glandular areas of the biopsy specimen, no sarcomatous areas were present. the majority of the tumor was composed of sheets of round to polygonal cells with interspersed areas of geographic necrosis. most of the cells contained single, spherical eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions that sometimes compressed the nucleus (fig. 2, inset). in some areas of the tumor, nucleoli were prominent, whereas in other areas they were less conspicuous. the cytoplasmic inclusions were striking and easily seen in sections fixed in omnifix, but much less distinct and more subtle in formalin-fixed tissue. these cells were identical to those seen in malignant rhabdoid tumor of the kidney. cells with these rhabdoid features were especially evident adjacent to areas of necrosis, but were the predominant component throughout the tumor. the tumor infiltrated through approximately 50% of the myometrium and vascular invasion was present; immunohistochemistry: the eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions reacted strongly with anti-vimentin and were negative for cytokeratins, a- smooth muscle actin, desmin, and myoglobin. ema staining was not observed in rhabdoid appearing tumor cells. strong positivity for both ema and cytokeratins was present in the small epithelial portions of the tumor forming glandular and cribriform patterns. these glandular areas were negative for all other antibodies including anti-vimentin; immunoelectron microscopy: colloidal gold particles indicative of vimentin antigenicity were concentrated over whorls of paranuclear intermediate filaments. immunostaining for cytokeratin ae1/ae3 and ema were negative (not shown)

Medical/Surgical History: had no history of symptoms of heart failure in childhood; however, was aware of having reduced exercise ability from the age of 12 years; he recognized having muscle weakness in his lower limbs from about age 16 years; when approximately 19 years old, he needed to assist his knee with a hand when ascending stairs; later on, he needed to use his arms as support when standing up; the patient experienced progressive muscle weakness in the proximal limbs at age 24 years, and visited a hospital for a neurological examination; his laboratory test results showed a high creatinine phosphokinase (cpk) level (6678 iu/l), and partial loss of the immunohistochemical stain with anti-dystrophin antibody was observed in a muscle biopsy, which led to the diagnosis of bmd; at the time of the first medical evaluation, an echocardiogram revealed dilatation of the left ventricle (lv) and diffuse hypokinesis, with the following measurements: lv diastolic dimension (dd) of 71 mm, systolic dimension (ds) of 61 mm, and an ejection fraction (ef) of 28%; enalapril 5 mg was started in may 2009; his medical history included both liver damage and arrhythmia diagnosed in infancy
Signs and Symptoms: he complained of shortness of breath, abdominal distention, and coughing during work hours in may 2011 at age 26 years
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: june 2011: physical examination (showed a height of 161 cm, body weight of 74 kg, blood pressure of 110/60 mmhg, heart rate of 96 beats/minute regularly, respiratory rate of 24 times/minute, body temperature of 37.0°c, and spo2 of 97% under 2 l/minute oxygen; jugular vein dilatation in the neck was present; a chest examination revealed audible wheezes and crackles in both lungs; cardiac auscultation revealed that the third and fourth heart sounds had a gallop rhythm; his abdomen was distended; generalized edema and ascites indicated anasarca; the patient showed wing-like shoulder blades and mild lordosis; no pseudohypertrophy of the gastrocnemius muscle was observed; gower’s sign was positive); electrocardiography (showed a normal sinus rhythm of 90 beats/minute; qrs width of 105 ms; negative t wave in the iii, avf, v1-2, and v6 leads; st depression in the ii, iii, and avf leads; and qs pattern in the i and avl leads); chest radiography (remarkable cardiac enlargement with pulmonary congestion and pleural effusion were observed); echocardiography (revealed an lvef of 19% with marked dilatation and diffuse hypokinesis, moderate mitral regurgitation of grade 2 of 4, and lv dyssynchrony with septal flash and apical shuffle); 20th day of hospitalisation: the patient had fever, hemosputum, and hypoxemia, and pulmonary infiltration was detected on a chest radiograph; alveolar hemorrhage was detected on a chest computed tomography scan; after methylprednisolone and prednisolone, the fever and hemosputum improved, the pulmonary congestion was improved, and his body weight was reduced to 53 kg; 47th day of hospitalisation: cardiac catheterisation (showed right atrial pressure of 8 mmhg, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 29 mmhg, mean pulmonary artery pressure of 34 mmhg, and cardiac output and cardiac index of 5.9 l/minute, 3.7 l·minute-1·m-2, respectively; left ventriculography showed a considerably reduced lvef of 17% and elevated lv end-diastolic pressure of 33 mmhg); after psl dose was gradualy tapered, ventricular tachycardia frequently occurred: electrocardiogram (dyssynchrony was detected on echocardiography despite a narrow qrs width of 105 ms in the electrocardiogram); 59th day of hospitalisation: chest radiograph (shortness of breath appeared again, and the cardiothoracic ratio (ctr) was found to be deteriorated on a chest radiograph); during the corticosteroid therapy for alveolar hemorrhage, the patient’s heart failure improved with a reduction of the ctr on the chest roentgenogram and normalization of the serum cpk level
Diagnosis: refractory heart failure
Laboratory Values: june 2011: the laboratory tests showed the following results: white blood cell count, 6700/?l with normal segment (neutrophils 63.4%, lymphocytes 22.1%, monocytes 9.8%, eosinophils 2.1%, and basophils 0.6%); hemoglobin, 15.1 g/dl; and platelet count, 21.0 × 104/?l. biochemical examination showed a sodium concentration of 135 meq/l, potassium of 4.2 meq/l, chloride of 100 meq/l, blood urea nitrogen of 21 mg/dl, and creatinine of 0.5 mg/dl. his total bilirubin level was increased to 2.7 mg/dl, and liver enzyme levels were elevated, as follows: aspartate aminotransferase, 110 iu/l; alanine aminotransferase, 222 iu/l; alkaline phosphatase, 173 iu/l; and lactate dehydrogenase, 460 iu/l. cpk level was markedly elevated to 2697 iu/l without isoenzyme level elevation of cpk-mb. his b-type natriuretic peptide (bnp) level was markedly elevated to 1393.5 pg/ml. an antinuclear antibody test was negative. after methylprednisolone and prednisolone, the elevated cpk level decreased
Pathology: 47th day of illness: an endomyocardial biopsy was performed, which revealed slight interstitial fibrosis, enlarged nuclei, interstitial edema, and little lymphocyte infiltration between the myocardial fibers. granuloma, giant cells, and eosinophils were not observed, and cd8- positive t lymphocytes were detected by immunohistochemistry staining. there were no findings of a specific myocardial disease
Pharmacological Therapy: may 2011: he received furosemide 10 mg and carvedilol 15 mg. june 2011: we provided continuous infusion of dobutamine, milrinone, and carperitide to the patient, and we administered oral carvedilol 5 mg and enalapril 2.5 mg. the pulmonary congestion gradually improved. administration of amiodarone was started on the third day of hospitalization because of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia. enalapril was changed to 2.5 mg imidapril because of liver enzyme elevation. alveolar hemorrhage was detected on a chest computed tomography scan, which was probably an adverse effect of amiodarone. therefore, amiodarone was discontinued and intravenous infusion of methylprednisolone was started, at 1 g/day for 3 days followed by oral prednisolone (psl) at 1 mg/kg body weight. the intravenous infusions of dobutamine and the other medications were stopped on the 30th day of illness. the ?-blocker was changed from 5 mg carvedilol to 1.25 mg bisoprolol because of frequent ventricular tachycardia. the psl dose could be gradually tapered without the recurrence of alveolar bleeding. the psl dose was gradually tapered after improvement of the alveolar hemorrhage. thereafter, ventricular tachycardia frequently occurred despite the increase of bisoprolol dose to 1.875 mg. dobutamine infusion was required for the worsening heart failure on the 113th day of illness. during the corticosteroid therapy for alveolar hemorrhage, the patient’s heart failure improved with a reduction of the ctr on the chest roentgenogram and normalization of the serum cpk level. there was a possibility that the improvement in heart failure was due to the effect of the corticosteroid. therefore, psl administration was restarted from the 148th day of illness, at doses of 30 mg for 7 days, 15 mg for 7 days, and 7.5 mg for 7 days. thereafter, the cardiomegaly improved and the cpk level decreased. the dobutamine infusion, which had been difficult to stop for 43 days, could be discontinued at 8 days after the psl administration
Interventional Therapy: a cardiac resynchronization therapy defibrillator was implanted on the 59th day of hospitalisation; the patient seemed to be a nonresponder to cardiac resynchronization therapy (crt)
Patient Outcome Assessment: the patient was discharged from the hospital on foot thereafter; he continued taking psl as an outpatient, and returned to normal daily life without the exacerbation of heart failure; after 1 year, echocardiography showed that the lvef was slightly improved from 20% to 24%; two years after hospital discharge, the patient regularly visited the outpatient department of our hospital without rehospitalization for heart failure exacerbation; he maintained a stable cardiac condition with a 7.5 mg maintenance dose of psl, with a bnp level of about 130–200 pg/ml

Diagnosis: sjögren–larsson syndrome
Laboratory Values: NA
Pathology: dermatopathologic study of a biopsy specimen confirmed the presence of laminar ichthyosis. we observed a slight acanthosis with papillomatosis, orthokeratotic keratinization without prominent hyperkeratosis, and areas of hypogranulosis

Pathology: the bone marrow aspirate revealed that 86.4% of blasts had lymphoblastic morphology, consistent with the criteria for french, american, and british (fab) sub-type l2. cytochemically, all stains were negative except for periodic acid-schiff. the blasts were myeloid antigen-positive t-all. lab results of cell surface markers by fluorescence activated cell sorting analyses for the patient’s bone marrow sample are presented as follows: cd34(44.9%), cd7(81.1%), ccd3(29.9%), cd13(41.1%), cd33 (72.2%), cd2 (10.6%), cd10 (14.1%), cd79 (2.1%), cd19 (2.0%), cd20 (1.4%), hla-dr (11.1%), cd14 (0.5%), cd15 (2.2%), and cd117 (1.2%). a direct cytogenetic analysis of a bone marrow sample was performed at diagnosis, and showed a normal male karyotype, 46, xy, and an abnormal karyotype, 47, xy, +10, t(14;18)(q32;21), in 40% and 60% of metaphase cells analyzed, respectively. fusion transcripts were not detected by a multiplex nested rt-pcr for 29 types of leukemia-associated genes. although the blast cells had both t cell markers (ccd3 and cd7) and myeloid markers (cd13 and cd33), diagnosis of my+t-all was confirmed in accordance with criteria of the fab and the european group for the immunological characterization of leukemias (egil)
Pharmacological Therapy: initial antibiotic treatments; the patient achieved morphological remission after the first course of induction chemotherapy with vindesine, daunorubicin, l-asparaginase, and dexamethasone. thereafter, the patient continued intensive chemotherapy and maintenance therapy with various combinations of anthracyclines, vindesine, dexamethasone, l-asparaginase, etoposide, cyclophosphamide, high-dose methotrexate, cytarabine, and mercaptopurine; further received prophylactic treatment with methotrexate, cytarabine, and dexamethasone for four rounds
Patient Outcome Assessment: relapse occured after a 3-year remission; fortunately, morphological remission was achieved again after prompt re-induction therapy; the patient has remained in remission since then
Disclosures: all authors declare that there is no conflict interests involved

Pathology: inspection of the gastrectomy specimen confirmed the operative findings: the gastric mucosa was rugose and markedly hypertrophic, and thickened up to 15mm in places. this change was most conspicuous proximally and on the lesser curve where there was almost a polypoidal appearance. odd areas of mucosal erosion and haemorrhage were apparent but there was no discreet bleeding lesion and no suggestion of old or recent peptic ulceration. histologically the mucosal thickening proved to be due to epithelial hyperplasia involving the mucus-secreting cells of the gastric pit region as well as the gastric glands. within the latter there was hyperplasia of both parietal and oxyntic cells, but mucous metaplasia was also seen. cystic dilatation of such glands was conspicuous, and in the lamina propria between the elongated pit/crypt structures vertically running strands of smooth muscle were a further feature. in the pyloric region of the stomach mucosal hyperplasia was less pronounced but there was evidence of metaplasia to an acid-secreting type of epithelium in some of the pyloric glands. superimposed on the hyper plastic state there was quite marked active chronic non-specific gastritis. overall the pathological changes were considered to be consistent with menetrier’s disease, but in view of the involvemen to facid-secreting glands in the hyperplastic process and the presence of acid-secreting glands in the antrum the possibility of the co-existence of a gastrinoma was raised
Interventional Therapy: hypovolaemic shock was corrected by intravenous fluids and blood transfusion, and emergency laparotomy through an upper midline incision was carried out without prior gastroscopy, because of the rate at which the patient was continuing to bleed; the stomach was distended with blood clot; the gastric wall was grossly thickened and had the consistency of soggy wash-leather; the liver and duodenum appeared to be normal; a wide gastrotomy was made and large quantities of blood clot removed; the gastric mucosa showed markedly hypertrophic rugal folds with an almost polypoidal appearance in the proximal part of the body of the stomach; the mucosa was reddened with diffuse bleeding; only one site of pin-point pulsatile haemorrhage was seen, and this was controlled by undersewing; in view of the hypertrophic appearance of the gastric mucosa it was assumed that the patient was suffering from some form of hypertrophic hypersecretory gastropathy and bilateral truncal vagotomy and a pyloroplasty were carried out; in total the patient had received 22 units of whole blood and 10 units of blood products

Title: acute congestive heart failure due to the arteritis of rheumatoid arthritis: early diagnosis by endomyocardial biopsy: a case report.
Authors: Slack JD;Waller B
Institution: cardiology section, department of medicine, saint vincent hospital, department of pathology, indiana university medical center, indianapolis, indiana

Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: physical examination (revealed a blood pressure of 160/100 with a resting pulse rate of 110; bibasilar rales were present); cardiac examination (revealed a grade ii/vi murmur of mitral regurgitation and a prominent summation gallop); electrocardiogram (revealed st-t abnormalities); echocardiogram (revealed four chamber enlargement with normal valvular structures, no evidence of pericardial effusion, and generalized hypokinesis of both the right and left ventricular chambers); cardiac catheterization (revealed normal right heart pressures; the left ventricular pressure was 95/10); left ventriculography (revealed generalized hypokinesis and left ventricular enlargement with mild mitral regurgitation); aortography (there was a trace of aortic insufficency) coronary arteriography (luminal irregularities were noted); nuclear studies (revealed the left ventricular ejection fraction to be .35; global left ventricular enlargement with generalized hypokinesis was present); gallium-67 scan of the heart (showed 3+ myocardial uptake at 48 hours)

Laboratory Values: the sedimentation rate was 100 (10 x normal). the serum viscosity was slightly elevated. the ra titer was geater than 1:10, 240 and the lefa was positive with an ana greater than 1:320 in a diffuse pattern. the dna antibody screening was negative. c4 complement level was normal. the igg, igm, and iga were elevated at 1785, 407, and 544 mg/dl respectively. immune complex assay was high at 91% (c1q binding) and 818 mcg ahg eg/ml (raji cell)

Institution: royal coll surgeons ireland, rotunda hosp dublin, dept obstet & gynaecol, dublin 2, ireland
Medical/Surgical History: a 35-year-old woman, para 2?1 was referred to the fetal medicine unit at the rotunda hospital at 18 weeks’ gestation, after a routine ultrasound scan at an outside hospital suggested the presence of a fetal neck mass

Comorbidities: echogenic intracardiac focus in the left ventricle

Pathology: subsequent histological examination of the tongue mass confirmed the prenatal diagnosis of a mature teratoma
Interventional Therapy: caesarean delivery including the exit procedure (ex-utero intra-partum treatment); the pre-arranged multidisciplinary team was gathered and consisted of a high risk obstetrician, obstetric anaesthetist, paediatric otolaryngologist, paediatric anaesthetist and neonatologist, together with each of their relevant specialist nursing support staff and equipment; sonographic evaluation of the maternal abdomen was performed immediately prior to the procedure to map the location of the placenta and confirm a placenta-free area for uterine incision; general endotracheal anaesthesia was administered using intravenous vecuronium, for maximum uterine relaxation; the patient was placed in a modified lithotomy position with her legs supported in stirrups to allow optimal access for the paediatric surgeons to the fetal head; the abdomen was incised using a low vertical midline incision to allow maximum uterine exposure; a wide transverse lower uterine segment hysterotomy was performed and the fetal head was exteriorised easily, with the fetal shoulders, abdomen and limbs remained within the uterine cavity; the fetal head was rotated gently to the occipito-posterior position, and the large tongue mass was clearly visualised as a solid mass arising from the tip and lateral aspects of the tongue, with its base measuring 2.53.0 cm in diameter; uterine hypotonia and continuous fetal heart monitoring were maintained throughout the exit procedure; delivery of the rest of the fetal body was completed 16 min after initial exteriorisa- tion of the fetal head; Patient Outcome Assessment: successful primary resection of the tongue mass; immediately after delivery, the baby was admitted to the neonatal special care unit and was successfully extubated shortly thereafter due to its vigorous state; on the 8th day-of-life, the baby was brought back to theatre for refashioning of the tongue tip, and release of tongue tie; the baby had an otherwise uncomplicated neonatal course, and was discharged home shortly thereafter

Title: isolated cytochrome c oxidase deficiency as a cause of melas.
Authors: Rossmanith W;Freilinger M;Roka J;Raffelsberger T;Moser-Thier K;Prayer D;Bernert G;Bittner RE
Institution: center for anatomy & cell biology, medical university of vienna, währinger str. 13, 1090 wien, austria

Signs and Symptoms: clinical symptoms and laboratory abnormalities typical of melas; devoid of any mutation in a gene previously associated with this disease; instead, the deletion of a single nucleotide (7630delt) within mt-co2, the gene of cytochrome c oxidase (cox) subunit ii (coii), was identified as the cause of his condition; this patient has previously been described in detail,8 and is thus only briefly summarised and updated here; at the age of 13 years, the patient experienced his first stroke-like episode with reversible aphasia, right hemiparesis and hemianopsia; exercise intolerance, progressive mental impairment and short stature had previously been noted; serum lactate was constantly raised; the patient developed secondarily generalised and myoclonic seizures, left ventricular hypertrophy, retinopathy and progressive nephropathy, and had recurrent headaches and vomiting; repeated mri of the brain over the years revealed an increasing number of focal lesions and progressive cortical atrophy throughout the cere- bral cortex, beginning and most pronounced in the left parieto-occipital lobe (fig 1); brain angiography showed no angiopathic alterations; basal ganglia calcifications were noted from the first neuroradiological examination (fig 1), and the most last mri scan taken showed moderate cerebellar lesions

Diagnosis: cytochrome-c oxidase deficiency
Laboratory Values: given the overt pathogenic role of 7630delt, we refrained from doing a single-fibre pcr-rflp correlation analysis, but instead used the scarce amount of biopsy material to analyse protein and mrna steady-state levels of various subunits of the respiratory chain to throw light on the pathogenic mechanism of 7630delt. as predicted, the protein levels of coii were dramatically reduced (fig 4a). however, levels of other subunits of respiratory complex iv were also diminished, although not all to the same extent. in stark contrast, (selected) subunits of the other four complexes of the respiratory chain, as well as a mitochondrial marker protein, voltage-dependent anion channel (vdac), were generally upregulated (fig 4b). expression of a nuclear protein (emerin) was comparable with controls
Pathology: a biopsy from the vastus lateralis muscle taken at 13 years of age was processed for routine histo- chemical staining. a small fibre bundle was fixed and processed for transmission electron microscopy. activities of respiratory chain enzymes and citrate synthase (cs) were measured in the homogenate of the frozen muscle; the muscle biopsy revealed pronounced, generalised cox hyporeactivity (.90% of muscle fibres) with numerous fibres completely non-reactive and only a few with near-normal reactivity (fig 2a,b). succinate dehydrogenase (sdh) staining showed the complementary pattern of mitochondrial prolifera- tion in muscle fibres (fig 2c). however, of the few arterioles identified in the muscle section, only one displayed pronounced sdh reactivity. the presence of ragged-red fibres (,2%) indicated subsarcolemmal as well as sarcoplasmic accumulation of mitochondria, which was also seen by transmission electron microscopy (fig 2d). like most muscle fibres of normal appearance, ragged-red fibres were hyporeactive or non-reactive for cox. mitochondrial proliferation was also reflected by the marked increase in cs activity in the muscle homogenate (table 1). assessment of respiratory chain enzymes corroborated the complex iv deficiency already denoted by histology; cox activity was barely detectable. other respiratory chain enzyme measurements independent from complex iv were either in the normal range or were also increased (table 1). southern blotting excluded large-scale rearrangements of muscle mtdna. as none of the previously reported melas mutations was found by the initial, partial sequence analysis,8 the entire muscle mtdna was finally sequenced. in total, 15 discrepancies from the revised cambridge reference sequence were found,12 14 of which were previously reported polymorph- isms16 17 (see supplementary materials for a complete listing). the 15th, a deletion of t at position 7630 (7630delt; fig 3a), however, is obviously pathogenic. this mutation, 7630delt, gives rise to a frameshift in the reading frame of mt-co2, resulting in a premature stop of translation (fig 3c). a peptide translated from mt-co2 harbouring 7630delt will thus consist of only 16 amino acids instead of 227. this mutation was not found in the two major collections of mtdna mutations.16 17 pcr-rflp analysis showed that 7630delt was in fact heteroplasmic in the patient’s muscle also (fig 3b). the deletion was also found in the patient’s blood, although at a much lower frequency
Patient Outcome Assessment: the patient died at the age of 23 years; no postmortem examination was carried out

Institution: department of pathology, provincial clinical medical college of fujian medical university, fujian provincial hospital, fuzhou, 350001, fujian province, people's republic of china;the state key laboratory of organ failure research, national clinical research center of kidney disease, nanfang hospital, southern medical university, guangzhou, 510515, people's republic of china; department of pathology, the eighth affiliated hospital, sun yat-sen university, 3025 shennan middle road, shenzhen, 518033, guangdong province, people's republic of china

Medical/Surgical History: no history of cutaneous malignancy
Signs and Symptoms: 1-month history of chest distending pain
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: chest ct revealed a giant lobulated mass with uneven density approximately 12 × 12 × 7.5 cm in size occupying the anterior mediastinum (fig; 1a and ?andb).b); there were no obvious calcification and fat density shadows; the mass showed a slight heterogeneous enhancement on a contrast-enhanced ct scan
Diagnosis: primary mediastinal clear cell sarcoma
Laboratory Values: the serum levels of tumour markers, namely alpha-fetoprotein (afp) and carcinoembryonic antigen (cea), were within normal limits
Pathology: grossly, the mass was well-demarcated, measuring 10 × 10 × 5 cm in size and yellow-grey on the cut surface. a massive necrosis was identified; histologically, the tumour demonstrated expansive growth and infiltrated the adjacent lung tissue (fig. 2a). the tumour mainly consisted of epithelioid or polygonal cells arranged in sheets; clusters of tumour cells were set in a fibrous stroma (fig. 2c). these tumour cells had oval vesicular nuclei with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli and palely eosinophilic cytoplasm (fig. 2d). a large necrosis was found (fig. 2e). a proportion of the cells contained melanin; immunohistochemical studies showed a strong but diffuse distribution of the markers vimentin (fig. 3a) and hmb-45 (fig. 3b). these cells were negative for melan-a, s-100, cd117, ck19, cd56, cd99, synaptophysin, chromogranin a, cd34, ttf-1, cd2, cd5, cd20, and alkp80. the ki-67 index was about 30% (fig. 3c).dual colour interphase fluorescence in situ hybridisation utilising the ewsr1 break-apart probe was performed on a paraffin section. a clear separation of red and green signals within a single cell was identified in most cells, which demonstrated the presence of the ewsr1 rearrangement (fig. 3d). no braf mutation was detected
Patient Outcome Assessment: to date, 8 months after operation, the patient is well and without evidence of a recurrence or metastasis

Geographic Locations: aboriginal female from a remote area
Medical/Surgical History: had an area of congenital pigmentation at the left corner of the mouth and had been investigated with cranial computed tomography (ct) at 15 months because of increasing head circumference; no concerns were raised at that time about any mass but the pigmentation was well described in her case notes; the ct scan revealed no abnormality but failed to pass inferiorly enough to include the area of swelling observed subsequently
Signs and Symptoms: left facial swelling in the region of the cheek, measuring 3 x 3 cm; slow but progressive increase in the size of this tumor over the preceding year; on admission she had a swelling measuring 8 x 8 cm and occupying the anterior part of the left cheek ; the swelling was lobulated, felt firm and was attached to her upper jaw; the rest of the systemic examination was unremarkable; an mri scan of the face demonstrated a large heterogeneous mass occupying most of the left cheek, predominantly of low t1 and high t2 signal, without evidence of intracranial or intra orbital extension ; a ct scan of the chest demonstrated a 9 mm nodule in the inferior part of the right upper lobe and a few more opacities, suspected to be metastases in the lower lobes; a right thoracotomy and anterior segmentectomy of the upper lobe was done; it confirmed the presence of tumor deposits, which consisted of nests of cells with enlarged nuclei showing an extremely high mitotic rate; these tumor cells were essentially the same as those seen in the primary lesion from the cheek; a repeat mri scan [after three cycles of chemotherapy] demonstrated significant reduction in the size of the tumor (now measuring 4 x 2.2 cm) in the left cheek but still abutting the maxilla at the level of the hard palate and extending anteriorly and superiorly to the neck of the mandible; a ct chest demonstrated a reduction in the size of the previously documented pulmonary metastases; after a total of six courses of chemotherapy, an mri of the face demonstrated a further decrease of the tumor size; ; the tumor was found infiltrating the masseter
Comorbidities: congenital nevus in the left cheek; during [chemotherapy] treatment she had episodes of febrile neutropenia; tinea capitis; chicken pox; impetigo; which were treated appropriately
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: cranial computed tomography (ct) scans; biopsy; mri scan
Diagnosis: progressive sialoblastoma, which originated from the area of an existing nevus
Laboratory Values: NA
Pathology: the biopsy taken from the mass previously showed islands of primitive cells that demonstrated vague peripheral palisading separated by a fibro-myxoid stroma. there were grouped lobules of basaloid cells with open chromatin and mitotic activity. the tumor cells had large round to oval nuclei generally with one to two nucleoli demonstrating high mitotic activity. focal areas of necrosis were seen. the tumor cells stained positively for the epithelial markers ae1/ae3 (cytokeratin) and epithelial membrane antigen (ema), as well as smooth muscle actin and vimentin
Pharmacological Therapy: chemotherapy […] was begun according to the siop mmt953b protocol, consisting of carboplatin, epirubicin, vincristine, etoposide, ifosfamide, and dactinomycin which she received for an initial period of 27 weeks; total of nine courses of chemotherapy; surgical removal of the left cheek tumor was performed together with subtotal parotidectomy through a doubly modified blair incision. the tumor was found infiltrating the masseter. the tumor and part of the masseter muscle was removed en bloc. the facial nerve was preserved
Patient Outcome Assessment: six months after the surgery, she is clinically well with normal facial nerve examination; there is no sign of recurrence on imaging with mri

Diagnosis: heart failure
Laboratory Values: initial workup revealed normal levels of troponine (<0.01 ng/ml) and cpk-mb (4.6 ng/ml), thereby ruling out acute coronary syndrome. the level of bnp was 1230 pg/ml confirming the diagnosis of heart failure. prior to opcab, his renal function was monitored regularly to adjust diuretic dose. there was no feature of end organ dysfunction

Pharmacological Therapy: intensive decongestive therapy. prior to opcab, the patient was put on frusemide infusion with oral ramipril and aldactone
Interventional Therapy: prior to off pump coronary artery bypass grafting (opcab), sts risk of mortality was 2.4%; repeat echocardiographic assessment revealed improvement of lvef to 15% and decrease in pasp to 30 mm hg and decrease in lv filling pressure; opcab was performed through median sternotomy; left ita was used for grafting left anterior descending artery (lad); after revascularizing lad, right ita (rita) and ra composite, graft was prepared; the distal end of rita was used for revascularizing the diagonal artery; there was significant improvement in systolic blood pressure after this distal anastomosis; after these two grafts, heart was lifted for lateral and posterior wall vessels; we make a longer skin incision, open the sternum widely, and release pericardium on the right side to displace the heart gradually; this was supplemented with headlow and lateral tilt position; liberal doses of inotropic support were used; ra was used for sequential grafting of obtuse marginal, posterior lv branch, and posterior descending artery; all these five distal anastamoses were performed uneventfully
Patient Outcome Assessment: the patient was electively ventilated for 2 days; echocardiography on 1st pod revealed improvement in lvef to 20%; he was started on low dose beta blockers after inotropic supports were weaned off; he had slow and uneventful recovery; echocardiography on 4th pod revealed improvement in lvef to 30%; he had persistent pleural drainage requiring prolonged intensive care unit stay; after pleural drainage subsided and drains were removed, he was discharged on diuretics, low dose beta blocker, and ramipril

before therapy the patient was a sickly boy in whom minor respiratory infections might precipitate a reye's syndrome–like crisis and a full cardiac arrest; with therapy his vulnerability to these episodes abruptly ceased; the plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate level, always below 0.1 mm before treatment, rose to 0.42 mm — within the normal range. the total plasma carnitine level was 30.1 µm — at the lower end of the normal range; we had at first assumed that systemic carnitine deficiency was due to an inherited deficiency of an enzyme responsible for its biosynthesis.' the very high urinary excretion was taken as convincing evidence of excellent absorption from the gastrointestinal tract, and our failure to achieve normal fasting plasma values was unexplained; Title: acoustic neuroma in a 7-year-old girl. report of a case.
Authors: Krause CJ;McCabe BF
Institution: department of otolaryngology, university of iowa, iowa city
Family History: no family history of neurofibromatosis or café au lait spots
Medical/Surgical History: a school audiogram obtained a year earlier showed a marked high tone hearing loss in the right ear with excellent low tone hearing; right temporal headaches had been noted only since the myelogram was performed; the child was the product of a normal pregnancy and delivery with normal growth and development
Signs and Symptoms: she presented for evaluation of a right facial nerve paralysis of seven weeks' duration; the onset of paralysis had been sudden and apparently spontaneous, with no history of cerebral trauma, vertigo, otalgia, or otorrhea preceding it
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: local otolaryngologist consultation (revealed a total sensorineural hearing loss on the right, normal csf pressure and protein determinations); posterior fossa myelogram (demonstrated no cerebellopontine angle filling defect, but with indeterminate visualization of the internal auditory canal); upon admission after partial recovery from paralysis: physical examination (revealed a well-nourished, well-developed child in no distress; no subcutaneous masses were present, although two small areas of hyperpigmentation were present in the lower lumbar area; facial nerve function on the right had returned completely except for slight weakness of the orbicularis oculi muscle; corneal reflexes were present in both eyes; the tympanic membranes were normal in appearance and mobile bilaterally; normal pain sensation was present in each external canal; cranial nerves 1 through 6 and 9 through 12 were intact and cerebellar tests were normal; there was a normal caloric response to ice water in the left ear, with no response to 20 ml in the right ear; in the left ear the srt was 4 db and discrimination 100%; no measurable hearing could be demonstrated in the right ear; tone decay and bekesy audiometry could not be done.); posterior fossa myelograms (suggested an enlarged internal auditory canal on the right; the myelogram revealed filling of each cerebellopontine angle, but the right internal auditory canal did not fill; there was a suggestion of a curvilinear defect 1 cm in diameter at the meatus); 3 months later when facial function on the right was complete: audiogram (unchanged from the previous one); repeat tomographs of the petrous apices (revealed an increase in size of the internal auditory canal on the right during the three-month interval)
Diagnosis: acoustic neuroma
Laboratory Values: NA
Pathology: histologic evaluation of the tumor revealed an interlacing (fig 3). these cells were noted to be epithelioid and often spindle-shaped. a few areas of loose reticular tissue with many foam cells (antoni tissue) were noted, and large vascular spaces occurred throughout. in addition, a capsule of fibrous tissue was present. the diagnosis was acoustic neuroma
Interventional Therapy: because the lesion was continuing to expand the internal auditory canal, it was felt that surgical excision should be carried out; the apparent small size of the tumor and the absence of inner ear function on that side were indications for a translabyrinthine approach; this was done on june 4, 1969, revealing a tumor measuring 17 mm in diameter; the facial nerve had been flattened into a ribbon by the enlarging mass; it was carefully dissected free of the tumor, which was then removed without difficulty; following this step, facial nerve continuity was verified with electrical stimulation at the level of the brain stem
Patient Outcome Assessment: postoperatively the patient did well except for a total facial paralysis on the right; she was discharged on the eighth postoperative day; the patient is now 15 months postoperative and doing very well; facial function on the right began four months following the procedure and at this time represents approximately 60% of normal function; hearing in the left ear remains normal
