Title: bilateral temporal bone encephaloceles after cranial irradiation. case report.
Authors: Lalwani AK;Jackler RK;Harsh GR 4th;Butt FY
Institution: department of otolaryngology-head and neck surgery, school of medicine, university of california, san francisco
Family History: experienced recurrent otitis media during childhood, but had no history of hearing loss, otalgia, otorrhea, otological surgery, meningitis, or significant head trauma; at 2 years of age, he was diagnosed as having acute lymphocytic leukemia; he was treated with vincristine, prednisone, and intrathecal methotrexate, and received 24 gy of whole-brain radiation therapy to opposing 15 x 16-cm fields with a linear accelerator; a maintenance regimen of 6-mercaptopurine, methotrexate, prednisone, and vincristine was continued for 3 years; at 7 years of age, the patient suffered a testicular relapse of the acute lymphocytic leukemia, which was treated with an additional 18 gy of radiation to the whole brain and 28 gy to the scrotum, as well as with vincristine, prednisone, and l-asparaginase; a maintenance drug regimen of 6-mercaptopufine and methotrexate was continued for 4 years
Medical/Surgical History: NA
Signs and Symptoms: middle ear mass that caused bilateral intermittent tonal tinnitus and a vague echo in the fight ear; at his current presentation, the patient's acute lymphocytic leukemia was in remission; he was receiving replacement testosterone and growth hormone to compensate for pituitary insufficiency; his intellectual development, which previously had been delayed, was normal; otoscopy of the right ear revealed a posterior mesotympanic mass with a pial vascular pattern; the anterior tympanic membrane was normal; the left tympanic membrane was minimally retracted; weber's and rinne's auditory tests showed no abnormalities; a 10- to 20-db low-frequency conductive hearing loss and normal sensorineural function were revealed on an audiogram; the speech reception threshold was 5 db, and the speech discrimination score was 100%; computerized tomography (ct) demonstrated a grossly dystrophic skull with widened internal auditory canals bilaterally; there was a soft-tissue mass in the right mesotympanum, epitympanum, and mastoid cavity; on the left side, the soft tissue was confined to the mastoid antrum ; magnetic resonance (mr) imaging demonstrated bilateral endaural encephaloceles, larger on the left than on the right, that were isointense with brain on t1-weighted images and showed minimal enhancement after administration of gadolinium ; basal temporal lobe had herniated through a 2-cm defect, which represented diastasis of the petrosquamous suture line, on the floor of the middle fossa; the encephalocele was not covered with dura and occupied the mastoid cavity; the arachnoid coveting of the encephalocele was only mildly hyperemic; herniated brain enveloped the ossicles, necessitating a tympanotomy to remove the encephalocele completely without causing ossicular injury; to minimize transmitted vibratory trauma, the ktp laser* (2 w, 0; l second) was used to vaporize the brain from the ossicular chain; the herniating temporal lobe appeared nonviable and was divided; the defect was repaired in three layers: a free temporalis fascia graft was placed intradurally, the inner table of the middle fossa craniotomy bone flap was placed extradurally along the middle fossa floor, and an inferiorly based temporalis muscle flap was placed between the dura and the bone graft ; six months after the operation, the left mastoid encephalocele was repaired through a middle fossa craniotomy and mastoidectomy; the defect in the petrosquamous suture line extended from the mallear head anteriorly to the junction of the transverse and sigmoid sinuses posteriorly; nonviable herniating temporal lobe was divided, and the defect was repaired in three layers with intradural temporalis fascia, temporalis muscle between the dura and the temporal floor, and cortical bone bridging the bone defect
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: weber's and rinne's auditory tests, audiogram, computerized tomography (ct), magnetic resonance (mr) imaging, mr image

Laboratory Values: NA

Pharmacological Therapy: vincristine, prednisone, and intrathecal methotrexate, and received 24 gy of whole-brain radiation therapy to opposing 15 x 16-cm fields with a linear accelerator, maintenance regimen of 6-mercaptopurine, methotrexate, prednisone, and vincristine was continued for 3 years, treated with an additional 18 gy of radiation to the whole brain and 28 gy to the scrotum, as well as with vincristine, prednisone, and l-asparaginase, maintenance drug regimen of 6-mercaptopufine and methotrexate was continued for 4 years, replacement testosterone and growth hormone
Interventional Therapy: combined tight transmastoid and middle fossa craniotomy procedure, tympanotomy to remove the encephalocele completely, ktp laser, herniating temporal lobe appeared nonviable and was divided , the defect was repaired in three layers: a free temporalis fascia graft was placed intradurally, the inner table of the middle fossa craniotomy bone flap was placed extradurally along the middle fossa floor, and an inferiorly based temporalis muscle flap was placed between the dura and the bone graft, left mastoid encephalocele was repaired through a middle fossa craniotomy and mastoidectomy, nonviable herniating temporal lobe was divided, defect was repaired in three layers with intradural temporalis fascia, temporalis muscle between the dura and the temporal floor, and cortical bone bridging the bone defect

Title: spontaneous intraventricular hemorrhage: a rare presentation of a skull base mesenchymal chondrosarcoma.
Authors: Laghari AA;Javed G;Khan MF;Ahmed SI;Nathani KR;Ahmed R

Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: computed tomography scan of the brain showed an isodense lesion arising from the left petroclival region occupying the left cerebellopontine angle and extending into the left middle fossa, with areas of calcification, bony destruction, brainstem compression, and distortion of the fourth ventricle; the lesion showed dense homogeneous contrast enhancement with no hydrocephalus; magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with and without gadolinium enhancement was ordered along with pure tone audiometry and ear, nose, and throat evaluation; a follow-up magnetic resonance imaging scan showed a large well-defined multilobulated extraaxial lesion extending from the left cerebellopontine angle and reaching up to the middle fossa with mass effect, minimal edema, and homogeneous gadolinium enhancement; , non-contrast computed tomography scan of the brain showed hemorrhage in bilateral lateral ventricles, third ventricle, and fourth ventricle and enlargement of the temporal horns, third ventricle, and lateral ventricles reflecting acute hydrocephalus; his coagulation profile including prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time were within normal range
Diagnosis: chondrosarcoma, mesenchymal, skull base neoplasms

Title: cardiac failure in a trisomy 9 patient undergoing anesthesia: a case report.
Authors: Riley CJ;Moore T;Eagelston L;Burkett D;Auerbach S;Ing RJ
Institution: department of anesthesiology, children's hospital colorado, aurora, colorado
Medical/Surgical History: her past medical history was significant for premature birth (as a twin born at 34 weeks' gestation), developmental delay, scoliosis, and ger; she exhibits mosaic trisomy of chromosome 9; all reviewed previous anesthetic records showed normal sinus rhythm as the patient's electrocardiogram (ecg) pattern; the patient's general anesthesia history included magnetic resonance imaging, tethered cord release/laminectomy, simple mastoidectomy, posterior spinal fusion, multiple nuclear medicine bone scans, dental surgery, and an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy; a review of the anesthetic records did reveal a history of moderate to severe obstruction with mask ventilation, but successful one-attempt direct visual laryngoscopies for intubation with cormack-lehane grade 1 or 2 views of the vocal cords; one previous attempt at using a laryngeal mask airway had been converted to an oral endotracheal tube (ett); also noted were 2 separate episodes of emesis on induction, both promptly treated with positioning, suctioning, and intubation; the first episode demonstrated decreased breath sounds on the left, but bronchoscopy and chest radiography showed no evidence of aspiration; the remainder of that anesthetic was uneventful; the second episode of emesis on induction occurred during a dental rehabilitation, and similarly no evidence of aspiration was identified on further investigation; the patient later showed signs of bronchospasm with oxygen saturations ranging from the low 80s% to mid 90s%, and the anesthetic was terminated after the most urgent dental needs were addressed; two other anesthetic records noted laryngospasm and coughing, easily treated, with uneventful courses thereafter
Signs and Symptoms: the patient was reportedly asymptomatic from a cardiac standpoint, although her mother mentioned that she had gained weight recently and perhaps tired more easily with exertion
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: she presented for a 2.5 hour dental rehabilitation with extractions under general anesthesia: physical examination before dental surgery (she exhibited a bulbous nose, low-set ears, and microcephaly; on the morning of surgery, she weighed 72.2 kg, her height was 138.1 cm, and her body mass index was 37.9 kg/m2; preoperative blood pressure was 118/87 mm hg measured in her right arm, pulse rate was 99/min and regular, respiratory rate was 16/min, and her peripheral oxygen saturation was 93% on room air; her chest and cardiac exams were within normal limits.); during surgery: ecg (demonstrated widened qrs segments suggestive of bundle branch block); physical examination (a decrease in blood pressure from 118/87 mm hg to 60/30 mm hg occurred, associated with possible st segment depression by ecg, but this was difficult to interpret in the presence of bundle branch block; the heart rate dropped to the low 70s.); after receiving medication during surgery: physical examination (simultaneously, oxygen saturation decreased from 97% to the low 70s%; breath sounds appeared diminished, especially in the left lung fields.); post surgery: transthoracic echocardiogram (these tests demonstrated an ejection fraction of 25–30% with left ventricular dilation and moderate systolic dysfunction; with the images thus obtained, a thrombus in the apex of the left ventricle could not be ruled out, nor could the coronary arteries be optimally visualized); repeat transthoracic echocardiogram (was unchanged from the intraoperative exam); repeat ecg (demonstrated left bundle branch block, which was then noted to be similar to an ecg from 7 years prior that was found during a deeper exploration of the patient's medical record)
Diagnosis: cardiac failure during anesthesia
Laboratory Values: lab work for acute myocardial injury was negative: creatine kinase-mb isoenzyme was 3.2 ng/ml (normal is 0–3.4) and troponin was <0.01 ng/ml (normal is 0–0.119). bnp was 94 ng/l (normal is <99)
Pathology: NA
Pharmacological Therapy: her daily medications included lansoprazole for ger, hydrocodone/acetaminophen for dental pain, as well as paroxetine and risperidone as mood-stabilizing medications. for this anesthetic before the dental surgery, we secured a 22-gauge peripheral intravenous (iv) catheter in the preoperative area. the patient received 2 mg iv midazolam for anxiolysis and was transported to the operating room. induction of anesthesia was carefully titrated with a total of 200 mg of propofol (2.8 mg/kg) over 6 minutes, 50 mg of lidocaine (0.7 mg/kg), and 100 mcg of fentanyl (1.4 mcg/kg). sevoflurane (1%) was initiated once the patient was asleep to aid with intubation. upon blood pressure drop after anesthesia induction, glycopyrrolate, crystalloid, and 3 ephedrine boluses, with a sluggish but adequate response. hemodynamics and oxygen saturation improved and remained stable for the remainder of the surgery, with the patient requiring 2 more boluses of ephedrine over the course of the dental treatment. the patient was maintained on sevoflurane (0.8–2%) combined with a propofol infusion (30–100 mcg/kg/min), and received a dose of 200 mcg hydromorphone approximately halfway through the anesthetic
Interventional Therapy: dental procedure after anesthetic induction: at the same time, standard american society of anesthesiologists monitors were placed; moderate obstruction was noted on mask ventilation; after administration of topical oxymetazoline, nasal intubation was successfully and atraumatically performed with a 6.0 nasal rae ett utilizing a size 4 glidescope (verathon, inc, bothell, wa, usa) as well as a red rubber catheter to guide the nasal rae through the right naris; there was no vomiting or esophageal regurgitation noted during intubation; oxygen saturation began to improve with 100% oxygen, airway suctioning, albuterol sprayed down the ett, and recruitment maneuvers, recovering to the mid to high 90s%; we placed a fiber optic scope down the ett to ensure correct positioning above the carina, as well as performed direct laryngoscopy to ensure that the cuff was below the vocal cords; the ett was secured in the appropriate location, but the patient would intermittently cough and buck, and the decision was made to use rocuronium to better control her ventilation; the anesthesia team had kept the patient spontaneously ventilating until this point; once she began to breathe over the ventilator, she was switched to pressure support ventilation, and then to spontaneous ventilation at the end of the case; after echocardiogram, the patient was extubated awake without incident
Patient Outcome Assessment: the patient was recommended for a computed tomography angiogram of the coronary arteries or a cardiac magnetic resonance imaging; she was discharged from children's hospital colorado post-op day 1, with newly prescribed lisinopril 5 mg and aspirin 81 mg once per day

Title: isolated cardiac metastasis from sacral chordoma.
Authors: Oda Y;Takada R;Koitabashi K;Kurasawa T;Inoue T;Suzuki H;Kawai S;Aoki K;Ohmiya K
Institution: department of internal medicine, tokyo koseinenkin hospital, japan
Medical/Surgical History: her past medical history included uterine fibroidectomy in 1969, gastrectomy (billroth 1 method) in 1989 for gastric cancer (adenocarcinoma), and local resection of a sacrococcygeal tumor in 1992, with re-excision 2 years later due to local recurrence; the diagnosis of chordoma was made then, and radiotherapy given postoperatively
Signs and Symptoms: shortness of breath on exertion occurring since october 1996, and edema of the face, neck, and lower limbs from 1 month later
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: physical examination (revealed a heart rate of 70 beats/min and blood pressure of 110/70 mmhg; heart sounds were diminished and a pericardial friction rub was audible, as well as a systolic ejection murmur maximal at the 4th interspace on the left sternal border; no hepatosplenomegaly was palpable, but the jugular venous pulse was raised); chest radiography (the cardiothoracic ratio was 74%, indicated cardiomegaly); ecg (low voltage in limb leads was seen); echocardiography (revealed a massive pericardial effusion and 3x5 cm tumor centered in the free wall of the right ventricle; the tumor could be clearly seen on the parasternal long-axis view to diffusely involve the right ventricle, causing outflow tract obstruction, which was suggestive of metastatic cardiac tumor); chest computed tomography scan (showed pericardial effusion and a large tumor along eth right ventricular wall that was not enhanced by contrast media); cardiac catheterization (revealed no significant right ventricle-pulmonary artery pressure gradient; right coronary arteriography showed outward deviation, likely due to the tumor, in the right ventricular branch, but no tumor filling the artery); postoperative: echocardiography (no pericardial effusionw as found, but the tumor was proliferative and invaded the right ventricle; with doppler flow measurement, the flow speed gradually increased in the right ventricular outflow tract; peripheral edema, having improved following the procedure, later recurred, so we planned excision of the right ventricle, even though it was more palliative than curative, because other modalities such as radiotherapy and chemotherapy are ineffective against this tumor)
Diagnosis: isolated cardiac metastasis from sacral chordoma
Laboratory Values: apart from mild anemia, no abnormalities were found in the blood tests, which included tumor markers. during the admission, pericardiocentesis was performed, yielding a bloody pericardial effusion. aspiration cytology revealed malignant cells, indicative of mucinous adenocarcinoma. the pericardial effusion showed high levels of lactate dehydrogenase (ldh) (3,585 iu/l), adenosine deaminase (32.6 iu/l), and hialuroic acid (5,710 ng/ml)
Pathology: because there was no recurrence of the pericardial effusion following pericardiocentesis, open biopsy was performed. histologically, the tumor cells were arranged in sheets, clusters, or trabeculae with chondroid stroma. the cytoplasm was markedly vacuolated or eosinophilic, positive for pas and diastase. these findings were identical to those for sacrococcygeal chondroma resected at another institution 6 years before. immunohistochemical staining gave the same results; namely, positive for s-100 protein, vimentin, cytokeratin and epithelial membrane antigens. sacroccocygeal chordoma metastasis to the right ventricle of the heart was diagnosed
Pharmacological Therapy: the patient is on anticoagulant therapy with warfarin after her procedures
Interventional Therapy: pericardotomy was performed via an oblique incision over the left costal margin, and 545 ml of bloody effusion was extracted; a solid scleroid tumor was observed on the diaphragmatic edge of the right atrioventricular groove; the tumor measured approximately 5 cm in diameter, and was relatively discrete with a smooth surface; after follow up echocardiography, removal of the right ventricle was planned even though it was more palliative than curative, because other modalities such as radiotherapy and chemotherapy are ineffective against this tumor; median sternotomy was performed, and after cardiac arrest was obtained using the usual cardioplegia, cardiopulmonary bypass was commenced; resection of the tumor, right ventriculoplasty and tricuspid valve replacement had been planned prior to the procedure, but as the extent of tumor infiltration was greater than expected, the planned procedures were abandoned; instead, direct anastomosis of the right atrium to the pulmonary artery using a vascular prosthesis (fontan procedure) was performed to correct impairment of the right ventricular inflow; after hte heart had resumed beating spontaneously, significant hypotension resulted in cardiac arrest and the prosthetic vessel failed to maintain blood flow
Patient Outcome Assessment: the only treatment options available now are palliative in nature, including radiotherapy, anticoagulationf or prevention of thromboses adherent to the tumor causing pulmonary emboli, and diuretics to reduce edema

Title: case records of the massachusetts general hospital. weekly clinicopathological exercises. case 47-1969.
Authors: NA
Institution: massachusetts general hospital
Medical/Surgical History: he was the product of a full-term, uneventful gestation and uncomplicated delivery; the weight at birth was 3.64 kg; was apparently healthy
Signs and Symptoms: for a routine examination, he was active, with normal color; the pulse was 120; no cardiac murmurs were heard; the liver was felt 3 fingerbreadths below the right costal margin, and the spleen was palpable below the left costal margin; three days later he vomited in the morning, and during the day episodes of rapid breathing were observed; the respirations were 80, and the pulse 140; his color was dusky; no murmurs were heard, and the breath sounds were normal; the liver and spleen were unchanged; dusky coloration; the patient was active, well nourished and alert, with an occasional cough; he was breathing rapidly and appeared slightly cyanotic while breathing room air; the length was 56 cm, and the weight 4.86 kg; diminished breath sounds and a few inspiratory rales were audible in the right-lung field; the point of maximum cardiac impulse was in the fifth intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line; the heart sounds were normal, and no rub, murmur or gallop was heard; the edge of the liver, which was not tender, was felt 2.5 cm below the right costal margin; the edge of the spleen was felt 2 cm below the left costal margin; the genitalia and extremities were normal; the femoral pulses were normal; neurologic examination was negative; the temperature was 99.2°f, the pulse 160, and the respirations 88; the blood pressure, by flush technic, was 60 systolic in the upper extremities and 80 systolic in the lower extremities; on the sixth hospital day the respirations were more rapid, and he became increasingly dusky; examination of the chest and abdomen revealed no change
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: an electrocardiogram demonstrated a normal sinus rhythm; the qrs axis and right ventricular predominance were normal for the patient's age, and the tracing was interpreted as within normal limits; an x-ray film of the chest revealed no change; fluoroscopic examination and x-ray films of the chest: moderate cardiomegaly involving all chambers and pulmonary vascular congestion; the cardiac and main-pulmonary-artery pulsations were normal, and the trachea and esophagus were normal; an electrocardiogram: disclosed a sinus rhythm at a rate of 160; the pr and qrs intervals were normal, and the axis was + 90°; cardiac catheterization and a pulmonary-artery angiographic study were performed on the seventh hospital day: the catheter was passed to the inferior periphery of the left lung, where a mean pressure of 25 mm of mercury was recorded, with marked respiratory swings at 90 per minute; pullback to the pulmonary artery showed a distinct stepup in pressure; the pulmonary-artery pressure was 85 systolic, 45 diastolic; the right atrial pressure and right ventricular end diastolic pressure were 10 mm of mercury; there was a distinct oxygen stepup at the atrial level in comparison with the inferior vena cava below the liver; no samples of blood were taken from the superior vena cava; biplane pulmonary-artery angiograms demonstrated slight enlargement of the main pulmonary artery; the circulation time was normal in the left upper lobe but delayed elsewhere; the contrast material from the left-upper-lobe veins drained into the left innominate vein, the superior vena cava and the right atrium; the drainage of the remaining pulmonary veins was not adequately visualized; the left atrium was well opacified; the left ventricle was poorly opacified; biplane angiocardiographic study was done with injection of contrast material into the main pulmonary artery; that vessel appears slightly enlarged
Diagnosis: cor triatriatum; anomalous drainage of left superior pulmonary vein into persistent left superior vena cava; pulmonary vascular obstruction; right ventricular failure; congenital stenosis of common pulmonary vein (cor triatriatum); partial anomalous pulmonary venous return (left pulmonary vein to persistent left superior vena cava)
Laboratory Values: the urine was normal. the hematocrit was 38 per cent, and the white-cell count 7900, with 37 per cent neutrophils, 45 per cent lymphocytes, 11 percent monocytes, 2 per cent eosinophils, 1 per cent basophils and 4 per cent atypical lymphocytes. the glucose was 102 mg per 100 ml. the sodium was 142 meq, and the potassium 4.8 meq per liter. the glutamic oxalacetic transaminase (sgot) was 31 units. cultures of the throat grew out beta-hemolytic streptococci, which were not group a; culture of a nasopharyngeal swab yielded no growth; culture of the stool was negative; partial pressure of oxygen was 60 mm of mercury, the partial pressure of carbon dioxide 35 mm of mercury, and the ph 7.38; a sample of arterial blood showed that the partial pressure of oxygen was 12 mm of mercury, the partial pressure of carbon dioxide 94 mm of mercury, and the ph less than 6.8
Pathology: at autopsy the heart weighed 42 gm, about half again the normal weight at this age. the anomalous left-upper-lobe pulmonary vein was drained by a persistent left superior vena cava, which passed anterior to the pulmonary artery into the left innominate vein. the right ventricle was dilated, with a hypertrophied myocardium 4 to 6 mm in thickness. the left ventricle appeared to be of normal size for the patient's age, with a myocardial thickness of 5 mm. the right atrium was normally formed. the left atrium was divided into two chambers by a diaphragm that passed from above the foramen ovale across the left atrium, roughly parallel to the plane of the mitral valve . the presence of this diaphragm in the absence of other major cardiac anomalies defines the condition known as cor triatriatum sinister. there were struts with the appearance of trabeculae arising from the left atrial wall and entering the substance of the diaphragm. blood from the right lung and left lower lobe entered normally into the posterosuperior chamber of the left atrium through three openings. the finding of two tiny foramina, of roughly 1 and 2 mm in diameter, in the diaphragm explains the clinical picture, which mimicked mitral stenosis physiologically. the normally formed foramen ovale was valvar and entered the left atrium between the abnormal diaphragm and the mitral valve, as is usually seen in cases of cor triatriatum. the mitral valve, the left ventricle and its outflow tract, the interventricular septum and the right side of the heart were all normally formed. the abnormal diaphragm of the left atrium was composed of myocardial and fibroelastic tissue. it is interesting that the endocardium of the left atrial posterosuperior chamber was thicker than that of the lower chamber, each consisting of fibrous tissue interspersed with elastic fibers
Pharmacological Therapy: oxacillin; ampicillin; digoxin; sodium bicarbonate and methylprednisolone sodium succinate (solu-medrol); morphine; ventilatory assistance
Patient Outcome Assessment: died

Title: hemicrania continua: beneficial effect of non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation in a patient with a contraindication for indomethacin.
Authors: Eren O;Straube A;Schöberl F;Schankin C
Institution: klinikum der universit€at m€unchen – neurologische klinik und poliklinik & deutsches schwindel- und gleichgewichtszentrum dsgz, munich, german
Keywords: hemicrania continua;treatment;indomethacin contraindication;non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation;gammacore;neuromodulation
Medical/Surgical History: patient reported hc in 1987, and controlled it for many years by indomethacin 150 mg/day; he developed several myocardial infarctions resulting in consecutive coronary artery stenting (rca 2010, 2012, lad, rcx 2013); he also took aspirin after these stenting operations; patient tried multiple medication trials (gabapentin, valsartan, celecoxib, melatonin, boswelia serrate, antidepressants including citalopram and amitriptyline) and these were unsuccessful for pain tolerance; only under continuous opioids (tilidine retard 100 mg, three times a day) with additional intake of opiods (tilidine gtt) when required (prn) up to four times a day was pain tolerable for the patient; but the continuous intake of tilidine presented other side effects: fatigue and problems related to concentration and attention which had a significant impact on his quality of life and ability to work
Signs and Symptoms: patient suffers from left-sided hc; patient wanted to control his hc via new methods given dissatisfaction with opioids and other medications he tried either due to their inability to control his pain or negative side effects
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: condition already established; patient was simply seeking new treatmentn options for an established diagnosis
Diagnosis: hemicrania continua, classified as a trigeminal autonomic cephalagia (tac)
Laboratory Values: NA
Pathology: NA
Pharmacological Therapy: treatment with tilidine prn was reduced from 4 times a day every day at the beginning of stimulation to 14/28 days completely free of acute medication in the first part of our study, and at least 9/27 days completely free of the acute medication in the second part of our study. but, regular intake of tilidine 100 mg three times a day was continued by our patient
Interventional Therapy: therapeutic trials with non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation with gammacore; the patient was advised to stimulate the left vagus nerve in the region of the ventral neck with a handheld (battery-driven) transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulator (gammacorevr ) according to the following protocol: (1) prophylactic stimulation: three times per stimulation of 90 seconds in the morning and evening with the maximum individually tolerated current intensity; (2) acute stimulation during exacerbations: additional three times per 90 seconds; the patient reached maximum stimulation levels provided by the device (40/40)
Patient Outcome Assessment: we saw a highly significant and constant decline of pain intensity during the exacerbation periods from initially 8/10 to 5/10 on the nas; this reduction of pain intensity took place immediately after the stimulation; our patient reported a significant increase of his individual working capability and a significat increase in his quality of life; the patient reported a subjective reduction in intensity of his permanent background pain

Title: skin necrosis complicated by warfarin-induced protein s deficiency.
Authors: Liaw TY;Chang CH
Journal: journal of the formosan medical association
Institution: department of dermatology, kaohsiung medical university hospital, kaohsiung, taiwan; department of dermatology, college of medicine, kaohsiung medical university, kaohsiung, taiwan; graduate institute of medicine, school of medicine, kaohsiung medical university, kaohsiung, taiwan
Medical/Surgical History: NA
Signs and Symptoms: multiple progressive painful ulcers and atrophie blanche over bilateral lower legs and feet for 4 months
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: biopsy
Diagnosis: warfarin-induced skin necrosis; protein s deficiency
Laboratory Values: prothrombin time was prolonged to 14.8 seconds (control: 10.7 seconds) and the international normalized ratio was 1.47. partial thromboplastin time was 28.8 seconds (control: 27.1 seconds); elevation of dedimer (0.6 mg/l, normal range: <0.55 mg/l) was noted. a de?ciency of protein s (29% activity, normal range: 55%e130%) was identi?ed without evidence for a de?ciency of protein c (105% activity, normal range: 80%e 132%). antithrombin iii, ?brinogen, clotting factors (viii, ix, xi), and von willebrand factor were all within normal ranges. serum homocysteine was not elevated and cryoglobulin was negative. survey of the autoimmune antibodies showed negative results. serum immunoglobulin g, immunoglobulin a, immunoglobulin m, complement 3, complement 4, c-reactive protein, complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, liver function, renal function, electrolytes, electrocardiography, stool, and urine examinations were all normal. parents and siblings of the patient were tested for serum protein c and protein s, which turned out to be normal

Title: an infant with dilated cardiomyopathy confirmed as myocarditis by endomyocardial biopsy.
Authors: Nishikawa T;Sekiguchi M;Kunimine Y;Momma K;Ando M;Takao A
Institution: heart institute of japan, tokyo women's medical college
Family History: there is no family history of heart muscle disease
Medical/Surgical History: there was no notable previous medical history and no preceding episode of viral infection; at birth, the delivery was uneventful and the weight was 3750 g
Signs and Symptoms: she was admitted for heart failure
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: physical examination (distant heart sounds and gallop rhythm without heart murmur were noted on admission); chest x-ray (showed cardiomegaly with a cardiothoracic ratio of 67% and pulmonary congestion); electrocardiogram (revealed decreased voltage, right axis deviation, tall p waves in leads ii and v1, rr' pattern in v3r and v1, and negative t waves in leads v3r-v5); two-dimensional echocardiography (demonstrated biventricular dilatation and global hypokinesis; the left ventricular end-diastolic dimension was 33 mm; fractional shortening and ejection fraction were 18.2% and 46%, respectively); cardiac catheterization (was performed on the 7th day of hospitalization; systolic pressure was 47.5 mmhg with end-diastolic pressure (edp) of 15 mmhg in the right ventricle and 85 mmhg with edp of 18 mmhg in the left ventricle; mean pulmonary wedge pressure was 19.5 mmhg; ventriculography showed an enlarged left ventricle with diffuse hypokinesis)
Diagnosis: dilated cardiomyopathy
Laboratory Values: the results of routine laboratory examinations including blood count, serum chemistry, serological test (c-reactive protein), and urinalysis were within normal limits. no significant increase in complement fixation titers for influenza a, influenza b, mumps, herpes, coxsackievirus b1-b5, and adenovirus was observed in paired sera
Pathology: endomyocardial biopsy employing konno's small bioptome from both ventricles was performed via the jugular vein and carotid artery during the catheterization. the right ventricular biopsy specimen showed marked interstitial cell infiltration composed of lymphocytes, macrophages, fibroblasts, fragmentation of muscle bundles, myocytolytic changes, hypertrophy, disarrangement of muscle bundles, abnormal branching of myocytes, and mild interstitial edema. the left ventricular biopsy specimen showed moderately increased interstitial fibrosis and interstitial cell infiltration, including fibroblasts and fibrocytes with fragmentation and disarrangement of muscle bundles
Pharmacological Therapy: she was treated with digitalis and diuretics
Patient Outcome Assessment: following treatment with digitalis and diuretics, heart failure was relieved and the patient was discharged after 1 month of hospitalization; six months after discharge, the patient was in good health, a chest x-ray showed normal cardiac size, and she required no drug treatment; echocardiography 6 years after discharge revealed no abnormality of wall motion of the left ventricle or abnormal thickness of the ventricular wall; ejection fraction of the left ventricle was within normal limits (68%)

Title: early-onset cerebellar ataxia, myoclonus and hypogonadism in a case of mitochondrial complex iii deficiency treated with vitamins k3 and c.
Authors: Toscano A;Fazio MC;Vita G;Cannavó S;Bresolin N;Bet L;Prelle A;Barbiroli B;Iotti S;Zaniol P;et al
Institution: univ messina policlin,neurol clin 2,i-98125 messina,italy
Keywords: early-onset cerebellar ataxia;myoclonus;mitochondrial complex iii deficiency;hypogonadotropic hypogonadism;31p-mr spectroscopy
Family History: the patient's parents were first-degree cousins
Medical/Surgical History: at age 9 years she started to complain of sudden episodes of falling to the ground without loss of consciousness, and of involuntary movements at the trunk and upper and lower limbs; at that time her eeg showed normal background activity and asynchronous slow spikes in the occipital regions with brief bursts of irregular diffuse spike and wave complexes; therapy with carbamazepine (cbz) and sodium valproate led to the disappearance of drop attacks but no improvement in myoclonus
Signs and Symptoms: when she was first seen in our department at age 16, she had an ataxic gait, nystagmus, hearing loss and repetitive myoclonic jerks at the tongue, trunk and four limbs exacerbated by movements and emotion; muscular hypotonia and areflexia were present but muscle strength was normal; there was scanning speech, mild dysartria and dysmetria; she was obese and showed some dysmorphic features such as a high-arched palate and a supernumerary nipple; her wechsler adult intelligence full- scale iq showed verbal and performance scores of 79 and 80 re- spectively; polygraphic recordings during wakefulness showed a normal background activity and rare asynchronous bilateral occipital slow spikes, which did not increase during sleep; intermittent photic stimulation did not evoke paroxysmal responses; action myoclonus was decreased in sleep but it was triggered by movements either in slow or rapid eye movement sleep; brain ct and mri revealed mild cortical and cerebellar atrophy; electromyography, motor and sensory conduction velocity study, single fibre electromyography, visual and brainstem auditory evoked potentials were normal, whereas somatosensory evoked potentials by median nerve stimulation showed a marked increase of p25/n33 complex that was about five times the control value; serum creatine kinase level was normal; resting blood lactate concentration was 2.64 mmol/1 [control values (c.v.) ranging from 0.6 to 2.2] and pyruvate 0.17 mmol/1 (c.v; from 0.09 to 0.14); after 15 min of exercise on a cycle ergometer, lactate concentration increased to 7.09 mmol/1 (c.v; 1.86, sd 0.64) and pyruvate to 0.25 mmol/1 (c.v; 0.12, sd 0.04); karyotype was 46,xx; at 16 years of age she developed secondary amenorrhoea; at age 17, because of myoclonus had worsend, clonazepam and l-5-hydroxytryptophan (l-5-h) were administered in addition to sodium valproate, and cbz was dis- continued, resulting in a suppression of myoclonus
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: endocrinological study; morphology quadriceps muscle biopsy specimen; 31p-mr spectroscopy
Diagnosis: electron transport complex iii deficiency
Laboratory Values: low levels of serum oestradiol [< 10 pg/ml; normal value (n.v.) 30-150] and progesterone (< 0.1 ng/ml; n.y. 3-12) were detected. basal follicle-stimulating hormone (fsh) values were in the nor- mal range but luteinizing hormone (lh) values were very low (< 0.6 mu/ml; n.y. 0.5-18) and the intravenous administration of gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (gnrh) (100 ~tg in bolus) did not increase the gonadotropin levels. further gnrh injections, 90 min after the first gnrh bolus and 1 week after a daily intramuscular gnrh administration (100 mu/ml), did not significantly modify lh and fsh secretion, suggesting a hypogonadotropic hypogonadism due to a pituitary deficiency. basal serum thyroid-stim- ulating hormone (tsh), prolactin (prl), growth hormone (gh), free thyroxine and cortisol were in the normal range. the tsh and prl increases after thyroid-releasing hormone injection (200 t,tg i.v.), the gh response to growth hormone-releasing hormone ad- ministration (t00 j,tg i.v.) and cortisol peak after cortisol-releasing hormone injection (100 btg i.v.) were also within the normal range. although the whole endocrinological investigation revealed the in- capacity of pituitary lh- and fsh-secreting cells to release go- nadotropins, therapy with clomiphene (50 mg daily for 5 days/ week) induced periodic menstrual cycles; genetics southern blot analysis demonstrated a normal pattern of muscle mitochondrial dna (mtdna). mtdna point mutations at nu- cleotide (nt) 8344 (merrf mutation) and 3243 (melas mutation) were absent. the former was sought using a polymerase chain reaction (pcr) amplification [23] with modified primers to create a bgl i restriction site in the presence of an a to g transition at nt 8344 [26] whereas the latter was carried out using pcr am- plification and restriction site analysis; mtdna was amplified us- ing forward oligonucleotide primer 3150-3170 and reverse com- plementary 3360-3380, and the pcr product obtained was then subjected to restriction with apai [17], in addition, sequencing of a pcr-amplified dna fragment, obtained with forward oligonu- cleotide 8200-8230 and reverse complementary 8460-8490 to analyse the mtdna trnaly~gene, showed its wild-type sequence
Pathology: quadriceps muscle biopsy specimen was processed; on gomori trichrome staining about 30% of the muscle fibres appeared vacuolated and had a ragged appearance, particularly type 1 fibres. periodic acid-schiff staining showed normal glycogen distribution. sudan black stain showed increased lipid droplets (fig. 1a) and on succinate dehydrogenase and cytochrome c oxidase stains widespread intermyofibrillary hyperactive dots were seen in type 1 fibres (fig. 1b). electron microscopy showed subsarcolemmal and intermyofibrillary mitochondrial proliferation in association with lipid droplets and sporadic crystal-like inclusions (fig. 1c); biochemistry biochemical investigation of isolated muscle mitochondria [7] re- vealed a marked reduction of rotenone-sensitive nadh-cyto- chrome c reductase and succinate-cytochrome c reductase activities and a slight decrease of succinate dehydrogenase (table 1). cyto- chrome b and ccx concentrations were reduced whereas cytochrome aa 3 was normal (table 1). this biochemical pattern suggested a bct complex deficiency (complex iii) [20] with a mild involvement of complex ii of the mrc. the free and total carnitine contents were within the control range in urine, blood and skeletal muscle. urinary screening for oligosaccharides and organic acids were normal.
Pharmacological Therapy: therapy with carbamazepine (cbz) and sodium valproate led to the disappearance of drop attacks but no improvement in myoclonus; at age 17, because of myoclonus had worsend, clonazepam and l-5-hydroxytryptophan (l-5-h) were administered in addition to sodium valproate, and cbz was discontinued, resulting in a suppression of myoclonus; although the whole endocrinological investigation revealed the in- capacity of pituitary lh- and fsh-secreting cells to release go- nadotropins, therapy with clomiphene (50 mg daily for 5 days/ week) induced periodic menstrual cycles.
Interventional Therapy: therapy in accordance with the therapeutic protocol used by eleff et al; [13] in a patient with complex iii deficiency, we started treatment with vitamins k3 (40 rag/day) and vitamin c (4 g/day) to bypass the metabolic block at the complex iii level; the patient was tested every month for 9 months with an exercise test to check lactacidaemia; 31p-mrs was performed after 5 and 9 months; vitamin therapy was not followed by any significant change in lactacidaemia, whereas after 3 months of therapy, ataxia was mildly reduced
Patient Outcome Assessment: NA

Title: combined prednisolone and pirfenidone in bleomycin-induced lung disease.

Title: afebrile multi-valve infective endocarditis caused by lactococcus garvieae: a case report and literature review.
Authors: Suh Y;Ja Kim M;Seung Jung J;Pil Chong Y;Hwan Kim C;Kang Y;Wook Sohn J;Kyung Yoon Y
Institution: 1) division of infectious diseases, department of internal medicine, university of ulsan college of medicine, korea 2) department of thoracic and cardiovascular surgery, university of ulsan college of medicine, korea 3) department of infectious diseases, university of ulsan college of medicine, korea 4) department of pathology, korea university college of medicine, korea

Medical/Surgical History: a mitral valve replacement three years prior due to severe mitral stenosis with rheumatic etiology

Laboratory Values: NA
Pathology: smear cytology of the endometrium did not detect any malignant cells. magnetic resonance imaging and computed tomography of the pelvis revealed a mass in the anterior wall of the uterus; grossly, the tumor occupied the almost whole myometrium without tumorous lesion at the endometrial surface, suggesting that it was of myometrial origin. ; the uterine cavity of the resected uterus was filled with bloody materials. the endometrium was thin with partial erosion with hemorrhage and necrosis. the cut surfaces of the uterus showed the thickened anterior wall with hemorrhagic nodules (fig. 1a and fig. s2d), and the tumor measured 5 × 6 × 4.5 cm in size. the tumor did not show a polypoid growth protruding into the uterine cavity, which is a typical feature of uterine cs. histologically, it was a biphasic tumor consisted of mesen- chymal component mainly composed of angiosarcoma and epithelial component. the angiosarcoma were immunopositive for factor viii, cd31, cd34, and erythroblast transformation specific related gene (erg). another mesenchymal component demonstrated features of undifferentiated sarcoma (fig. s1). on the other hand, the epithelial component showed poorly differentiated carcinoma consisted of various-sized nests of polygonal cells with atypical round nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm, focally showed squamous differentiation positive for cytokeratin, p63 and p40 and negative for er, pgr, synaptophysin, and chromogranin a by immunohistochemistry (fig. s1). the tubular structures were immunoreactive for cea and also contained periodic-acid-schiff stain and alcian blue-positive secretion, suggesting glandular differentiation. both the epithelial and mesenchymal components were immunohistochemically negative for hcg. the results of the immunohistochemical studies are summarized in table s1. venous invasion of the angiosarcoma was diffusely distributed in the myometrium, and the epithelial component also revealed vascular and lymphatic invasion. transitions from the epithelial component to angiosarcoma were seen in several foci (fig. s2a–c). for other findings, multiple adenomyotic foci were widely distributed throughout the myometrium and inside the tumor (fig. 1b–d), leading to a diagnosis of carcinosarcoma associated with adenomyosis, figo stage iiic. some of them had irregular architecture with nuclear enlargement. these atypical glands and the tumor cells of the cs were negative immunostaining for pten, while the normal endometrial glands and adenomyosis with no atypical glands were positive. we performed a genetic analysis of the pten, using the vysis pten/cep10 fish probe (abbott, tokyo, japan). the deletion of pten by fish analysis was not found in any lesion. in addition, p53 and k-ras mutations were analyzed. four minute targets representing normal tissue, adenomyotic lesion, carcinoma and sarcoma were sampled directly unstained sections, and genomic dna was extracted from each representative lesion. exons 5–8 of the p53 gene and exon 1 of the k-ras gene were examined by direct sequencing of pcr products. no mutation of the analyzed p53 and k-ras gene was detected in any lesion
Interventional Therapy: total transabdominal hysterec- tomy and salpingo-oophorectomy were carried out

microscopic examination. the whole brain and spinal cord were formalin fixed for 3 weeks for the neuropathological examination. slight cerebral atrophy was evident, the meninges presented congestion, and mild focal atherosclerotic changes of the circle of willis arteries were found. on the surface of the left parietal lobe an excavation 3 / 2 cm was noticed. the whole brain cut sections disclosed multifocal decay in the form of irregular yellowish-rusty partially cystic foci within the white matter 0.5-5 cm, especially in parietal and temporal lobes (fig. 1a, b). moreover, discoloration, foci of spongy degeneration and lacunae of frontal white matter, and status cribrosus of the pons, basal ganglia, cerebellum, and the spinal cord were found (fig. 1c, d). a few bigger cystic foci with scarring were also present. the ventricular system showed dilatation. single linear cortical softening up to 1.5 cm in the left temporal region was observed. many topographically oriented samples were taken from the brain and the spinal cord for histopathology according to neuropathological recommendations [12]. all sections were stained with he, and further the selected sections were stained with histochemical methods – pas, masson trichrome, van gieson, gomori, spielmayer, and congo red. immunohistochemistry was performed with a routine procedure using anti-sma and gfap antibodies (anti smooth muscle actin, anti gfap; flex, dako) according to the producer’s description, with pt-linker for antigen retrieval; histological examination of the central nervous system (cns) showed multifocal metachronous vasogenic changes (fig. 1e–h). they were located primarily in the white matter of the whole cns, in the form of tissue rarefaction, as well as old and subacute ischemic infarcts of different size with foamy macrophages surrounded with the astroglial reaction. perivascular spaces were in general enlarged, containing focal hemosiderin deposits. status cribrosus and lacunaris, a few foci of recent cerebral softening, as well as confluent postapoplectic cysts were the next prominent findings. the relatively spared white matter showed demyelination with u-fibers sparing, intensive in periventricular regions. the arterioles and arteries of small and medium size, within the cerebrum, meninges, cerebellum, spinal cord, and the nerve roots exhibited specific changes (fig. 2a). the arteriolar wall was markedly thickened with a consequent vascular lumen narrowing. hypertrophic and degenerated, swollen myocytes with distinct hyperchromatic nuclei were seen within the media of many vessels. moreover, many vessels presented medial bluish discoloration, with accumulation of slightly brownish granular deposits (fig. 2b). consecutive fibrosis and hyalinization progressing from the external part of the vascular wall was seen in different stages up to completely glazed vessels. masson staining emphasized this phenomenon well (fig. 2e). pas staining visualized granular basophilic material within the vascular media (fig. 2c, d). sma immunohistochemical reaction revealed degeneration of medial smooth muscle cells (fig. 2f) along with depletion and thinning of this layer. the congo-red stain was negative. ultrastructurally, gom presence was confirmed in the form of round granular deposits located in smooth muscle cell/pericyte membrane infoldings (fig. 2g). the analysis of the systemic organ sections revealed that the small arteries in the liver, kidneys, fat tissue, and spleen presented analogous abnormalities, although of a lesser intensity (fig. 2h). all above findings supported the diagnosis of cadasil. the members of the patient’s family were informed about the diagnosis and hereditary character of the disease, but Laboratory Values: laboratory findings on admission were as follows: white blood cell count, 24.9x103/mm3 with left shift, red blood cell count, 5.17x103/ mm3, hemoglobin 17.3 g/dl, and hematocrit, 52.6%; c reactive protein, 29.9 mg/dl (normal <0.3 mg/dl), serum creatinine, 0.9 mg/dl, fibrinogen, 108 mg/dl (144-303 mg/dl), serum total bilirubin, 2 mg/dl, blood glucose, 190 mg/dl
Pathology: at laparotomy, the distal portion of the appendix was found to be adhered to the retroperitoneum with periappendiceal abscess formation. from its midportion to its tip, the appendicular tissue was necrotic, while the rest was merely inflammed. ascitis was noted, and the abscess was ruptured during appendectomy; histologically, the appendix showed phlegmonous and gangrenous inflammation, but neoplastic cells infiltrating through the mucosa to the subserosa were also found. the cancer cells involved only the tip of the appendix, and the surgical margin was free of malignant infiltration. in the mucosa, there were many tumoral goblet cell-like cell nests with mucin production (figs. 1 and 2), and in some areas, acinar and glandular formation or short cords were present (figs. 3 and 4). there was periappendiceal connective tissue and perineural invasion, but only slight vascular infiltration. nuclear atypia was slight, and mitotic configuration was not encountered. the appearance of the mucosa epithelium was normal. almost all tumoral cells that resembled goblet cells were stained by pas (neutral mucin), mucicarmin, and ab (acid mucin). argyrophil and argentaffin cells (endocrine differentiation) were frequently encountered among the tumoral cells (fig. 4-a), but the mucin-producing cells were predominant. immunoperoxidase reaction for chromogranin-a (fig. 4-b) was positive in a high percentage of the goblet cell-like nests, and some neoplastic cells were also stained by ab, when double staining was done (amphicrine cells). only a few tumoral cellspossibility of pericecal or peritoneal seeds, perhaps originally obscured by the presence of periappendiceal abscess (which was ruptured during the first operation). histologically, the resected specimens did not show any evidence of metastasis or invasion

Title: recovery of ventricular function with a left ventricular axial pump in a patient with end-stage toxic cardiomyopathy not a candidate for heart transplantation: first experience in spain.
Authors: Castells E;Roca J;Miralles A;Manito N;Ortiz D;Gonzalez J;Granados J;Benito M;Rabasa M;S'braga F;Toscano J;Toral D;López A;Fontanillas C
Institution: department of cardiac surgery, bellvitge university hospital idibell, hospitalet de llobregat, barcelona, spain
Medical/Surgical History: there was no history of heart disease, chest pain, alcohol abuse, or rheumatic fever; had one uneventful full-term pregnancy at the age of 23 years
Signs and Symptoms: symptoms at rest of progressive heart failure for 4 months
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: echocardiogram (her ejection fraction was 23% with inotropic treatment, the left ventricle was slightly dilated, and right ventricular function was almost normal)
Diagnosis: end-stage toxic cardiomyopathy
Laboratory Values: NA
Pathology: NA
Pharmacological Therapy: after her operation for breast cancer, she was treated with doxorubicin (300 mg/m2 from october 2005 to january 2006) and trastuzumab (2 mg/kg per week from march to october 2006). standard medical treatment with angiotensin-converting enzymes inhibitors, ?-blockers, and aldosterone antagonists at the highest tolerated doses was initiated after implantation of the left ventricular axial pump. over the following months, we observed 2 problems. first, the patient had a genetic resistance to antivitamin k anticoagulants and despite very high doses of acenocumarol or warfarin (both agents were tried), an international normalized ratio between 2.5 and 2.8 was rarely achieved, and during most of her stay she needed additional anticoagulation with subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin as well as aspirin and dypiridamol
Interventional Therapy: heart transplantation was contraindicted at this point; after 3 weeks, we decided to implant a left ventricular axial pump (incor), as a long-term therapy, as a bridge to heart transplantation 4 years later if the cancer remained in remission; on june 5, 2007 we implanted the pump under extracorporeal circulation and induced ventricular fibrillation, during the connection of the inflow cannula to the apex of the left ventricle; afterward, we sutured the outflow cannula of the device to the ascending aorta; the driver cable was tunnelled in the abdomen and through a hole in the skin; it was connected to the control unit; the pump flow administered was 4.5–4.6 l/m
Patient Outcome Assessment: by the end of the fourth month postoperatively, the left ventricular ejection fraction was 55% and remained so after reducing the pump flow to a minimum; after 135 days of support, we removed the device without extracorporeal circulation; the immediate postoperative course was again uneventful; after 2 weeks, she was discharged home in good condition; now, after 1.5 years, she is leading an active life and the left ventricular ejection fraction is currently 57%, under standard medical treatment

Title: a child with severe relapsing kawasaki disease rescued by il-1 receptor blockade and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.
Authors: Cohen S;Tacke CE;Straver B;Meijer N;Kuipers IM;Kuijpers TW
Institution: pediatric hematology, immunology and infectious diseases, academic medical center, amsterdam, the netherlands; pediatric cardiology, academic medical center, amsterdam, the netherlands; pediatric intensive care, erasmus medical center, rotterdam, the netherlands
Medical/Surgical History: had a history of progressive heart failure for 4 months, with symptoms at rest and need for treatment with dobutamine; had undergone bilateral resection for breast cancer; after the operation, was treated with doxorubicin (300 mg/m2 from october 2005 to january 2006) and trastuzumab (2 mg/kg per week from march to october 2006); she began to experience symptoms at the end of the treatment; after receiving medical treatment after the implantation of the left ventricular axial pump, had 2 had 2 transient ischemic cerebrovascular events, coinciding with suboptimal anticoagulation andbefore the next dose of low-molecular-weight heparin; second, there was an increasing frequency of suction events despite adequate preload, specially after 3 months of implantation; this caused nonsustained ventricular arrythmias and episodes of pump malfunction that resolved after reduction of the flow rate; these suction events were probably related to the nondilated left ventricle and the progressive recovery of the ventricular function; these complications did not allow the patient to be discharged home, despite the fact that was able to walk inside and outside and near the hospital
Signs and Symptoms: persistent fever, coughing and swollen cervical lymph nodes; he developed a rash, conjunctivitis and swollen extremities; the child was lethargic; tachycardia and hypotension developed the next day; fever;rash and skin desquamation subsequently reappeared
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: echocardiography showed diminished shortening fraction of 20% without caa; echocardiography showed dilations of the left descending (lad) and right coronary artery (rca); echocardiography at day 53 showed progression to giant caas; the maximal coronary artery diameter observed during admission was 6.6 mm (z-score 16.9) for the lad and 7.5 mm (z-score 16.2) for the rca; coronary angiography after 6 months showed normalisation of his coronary arteries (figure 2), which was unexpected in such a severe case of kd
Diagnosis: kd-associated myocarditis; respiratory and circulatory failure
Laboratory Values: increased c reactive protein (340 mg/l); his blood pro-b natriuretic peptide levels had risen to >70 000 ng/l (normal value <100 ng/l); escherichia coli was cultured from his urine
Pathology: NA
Pharmacological Therapy: empirical antibiotic treatment; ivig administration (2 g/kg); a second dose of ivig (2 g/kg) ; multiple methylprednisolone pulses; il-1ra was started (anakinra once daily, 1 mg/kg subcutaneously); ivig with low-dose prednisone; antibiotics
Patient Outcome Assessment: coronary angiography after 6 months showed normalisation of his coronary arteries, which was unexpected in such a severe case of kd

Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: physical examination (distended abdomen; large mass obscured splenic exam); mri of abdomen (revealed a markedly enlarged nodular liver extending into the pelvis, with areas of t1 and t2 hyperintensity as well as enlargement of the tail of the pancreas); a positron emission tomography ct scan (found abnormal metabolic activity in the pancreatic tail mass, heterogenous and patchy metabolism in the liver, and low grade but abnormal metabolic activity in the left axilla concerning for metastatic disease); octreotide scan (revealed increased uptake in the tail of the pancreas, diffuse hepatic uptake, and no definite uptake in the left axilla, where a previous pet ct scan had demonstrated activity); bone scan (negative for skeletal metastases); echocardiogram (revealed mild mitral valve prolapse with trace regurgitation); head ct scan (normal); repeat octreotide scan after transplant (demonstrated 3 new foci in the abdomen located beneath the right hemidiaphragm in the region of the epigastrium and medial to the lower pole of the right kidney, as well as focal uptake int he left suprarenal region); repeated mri of the abdomen and pelvis (did not demonstrate soft-tissue abnormalities beneath the hemidiaphragm, within the epigastric tissue or int he left suprarenal region as identified on previous octreotide scan); ct scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis (revealed a sclerotic lesion in the right transverse process of l1 vertebral body corresponding to findings on mri); repeated mri of abdomen and pelvis after second round of chemotherapy (demonstrated stable enhancing focus of signal abnormality in the right li transverse process); mri of spine (reveals abnormal signal involving the right transverse process of li, differential diagnosis includes metastatic lesion versus an incidental lesion such as an osteoid osteoma; in addition a disc bulge at l4-l5 and l5-s1 without evidence of central spinal canal stenosis or neural foraminal narrowing was noted); octreotide scan (revealed interval resolution fo the previously identified pentatreotide-avid foci)

Laboratory Values: laboratory evaluation revealed a fasting serum gastrin level of >100,000 pg/ml (normal<125 pg/ml) and a serum chromogranin a level of 10,300 ng/ml (normal<50 ng/ml). aspartate aminotransferase 42, alanine aminotransferase 21, alkaline phosphatase 98, lactate dehydrogenase 158, albumin 5.1, beta human chorionic gonadotrophin<2, alphafetoprotein 3, ammonia 54, amylase 83, and lipase 11.4. evaluation for multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 was negative: serum calcium, parathyroid hormone, prolactin, insulin-like growth factor-1, and thyroid function tests were normal. after liver transplant, the patient's serum gastrin level decreased to <1000 pg/ml. laboratory investigation after chemotherapy included serum gastrin level of 188 pg/ml and chromogranin a level of 1154 ng/ml. after repeated chemotherapy, serum gastrin level was 295 pg/ml and chromogranin a level was 168 ng/ml
Pathology: an ultrasound-guided liver biopsy confirmed metastatic gastrinoma; immunostains for chromogranin, synaptophysin, gastrin, and somatostatin receptor were strongly positive, stains for insulin and glucagon were negative. the ki67 index was approximately 3%. pathology after resection revealed disseminated intrahepatic metastases occupying approximately 80% of the liver parenchyma, ki67 index of approximately 2%. periportal lymph nodes (3 of 3) were positive for metastatic gastrinoma. disease was documented in 4 of 6 peripancreatic lymph nodes, with a ki67 index of 7%. vascular invasion was identified although the pancreatic and radial surgical margins were negative
Pharmacological Therapy: the patient was started on omeprazole and octreotide 100 mcg/dose twice daily before transplant. the patient began tacrolimus and sirolimus approximately 3 weeks after transplant. the patient received adjuvant chemotherapy per children’s oncology group protocol ahep0731 regimen f, a therapeutic study designed for children with hepatoblastoma, with cisplatin, doxorubicin, 5-flurouracil, and vincristine, but did not receive subsequent weekly doses of vincristine secondary to toxicity. the patient's side effects from chemotherapy were managed with histamine blockers, proton pump inhibitors, an octreotide drip, which was transition to subcutaneous injectiosn and subsequently to octreotide long-acting repeatable depot. the patient continued to receive immune modulation therapy with tacrolimus and sirolimus. after repeated mris and ct scans showing a sclerotic lesion in the right transverse process of l1 vertebral body, the patient again received chemotherapy with cisplatin, doxorubicin, 5-flurouracil, and vincristine, followed by granulocyte colony stimulating factor rescue
Interventional Therapy: she underwent a living related liver transplant with resection of the gallbladder, distal pancreas, and spleen
Patient Outcome Assessment: the patient remains asymptomatic >2 years after transplant and chemotherapy; since completion of chemotherapy, serum gastrin and chromogranin a levels remain <200 and 150 ng/ml, respectively; the patient continues to receive octreotide 10 mg intramuscularly monthly, sirolimus and tacrolimus

Title: case records of the massachusetts general hospital: case 5-2014: 2014: a 59-year-old man with fever, confusion, thrombocytopenia, rash, and renal failure.

Title: growth and regression of arteriovenous malformations in a patient with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. case report.
Authors: Du R;Hashimoto T;Tihan T;Young WL;Perry V;Lawton MT
Institution: department of neurological surgery, brigham and women's hospital, harvard medical school, boston, massachusetts, usa
Family History: in a linkage analysis, the patient’s father, father’s sister, father’s sister’s son, paternal grandmother, and paternal grandmother’s mother were genetically confirmed to have mutations in eng on chromosome 9 (fig; 4); there was no evidence of linkage to acvrl1 (also known as alk-1) on chromosome; the patient’s father, father’s sister, and paternal grandmother had frequent epistaxis; the father’s sister also had telangiectasias; the father’s sister had a child who died on day 1 of life due to an intracerebral hemorrhage, which on autopsy was confirmed to have been caused by an avm; this woman has another child who is asymptomatic; the paternal grandmother also had avms
Medical/Surgical History: well until one month earlier, when facial palsy developed and resolved in about one week; six days before entry a sore throat appeared, without fever or other symptoms; a physician prescribed penicillin taken by mouth, but the sore throat worsened and the patient began to feel progressively weaker, with difficulty in walking; three days before admission she came to this hospital, where examination showed that the temperature was 38.7°c; erythema without an exudate was noted over the left tonsil; a throat swab was obtained for culture, and benzathine penicillin was injected intramuscularly; the patient remained unimproved; her weakness worsened, and in the next two days she experienced chilliness; one day before entry she vomited several times, without noticing whether there was blood in the vomitus; on the following day was admitted to the hospital; the patient was a native of portugal who immigrated to the united states 19 years earlier; she spoke no english; a hysterectomy was performed seven years before admission; the patient had traveled to portugal five months before admission and returned in the following month, without obvious illness in that interval; had lost an unknown amount of weight during the five weeks before entry while on a low-fat diet; there was no history of dyspnea, cough, paranasal sinus pain, abdominal pain, urinary frequency, dysuria, or urgency, photophobia, stiff neck, exposure to communicable disease, heart disease, hepatitis, tuberculosis, seizures, rheumatic disease, renal disease, hématologie disorder, night sweats, tick bites, or receipt of blood transfusions; she used no tobacco and little alcohol
Signs and Symptoms: generalized seizure; the patient did not open his eyes to pain but symmetrically moved all four extremities in response to light touch; the patient had right hemiparesis postoperatively, which improved rapidly over the course of 2 weeks
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: head ultrasonography performed in utero at 37 weeks’ gestation and at birth were normal; a head ct revealed a 3.5×2.5 cm left frontopari-etal intraparenchymal hemorrhage; results of mr imaging of the brain showed a left parietal hematoma with subarachnoid and intraventricular extension; there were multiple foci of t 2 signal abnormality in the left frontal lobe, bilateral medial occipital lobes, left caudate nucleus, and left thalamus, which could represent small hemorrhages from telangiectases or avms; a cerebral angiogram revealed a 3.6×2.5×1.9 cm spetzler–martin grade iii avm in the left parietal lobe with superficial drainage into the superior sagittal sinus there was also a smaller 1.5-cm left parasagittal frontal avm with superficial venous drainage; two areas of hypervascularity were seen in the left frontal lobe and left temporal lobe without obvious shunting; chest and abdominal cts showed no vascular abnormalities; an mr image obtained 5 months later showed no significant changes; an angiogram obtained 5 months after the initial hemorrhage revealed an unchanged avm in the left parietal lobe, although the smaller left parasagittal frontal avm was less evident compared with its appearance on the previous angiogram; two new avms with early venous shunting had been previously seen as areas of abnormal hypervascularity: 1) a 1.5-cm left frontal lobe avm supplied by the middle cerebral artery; and 2) a 2-cm diffuse region of hypervascularity with some shunting in the anterior left temporal lobe that drained into the sphenopa-rietal sinus; a postoperative angiogram showed complete resection of the left parietal avm
Diagnosis: hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, cerebral arteriovenous malformation, cerebral hemorrhage
Laboratory Values: NA
Pathology: histopathological and immunohistochemical studies. staining with h & e, and van gieson and elastin showed abundant abnormal vessels with and without internal elastica as well as multiple infarcts and foci of hemorrhage with mineralization in the cortex, which are consistent with an avm. immunohistochemical stainings were performed on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissues by using antigen retrieval and the avidin-biotin meth-od. nuclear ki 67 protein expression was detected using the mab mib-1 (1:500 dilution, dakocytomation). the mab to cd34 (1:500 dilution, dakocytomation) was used to identify endothelial cells. the ki 67–positive endothelial cells can be seen indicating the presence of proliferating cells. the mabs to cd45 (1:100 dilution, dakocytomation) and cd68 (1:1500 dilution, dakocyto-mation) were used for the detection of lymphocytes and macrophages, respectively. 7 staining for cd45 and cd68 showed inflammatory cells in the vessel wall and perivascular region as well as in the intervening brain parenchyma. staining for cd45 and cd68 in a patient with a sporadic avm that hemorrhaged 2 days before resection demonstrated a similar distribution of inflammatory cells, whereas the stainings in a patient with an unruptured sporadic avm revealed many fewer inflammatory cells
Interventional Therapy: bifrontopa-rietal craniotomy for complete removal of the avm
Patient Outcome Assessment: at the 4-month follow up, the hemiparesis had completely re-solved; the patient has had no seizure episodes since the surgery

Title: autoimmune sensorineural hearing loss as presenting manifestation of paediatric behçet disease responding to adalimumab: a case report.

Institution: department of pediatrics, university of chieti, via dei vestini 5, chieti 66100, italy

Signs and Symptoms: a vestibular viral neuritis was diagnosed and the boy was continuously treated with oral steroids with partial improvement; on admission the boy was conscious, his body temperature was 37°c and blood pressure was within normal limits (100/60 mm hg); he had dizziness, horizontal nystagmus which was aggravated by head movements; he was not able to sit or stand up; romberg’s sign and head-thrust test were positive; no visual problems, meningeal signs, clonus or pathologic reflexes were noted; both tympanic membranes were normal; the haplotype hlab52 was found; audiometry revealed bilateral sensorineural hearing loss; two months later, however, febrile episodes recurred with associated oral ulcers, dizziness and tinnitus; at that time, eye examination showed anterior uveitis and retinitis in the right eye; endoscopic video capsule showed a few ulcers surrounded by healthy mucosa in jejunum and ileum; the association of oral ulcers, uveitis, recurrent fever and neuro-vestibular symptoms suggested bd; three months later, however, a new flare up of disease was observed
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: magnetic resonance imaging (mri) performed on day 7 post onset of symptoms excluded cerebral and brainstem lesions; audiometry revealed bilateral sensorineural hearing loss; chest x-ray, abdomen ultrasound and brain mri excluded any abnormality; an electroencephalogram showed normal results; colonoscopy and esophagogastroduodenoscopy were normal whereas endoscopic video capsule showed a few ulcers surrounded by healthy mucosa in jejunum and ileum; abdominal mri, however, excluded intestinal crohn's disease; follow-up audiometry, laboratory evaluation and ocular screening recorded normal values; in our patient, diagnosis was delayed and was possible only when the classic symptoms of bd disease appeared and one could assume that the ongoing steroid therapy contributed to delay the onset of symptoms and therefore the correct diagnosis

Interventional Therapy: the boy was continuously treated with oral steroids with partial improvement; an autoimmune audio-vestibular disease was suspected, the boy was treated with methylprednisolone (2 mg/kg/day); after clinical improvement, a few weeks later, steroid therapy was gradually tapered and discontinued

a grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur, so-called scratchy murmur, was heard most strongly along the left lower sternal border; lungs were clear on percussion and auscultation; hepatosplenomegaly was not observed); laboratory investigations (mild polycythemia); chest x-ray (disclosed mild cardiomegaly and a somewhat globular appearance to the overall cardiac silhouette; relative pulmonary hypovascularity was also demonstrated); electrocardiogram recorded when the patient felt no palpitation (showed a regular sinus rhythm with complete right bundle branch block and pulmonary p wave; qrs axis was +100' and non-specific st-t changes were found in lead iii., avf, and from v1 through v4; the ecg during the palpitation attack demonstrated a fairly regular rate of 86/min with almost the same qrs configuration as that taken before the attack; furthermore, we could not find an apparent p wave preceding qrs complex in the electrocardiogram during the attack); echocardiogram (tricuspid valve closed 70 msec after the closure of the mitral valve; the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve was found markedly displaced interiorly within the right ventricle); simultaneous recodings of intracavity potentials and pressures (disclosed the existence of the atrialized right ventricle, which showed the right atrial pressure pulse with intracardiac potentials of the right ventricle); intracardiac catheters used for electrophysiologic study (at the sinus rhythm, pa interval was 20 msec, ah interval 120 msec, and hv interval40 msec; wenckebach phenomenon in the av node appeared at the cycle length of 600 msec in repeat atrial pacing; effective and functional refractory periods of the av node were 645 msec and 690 msec respectively; these findings may indicate a deteriorated av nodal function; jump up phenomenon in the av conduction curve was not detected; va conduction through av node and concealed bypass tract was not found by repeat ventricular pacing; each v wave was preceded by his bundle depolarization with a hv interval of 40 msec; there was no retrograde his potential; the atrium was depolarized following his bundle depolarization; the high right atrium was activated earlier than the atrium recorded in the his bundle electrogram; the rate of atrial depolarization was nearly the same as that of his bundle depolarization; these electrophysiologic findings during the palpitation attack may indicate that this was an ectopic junctional tachycardia associated with isorhythmic av dissociation; we evaluated the simultaneous recording of right atrial pressure pulse and intracavitary electrogram; at the sinus rhythm, v: wave was slightly elevated, probably due to tr; once the tachycardia was initiated, however, right atrial pressure increased about twice as much as at the sinus rhythm, and then, the patient began to feel palpitation; the tachycardia occurred abruptly after a single atrial or ventricular premature contraction, resembling the form of an escape rhythm; however, the interval between the ventricular wave of the premature beat and that of the first junctional beat was shorter than that during the sinus rhythm; the cycle length of the ventricular depolarizations during the tachycardia was shorter than that during the sinus rhythm; other electrophysiologic procedures such as repeat atrial and ventricular pacing or atrial and ventricular extrastimulus methods failed to initiate the tachycardia; the termination came only after the timely depolarization of the atrium or after a single vpc; it was followed by regular sinus rhythm
Diagnosis: ectopic junctional tachycardia in ebstein's anomaly
Laboratory Values: there was a mild polycythemia; red blood cell count was 560 x 10^4/mm3, hemologin 17.2 g/dl, and hematocrit 51.6%. other hemogram tests, urinalysis, and blood chemical surveys were all within normal range

Pharmacological Therapy: we administered a small dose of disopyramide (200 mg/day, 3 x 1, po) to suppress the appearace of apc and/or vpc

Diagnosis: blount disease, associated femoral osteochondroma
Laboratory Values: NA
Pathology: NA
Interventional Therapy: the deformity was treated by asymmetric physeal distraction, applying a modified wagner fixator-distractor device (jacquet-howmedica, geneva, switzerland), which allows epiphyseal pin placement and progressive angular correction (5,8); in brief, a first modification consisted of substituting one of the conventional screw-holder clamps by a t-shaped clamp (t piece), which allowed the insertion of the epiphyseal screws perpendicular to the diaphyseal screws; second, to convert the longitudinal distraction applied to the device into an angular movement of the epiphyseal screws, a washer was interposed between the t piece and the body of the wagner device, leaving a free-moving hinge at the proximal end of the apparatus; , the device was assembled by using predrilled, self-tapered, 6-mm diameter screws (apex; howmedica, geneva, switzerland); an image intensifier was used to check the proper insertion of the screws; osteotomy of the fibula was not required; distraction started 24 h after surgery at a rate of 1.5 mm/day (2 × 0.75); the correction was completed in 25 days; at that moment, the free-moving hinge was blocked until the removal of the device; , full weight bearing was allowed from the first day after surgery, but the patient could do it comfortably only after 15 days; although the patient was encouraged to maintain the knee range of motion actively, some restriction of knee flexion was observed throughout the treatment period; the wagner device was removed in the outpatient clinic without anesthesia 10 weeks after surgery; the patient did not require any additional period of inmobilization and regained full range of knee motion a few days after the removal of the fixator
Patient Outcome Assessment: premature complete closure of the operated-on physis took place 6 months before the closure of the contralateral proximal tibial growth plate; the patient has been followed-up for 4 years; at last assessment, the correction was well maintained, and no leg-length discrepancy was observed; the range of motion showed no restrictions; the patient was asymptomatic and able to live a completely normal life including contact sport activities
