Title: zollinger-ellison syndrome with subsequent association of insulinoma.
Authors: Rustagi T;Siegel RD
Institution: department of internal medicine, university of connecticut. farmington, ct, usa. division of hematology and oncology, hartford hospital. hartford, ct, usa
Family History: past medical and family history were unrevealing for any endocrine tumors
Medical/Surgical History: NA
Signs and Symptoms: she was admitted to the hospital in 2000 for evaluation of severe epigastric pain, chronic diarrhea, and a 11.5 kg weight loss ove rthe last few years; in 2002, she again developed peptic symptoms including epigastric discomfort and recurrent bleeding gastric ulcers; in 2003, after her laparotomy, she presented with abdominal pain; in 2007, she developed recurrent episodes of diaphoresis, shakiness, and syncope; she also noted weight gain of 2.3 kg over last 3-4 months.]
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: esophagogastroduodenoscopy (showed severe duodenitis and an atypical post-bulbar ulcer); ct scan of the abdomen and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (showed a 3 cm mass in the head of the pancreas compressing the main pancreatic duct); octreotide scan (revealed an octreotide positive mass in head of the pancreas suggestive of a neuroendocrine tumor); octreotide scan in 2002 (negative); in 2003: ct scan of the abdomen (demonstrated a new area of low attenuation in the right lobe of the liver with a 3 cm ring-enhancing mass at the periphery); repeated octreotide scan (showed at least 4 octreotide-avid hepatic lesions involving both the lobes (largest measuring 2.5 cm in size) suggestive of metastatic neuroendocrine to liver); in 2004 after drug therapy: follow up ct scan ( showed post-embolization changes and reduction in size (3.5 to 2.5 cm; 3.8 to 3.0 cm; 2.2 to 1.9 cm) of the hepatic metastases suggestive of effective chemoembolization); follow up serial ct imaging (showed minimal increase in size of multiple hepatic lesions); in 2007: ct scan of the abdomen (showed multiple (n=10) richly peripherally-enhancing vascular metastatic nodular lesions in the liver, all of which had grown in size since last imaging)
Diagnosis: insulinoma with hypoglycemia secondary to zollinger-ellison syndrome
Laboratory Values: in 2000, her serum gastrin level was elevated (198 pg/ml; reference range: 0-42 pg/ml). serum insulin, glucagon, somatostatin and vasointestinal polypeptide (vip) levels were within normal range. in 2002, her serum gastrin level was found to be elevated (205 pg/ml). in 2003, serum gastrin level was 261 pg/ml. in 2003, laboratory investigations revealed elevated liver enzymes (ast 149 u/l, reference range: 9-36 u/l; alt 135 u/l, reference range: 7-49 u/l; alkaline phosphatase 671 u/l, reference range: 32-104 u/l). in 2003, few months after the emergency laparotomy, her serum gastrin elvel was 949 pg/ml. in 2004 after antibiotics and chemotherapy, the patient continued to have evidence of hypergastrinemia on interval follow-up with gastrin levels of more than 1,000, 3,694, 5,321, 6,786, 4,965 in december 2004, july 2005, november 2005, may 2006, and october 2006, respectively. in 2007, she had hypoglycemia (blood glucose levels: 47, 25, 51 mg/dl; reference range: 70-105 mg/dl). extensive evaluation of syncopal episodes revealed fasting hypoglycemia (25 mg/dl) with elevated insulin (29 µu/ml, reference range: 0-17 µu/ml), proinsulin (422 pmol/l, reference range: 0-18.8 pmol/l), insulin-like growth factor ii (897 ng/ml, reference range: 0-90 ng/ml) and c-peptide (3.8 ng/ml, reference range: 0.8-3.0 ng/ml) levels consistent with a functioning insulinoma
Pathology: the resected mas proved to be a 2.8 cm gastrinoma with focal venous and perineural invasion. all resected lymph nodes were negative on h&e and immunostaining (figure 2). immunohistochemically, tumor cells were diffusely positive for gastrin, and focally positive for chromogranin-a, synaptophysin and insulin (figure 3). tumor cells were negative for glucagon, vip or somatostatin. post-operatively, follow-up serum gastrin level was suppressed (18 pg/ml)
Pharmacological Therapy: she received no adjuvant chemotherapy or radiotherapy in 2000. after her laparotomy and after her elevated serum gastrin level in 2003, she was treated with depot-octreotide and proton-pump inhibitors with some symptomatic improvement but ultimately underwent chemoembolization (cisplatin 100 mg, doxorubicin 15 mg, mitomycin-c 30 mg) in 2004 for progressive disease, as evidenced by increase in number and size of hepatic metastases seen on ct scan. after her follow up ct scan after treatment with chemotherapy, depot-octreotide was discontinued without worsening of her symptoms. she developed small liver abscesses several weeks later, as a complication of chemoembolization, which were successfully treated with broad spectrum antibiotics and percutaneous drainage. in 2007, she was treated with depot-octreotide and diazoxide with poor control of her hypoglycemic episodes. subsequently, she underwent hepatic embolization with complete resolution of her hypoglycemic symptoms, and requires no medications other than proton-pump inhibitors
Interventional Therapy: she underwent a whipple procedure in 2000 with resection of the mass that proved to be a 2.8 cm gastrinoma with focal venous and perineural invasion; in 2003, she had an emergency laparotomy because of a perforated marginal ulcer and underwent revision of roux-en-y gastrojejunostomy and vagotomy
Patient Outcome Assessment: follow-up imaging has shown stable hepatic metastatic disease without localization of pancreatic or extra-pancreatic insulinoma as source of her hyperinsulinemia-hypoglycemia; patient has remained asymptomatic and is doing well on follow-up till date

Institution: department of radiology, university of british columbia, vancouver general hospital and health sciences center, vancouver, british columbia, canada
Medical/Surgical History: NA
Signs and Symptoms: worsening neck pain; the pain increased after treatment with nsaids and left arm pain and weakness began
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: physical exam (focal tenderness with no neurological deficits); radiographs (no fractures or soft-tissue abnormalities); repeat physical exam (local tenderness over the cervical spine); repeat radiograph (revealed destruction of the vertebral body of c7); ct examination (extensive destruction of bone was noted with cortical thinning, slight loss of height and an accompanying soft-tissue mass, which obliterated the epidural fat plane); bone scintigraphy (no other lesions were discovered)
Diagnosis: gorham disease
Laboratory Values: laboratory investigations were normal
Pathology: on macroscopic examination during surgery, there was marked loss of trabeculae within the c7 vertebral body with only a thin cortical rim of bone remaining. the majority of the c7 vertebral body was replaced with fibrous soft tissue with no evidence of malignancy
Interventional Therapy: physiotherapy; after pain did not subside, verbrectomy with bone grafting
Patient Outcome Assessment: no post-operative complications were encountered

Title: surf-1 gene mutation associated with leukoencephalopathy in a 2-year-old.
Authors: Timothy J;Geller T
Institution: department of neurology, division of child neurology, saint louis university school of medicine, st. louis, missouri, usa
Family History: he was an oldest child and there was no known history of miscarriage, sudden infant death syndrome, or other infant death in the extended family on either side; his family is of irish descent
Medical/Surgical History: head-on motor vehicle accident 4 months earlier

Comorbidities: acute disseminated encephalomyelitis; partial complex epilepsy
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: a cranial computed tomography (ct) scan showed bilateral cerebellar hypodensities in the area of the white matter and dentate nuclei (not shown); brain magnetic resonance imaging (mri; figure 1) showed dif- fuse, bilateral symmetrical t2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensity of white matter signal and the dentate nuclei of the cerebellum; diffusion-weighted imaging revealed symmetrical hyperintensity with corre- sponding apparent diffusion coefficient map hypointen- sity in the occipital lobes and cerebellum; a repeat mri (figures 2 and 3) showed exten- sive t2 and diffusion-weighted imaging periventricular white matter hyperintensity with continued apparent diffusion coefficient map hypointensity; additionally, t2 hyperintensity had spread to symmetrically include the brain stem

Pathology: NA
Pharmacological Therapy: the patient was started on carbamazepine with a good response, with a 4-month seizure-free period; the patient was given the presumptive diagnosis of acute disseminated encephalomyelitis and treated with a course of steroids.
Patient Outcome Assessment: he had a sudden deterioration 6 months after hospitalization, developing vertical nystagmus, impaired saccades, right optic nerve atrophy, spastic mus- cle tone in extremities, and truncal hypotonia with extensor plantar responses and ankle clonus present on neurologic examination
Disclosures: the authors have no conflicts of interest to disclose with regard to this article

Title: prolonged right ventricular failure after relief of cardiac tamponade.
Authors: Geffroy A;Beloeil H;Bouvier E;Chaumeil A;Albaladejo P;Marty J
Institution: service d’anesthe?sie re?animation, ho?pital beaujon, assistance publique-ho?pitaux de paris, universite? xavier bichat paris 7, 100 bvd ge?ne?ral leclerc, 92118 clichy cedex, france
Medical/Surgical History: a 13-month-old boy had the onset of partial complex epilepsy 1 month following a fall of 2 feet, with no loss of consciousness; his seizures consisted of rightward gaze deviation with tonic stiffening of neck, trunk, and extremities, lasting under 30 seconds but occurring 10 to 15 times per day; the patient was started on carbamazepine with a good response, with a 4-month seizure-free period
Signs and Symptoms: he had clinical signs of cardiac tamponade including pulsus paradoxus, turgescent jugular veins, tachycardia and dyspnea
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: the electrocardiogram (ekg) showed sinus tachycardia, an incomplete right bundle block and a low qrs voltage; the chest x-ray showed a globular heart with moderate bilateral pleural effusions; a transthoracic echocardiography (tte) confirmed the diagnosis of a circumferential pericardial effusion with complete end-diastolic collapse of right-sided cavities; a 12-lead ekg showed sinus rythm and an incomplete right bundle block (already present preoperatively); the chest x-ray showed moderate bilateral pleural effusions with no parenchymatous images; postoperative tte showed an akinetic and dilated rv, paradoxical septal wall motion and normal left ventricular function (the left ventricular ejection fraction was 55%); estimation of pulmonary arterial pressure was not possible due to the absence of tricuspid regurgitation; a contrast study revealed a right-to-left shunt which was thought to be consistent with a patent foramen ovale; no residual pericardial effusion was detectable; transesophageal echocardiography performed on days one, three, five and seven showed a persistent intracardiac shunt and rv akinesia; daily ekgs showed no modification; on day three, pulmonary angiography excluded a pulmonary embolism and a coronary angiogram was normal; right heart catheterization (performed while the patient was treated with dobutamine 10 ?g·kg–1·min–1) showed a cardiac output of 8.5 l·min–1, a right atrial pressure of 17 mmhg and rv pressure was 34/12 mmhg; mean pulmonary artery pressure and pulmonary artery occlusion pressure were within normal limits; we describe a severe and fatal cardiac complication following pericardiotomy; rv failure was responsible for major hypoxemia due to persistent shunt through a patent foramen ovale; appropriate investigations ruled out classic causes of rv failure (i.e., pulmonary embolism, right coronary occlusion, rv compression by residual pericardial effusion or mediastinal thrombi)
Diagnosis: hfpef
Laboratory Values: troponin ic started to raise postoperatively. the first troponin ic value was 2.65 ?g·l–1 after six hours which reached a peak of 3.78 ?g·l–1 after 30 hr. on day four, troponin ic returned to a normal range (normal: < 0.15 ?g·l–1)
Pathology: no autopsy was performed
Interventional Therapy: because of the right heart failure, the patient was immediately transferred to the operating room for an emergent pericardiotomy; on arrival in the operating room, oxygen saturation (spo2) was 97% in room air, arterial blood pressure was 140/90 mmhg and heart rate was 110 beats·min–1; after local anesthesia, a pericardiotomy was performed; as soon as the pericardium was incised, general anesthesia was induced with 20 mg of etomidate and 70 mg of succinylcholine, the trachea was intubated and the lungs were ventilated mechanically on fio2 1.0 without positive end-expiratory pressure; anesthesia was maintained with isoflurane and fentanyl; the volume of pericardial effusion was estimated at 1500 ml and a drainage tube was placed; throughout the procedure, 1500 ml of crystalloid were infused, blood pressures ranged between 150/80 and 180/120 mmhg and spo2 was stable at 100%; after recovery from anesthesia, shortly after extubation the patient became hypoxemic (spo2 < 80% despite supplemental oxygen) and showed systemic hypotension (80/35 mmhg) with turgescent jugular veins; the trachea was reintubated urgently; ten minutes after reintubation, arterial blood gas showed a pao2 of 40 mmhg on fio2 1.0; treatment, including mechanical ventilation and dobutamine, initially improved hemodynamic conditions markedly but hypoxemia persisted (pao2/fio2 ratio between 80 and 100); nitric oxide (5 to 30 ppm) was ineffective to improve oxygenation
Patient Outcome Assessment: on day six, while the rv failure was still present, the patient developed a lung infection and a septic shock; he died of refractory shock on day nine; no autopsy was performed

Title: reversible multiorgan system involvement in a neonate with complex iv deficiency.
Authors: Low E;Crushell EB;Harty SB;Ryan SP;Treacy EP
Institution: national centre for inherited metabolic disorders, children's university hospital, dublin, ireland
Family History: a female infant was born at term after a normal pregnancy and delivery to nonconsanguineous parents of irish ancestry; there were three other healthy children born to the family, and there was no family history of note
Medical/Surgical History: previous history of auricular fibrillation in treatment with a dicumarinic anticoagulant and a previous episode of abdominal pain which was diagnosed as spontaneous mesenchimal haematoma and treated non operatively
Signs and Symptoms: we report the case of a neonate who presented with acute liver failure and fulminant lactic acidosis with profound complex iv deficiency documented in muscle and liver biopsies; the neonate subsequently experienced clinical resolution by 3 months of age, and was observed to have reversibility of the biochemical deficiency noted in muscle; she presented at day 6 of life with poor feeding, jaundice, and weight loss; on evaluation, she was noted to be acidotic, with elevation of liver transaminases enzymes (aspartate aminotransferase, 195 iu/l [normal reference range, 0-54 iu/ l]; alanine aminotransferase, 114 iu/l [normal reference range, 0-67 iu/l]) and had mixed conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin, 181 mmol/l [normal reference range, 0 to 17 mmol/l]; conjugated biliru- bin, 145 mmol/l [normal reference range, 0-5 mmol/l]); in addition, a coa- gulopathy was noted: the prothrombin time was greater than 180 seconds (normal reference range, 11.5-15.3 seconds), and the activated partial thromboplastin time (aptt) was greater than 120 seconds (normal refer- ence range, 35.1-46.3 seconds); screening markers for sepsis were nega- tive; other investigations yielded normal results, including cholesterol and triglyceride levels, a copper–ceruloplasmin level, a-1 antitrypsin, serum ferritin, and plasma total iron binding capacity levels; the trans- ferrin saturation was high at 100 mmol/l (normal reference range, 15-50 mmol/l); however, a salivary gland biopsy to rule out neonatal hemach- romatosis yielded negative results for iron storage; a liver ultrasound did not show any abnormality; at presentation, the plasma lactate ranged from 7 to 18 mmol/l (normal reference range, 0.6-2.4 mmol/l), a plasma ammonia level was slightly elevated at 137 mmol/l; this subsequently decreased to normal values; the cerebrospinal fluid (csf) lactate was 2.4 mmol/l (normal reference range, 0.9-2.4 mmol/l); the csf protein analysis was normal, as was the csf amino acid analysis; plasma amino acid analysis showed a general- ized aminoaciduria, but this normalized 1 week later; analysis of urinary organic acids was consistent with liver dysfunction, with phenylalanine metabolites, phenyllactate and phenylpyruvate present and a mild eleva- tion of ethylmalonic acid; an acylcarnitine profile was within normal limits; on examination, her weight and length were on the 3rd percentile, the head circumference was on the 9th percentile; neurological findings were normal; the liver was slightly enlarged; other systems were normal; an echocardiogram showed mild left pulmonary artery stenosis; an oph- thalmologic review yielded normal findings; cranial magnetic resonance imaging performed on day 26 of life showed an abnormal high signal in the right thalamus and magnetic res- onance spectroscopy revealed a lactate peak (fig 1); the patient was commenced on a high caloric diet with coenzyme q and carnitine sup- plementation; she subsequently had diagnostic liver, muscle, and skin biopsies performed; the liver histology showed significant distortion of normal liver architecture, with evidence of individual cell necrosis as well as widespread balloon degeneration and microvesicular steatosis; staining for cytochrome oxidase activity in the muscle showed several cox-depleted fibers (fig 2); analysis of enzymatic activity performed showed a profound deficiency of complex iv activity in muscle and liver tissue (table 1); from analysis of dna isolated from liver, the common mutations in the dna polymerase gamma gene (polg) (p.a467t, p.w748s, and p.g848s) were absent; a screen for major mi- tochondrial dna rearrangements and for mitochondrial dna depletion analysis was also performed on the liver dna, and no abnormality was detected; at 3 months of age, the patient was noted to be progressing very well and gaining weight; at this time, the liver function tests had completely reverted to normal and all serial measurements of lactate were normal; a repeat mri of brain at 1 year old indicated resolution of the signal abnor- mality in the right thalamus, and repeat mrs study of the brain was normal; a repeat muscle biopsy was performed at 18 months of age; this showed cytochrome oxidase activity within the normal reference range (table 1); a repeat liver biopsy was not possible; when last reviewed at 2 years old, her head circumference was above the 9th percentile, her weight was above the 50th percentile, and her height was above the 50th percentile; she was noted to be developmentally normal; our patient presented with fulminant liver failure with hepatocyte involvement exemplified by a coa- gulopathy
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: a liver ultrasound did not show any abnormality; an echocardiogram showed mild left pulmonary artery stenosis; an oph- thalmologic review yielded normal findings; cranial magnetic resonance imaging performed on day 26 of life showed an abnormal high signal in the right thalamus and magnetic res- onance spectroscopy revealed a lactate peak (fig 1); a repeat mri of brain at 1 year old indicated resolution of the signal abnor- mality in the right thalamus, and repeat mrs study of the brain was normal
Diagnosis: complex iv deficiency
Laboratory Values: on evaluation, she was noted to be acidotic, with elevation of liver transaminases enzymes (aspartate aminotransferase, 195 iu/l [normal reference range, 0-54 iu/ l]; alanine aminotransferase, 114 iu/l [normal reference range, 0-67 iu/l]) and had mixed conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin, 181 mmol/l [normal reference range, 0 to 17 mmol/l]; conjugated biliru- bin, 145 mmol/l [normal reference range, 0-5 mmol/l]). in addition, a coa- gulopathy was noted: the prothrombin time was greater than 180 seconds (normal reference range, 11.5-15.3 seconds), and the activated partial thromboplastin time (aptt) was greater than 120 seconds (normal refer- ence range, 35.1-46.3 seconds). screening markers for sepsis were nega- tive. other investigations yielded normal results, including cholesterol and triglyceride levels, a copper–ceruloplasmin level, a-1 antitrypsin, serum ferritin, and plasma total iron binding capacity levels. the trans- ferrin saturation was high at 100 mmol/l (normal reference range, 15-50 mmol/l); however, a salivary gland biopsy to rule out neonatal hemach- romatosis yielded negative results for iron storage; at presentation, the plasma lactate ranged from 7 to 18 mmol/l (normal reference range, 0.6-2.4 mmol/l), a plasma ammonia level was slightly elevated at 137 mmol/l; this subsequently decreased to normal values. the cerebrospinal fluid (csf) lactate was 2.4 mmol/l (normal reference range, 0.9-2.4 mmol/l); the csf protein analysis was normal, as was the csf amino acid analysis. plasma amino acid analysis showed a general- ized aminoaciduria, but this normalized 1 week later. analysis of urinary organic acids was consistent with liver dysfunction, with phenylalanine metabolites, phenyllactate and phenylpyruvate present and a mild eleva- tion of ethylmalonic acid. an acylcarnitine profile was within normal limits
Pathology: she subsequently had diagnostic liver, muscle, and skin biopsies performed. the liver histology showed significant distortion of normal liver architecture, with evidence of individual cell necrosis as well as widespread balloon degeneration and microvesicular steatosis. staining for cytochrome oxidase activity in the muscle showed several cox-depleted fibers (fig 2). analysis of enzymatic activity performed showed a profound deficiency of complex iv activity in muscle and liver tissue (table 1). from analysis of dna isolated from liver, the common mutations in the dna polymerase gamma gene (polg) (p.a467t, p.w748s, and p.g848s) were absent. a screen for major mi- tochondrial dna rearrangements and for mitochondrial dna depletion analysis was also performed on the liver dna, and no abnormality was detected; a repeat muscle biopsy was performed at 18 months of age. this showed cytochrome oxidase activity within the normal reference range (table 1). a repeat liver biopsy was not possible
Interventional Therapy: the patient was commenced on a high caloric diet with coenzyme q and carnitine supplementation
Patient Outcome Assessment: at 3 months after presentation, the infant experienced clinical resolution, which was subsequently confirmed by the findings of normal complex iv activity from a muscle biopsy sample taken from the infant; when last reviewed at 2 years old, her head circumference was above the 9th percentile, her weight was above the 50th percentile, and her height was above the 50th percentile; she was noted to be developmentally normal

Title: ovarian steroid cell tumors, not otherwise specified: a case report and literature review.

in its absence p22-phox is degraded; to evaluate the reason for the gp91-phox deficiency we sequenced the gp91-phox gene on the genomic level and found that the patient was heterozygous for a nonsense mutation, 879g?a, trp289?stop, in exon 8 on one allele ; no mutation could be found on the patient's other gp91-phox allele; nevertheless, we had to consider two possibilities: the patient could have been compound heterozygous with a mutation on the second gp91-phox allele outside the sequenced regions or the patient's cells could have had an extremely skewed x chromosome inactivation (lyonization) pattern; 4, bottom); we conclude that the patient has an extremely skewed lyonization not only of her peripheral blood leukocytes but also in other tissues; to further confirm this extreme x inactivation pattern as a reason for the patient's cgd, we sequenced her gp91-phox cdna from ebv-transformed b-cells and found indeed that only the mutated sequence was expressed ; 8, omitting irrelevant crossovers for clarity); this confirms that the region framed by these markers did not generally determine an extreme x inactivation ratio; also, a huge alteration (such as a big deletion, insertion, or unequal crossover) of one of the patient's x chromosomes could not be found; a cytogenetic staining of chromosomal bands was normal; the patient's neutrophils were analyzed by a dhr assay, which can be used to measure rom (h2o2) production of many more cells than can nbt testing (fig; 7); the dhr assay revealed that the one-sided lyonization was not absolute because 1 in 2500 cells consistently produced rom at normal levels, whereas the bulk of the cells did not have any functional nadph–oxidase; Signs and Symptoms: dyspnea; muscular weakness; symptoms of heart failure; transthoracic echocardiography confirmed the location of the asd, with a left-to-right cardiac shunt, moderate to severe tricuspid insuficiency, moderate pulmonary hypertension (60 mm hg), four chamber dilatation and biventricular hypertrophy; dyspnea at rest, was alert, but anxious, and her blood pressure was 170/115 mmhg, with a heart rate of 112 beats per minute, and labored respiration at 32 breaths per minute; cardiac examination showed both lv and rv enlargement; cardiac auscultation detected a fixed split s2 with a loud component and a grade 3/6 ejection systolic murmur which was audible at the upper left sternal border and a diastolic gallop that could be heard at the cardiac apex; the lower limbs showed symmetric palpable pulses, no pedal edema, and no muscular atrophy; chest x-ray showed cardiomegaly, with a cardiothoracic ratio of 74.3% , and right atrial (ra) and rv enlargement with pulmonary edema; the electrocardiogram (ecg) showed sinus tachycardia with a ventricular rate of 112 beats per minute, left axis deviation, lv hypertrophy with strain, and alteration in ventricular repolarization consistent with hypokalemia with nonspecific st-t segment depression, and attened t wave with a prominent u wave; transthoracic echocardiography was performed and showed concentric hypertrophy of the lv, with an interventricular septal (ivs) thickness of 14 mm (n=6–9 mm); lv posterior wall thickness in end diastole of 17 mm (n=6–11 mm); lv mass of 473.6 g (n=66–150 g); lv mass index of 284.4 g/m2 (n=43–95 g/m2)); and rv wall thickness of 8 mm in diastole (n£5 mm); there was four-chamber cardiac dilatation, global ventricular hypokinetic and lv systolic dysfunction, with an ejection fraction of 17% (teichholz method); a large interatrial septum gap was present with a defect size of 2.4×2.7 cm, with a left-to-right shunt confirming the diagnosis of ostium secundum asd; the ra and the rv were dilated, and the right ventricular systolic pressure (rvsp) of 60 mmhg indicated moderately severe pulmonary arterial hypertension (pah); enlarged adrenal mass, from 3.4 cm in diameter in 2008 to approximately 4 cm in diameter in 2014; the tumor was minimally enhanced after contrast injection with low attenuation (+5 hounsfield units); the absolute washout was calculated as 68%, and the mass was considered as a lipid-poor adenoma
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: captopril suppression test; right cardiac catheterization; transthoracic echocardiography; endocrine function tests; cardiac auscultation; chest x-ray; electrocardiogram (ecg); abdominal ct scan
Diagnosis: primary aldosteronism; heart failure; atrial septal defect; biventricular cardiac hypertrophy; primary aldosteronsim due to conn’s adenoma who presented with biventricular cardiac hypertrophy, which reverses upon aldosterone normalization following adrenalectomy; exhibited ostium secundum-type atrial septal defect (asd); right adrenal adenoma and biochemical diagnosis of primary aldosteronism, with acute heart failure, decreased lv systolic dysfunction, hypertensive heart disease, severe hypokalemia, rhabdomyolysis, left-to-right cardiac shunt due to a secundum asd with moderate pulmonary hypertension (who functional class ii)
Laboratory Values: endocrine function tests showed a raised plasma aldosterone concentration (pac) to plasma renin activity (pra) ratio, which supported a diagnosis of primary aldosteronism. a captopril suppression test failed to suppress the patient’s pac; severe hypokalemia (2.2 mmol/l) which was refractory (range, 1.9–2.6 mmol/l) even with repeated potassium supplementation; urinary potassium excretion was 43 mmol/24 h; serum magnesium level was normal, while the sodium concentrations were in the high normal limit (143 mmol/l). serum creatine phosphokinase (cpk) was elevated at 1,257 iu/l, and creatine kinase isoenzyme myocardial band (ckmb) was 221 iu/l. arterial blood gas analysis showed metabolic alkalosis and ventilation-perfusion mismatch secondary to pulmonary edema. renal function tests showed normal serum urea and creatinine. urinalysis showed no proteinuria or myoglobinuria; serum potassium level was 2.1 mmol/l; pac failed to be suppressed after 120 minutes of captopril 50 mg, and the pac-to-pra ratio was still elevated further
Pathology: surgical pathology examination of the tumor revealed an adrenocortical adenoma; the resected adrenal gland was a single, well defined and encapsulated yellowish nodule which weighed 27.9 g and measured 4.1×2.6×1.5 cm; a benign adrenocortical adenoma (figure 4)

Signs and Symptoms: claudication and ischemic symptoms as well as morphological findings including arterial stenosis and occlusions; relevant stenosis of the popliteal artery; presented again with a recurrent ischemia of the right lower limb only 4 weeks after the initial treatment; an occlusion of the popliteal stent; 1 month later, the patient was readmitted to our department with massive ischemic symptoms of the same leg; one day after that surgery the patient had massive ischemic symptoms due to an occlusion of the bypass graft; postoperative magnetic resonance (mr) angiography of the aorta and lower extremities revealed only minimal circular stenoses of the bypass anastomoses with no abnormalities in the aorta or other arteries; within the next 4 years after the bypass surgery, the patient developed claudication of the right lower limb with a painless walking distance of approximately 100 m; however, the annually performed mr angiography imaging of the lower limb arteries was without pathological findings; in contrast to the mr, color-coded duplex ultrasonographies revealed a decreasing arterial perfusion; one month after the prostaglandine infusions, the patient suffered an incomplete ischemia of the right leg; mr angiography and color-coded duplex ultrasonography revealed an occlusion of the right superficial femoral artery and the bypass graft as well as stenoses of the popliteal artery and tibioperoneal trunk; the thrombolytic therapy was successful but an aneurysm of the distal bypass anastomosis was detected in the final angiography; that aneurysm had a diameter of 1.1 cm, was well perfused, and the patient had no limitations due to the popliteal aneurysm; two months later, a color-coded duplex ultrasonography control showed an increase of the popliteal aneurysm with a diameter of 1.4cm; claudication in the right leg again; one year after the surgical treatment, the patient was admitted again to our department due to massive ischemic symptoms of the right leg; walking distance of only 20 m; a mr angiography revealed a thrombotic reocclusion of the bypass graft
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: digital subtraction angiography; histopathological analysis; magnetic resonance (mr) angiography; color-coded duplex ultrasonographies
Diagnosis: multiple arterial stenoses and thromboses leading to peripheral artery occlusive disease caused by cystic medial degeneration erdheim-gsell; cystic medial degeneration of the lower limb vessels mimicking peripheral artery occlusive disease
Laboratory Values: NA
Pathology: minimal atherosclerotic changes in the arteries and degenerated vessel walls of the veins and arteries which were fragmented by a mucoid substance; that mucoid substance showed a clear blue coloring in alcain stain
Pharmacological Therapy: despite antiplatelet and anticoagulant treatment, the patient suffered multiple vascular stenosis and occlusions; oral antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy; dual antiplatelet therapy, anticoagulant therapy with rivaroxaban; clopidogrel and phenprocoumon; despite the endovascular treatment with stenting of the popliteal artery and the initiation of an oral antiplatelet therapy with 100mg acetylsalicylate and 75 mg clopidogrel daily, the patient presented again with a recurrent ischemia of the right lower limb only 4 weeks after the initial treatment; acetylsalicylate 100mg daily was continued as antiplatelet therapy for the following four years; the claudication was treated symptomatically with intravenous prostaglandine infusions; overall, 50mg alteplase and 30,000 iu heparin were administered via the catheter; discharged with anticoagulant treatment (rivaroxaban 20mg once daily) as well as due to elevated low-density cholesterol with statin treatment (atorvastatin 40 mg once daily); medication has not changed since the dismissal 2 years before; 50 mg alteplase and 36,000 iu heparin; unfractionated heparin was given for the next 5 days and was then changed to an oral anticoagulation with phenprocoumon due to a bypass occlusion under rivaroxaban treatment. additionally, clopidogrel 75 mg once daily was added as an antiplatelet therapy
Interventional Therapy: multiple surgical and endovascular interventions including bypass graft and intra-arterial thrombolysis; multiple surgical and endovascular interventions; underwent a peripheral transcutaneous angioplasty and stenting of the popliteal artery due to an ischemia of the right lower limb; stenting of the popliteal artery; an occlusion of the popliteal stent, which was successfully treated with a second angioplasty; occlusion was surgically treated with a stent removal and an implantation of a femoropopliteal bypass graft with an autologous vein; thrombotic material was surgically removed; due to the morphology an intra-arterial thrombolysis was performed; the thrombolysis-catheter was placed in the thrombus material at the bypass graft; a surgical treatment of the popliteal aneurysm was successfully performed; intra-arterial thrombolysis with an overall administration of 50 mg alteplase and 36,000 iu heparin was performed again successfully (fig; 4a); a dissection of the proximal bypass anastomosis was treated with a cordis smart stent 6/40 (fig; 4b)
Patient Outcome Assessment: despite dual antiplatelet therapy, anticoagulant therapy with rivaroxaban and multiple surgical and endovascular interventions, the patient developed recurrent arterial thromboses. the patient did not suffer further thrombotic events since clopidogrel and phenprocoumon were administered.

Title: spontaneous resolution of post-traumatic chronic subdural hematoma: a case report.
Authors: Yilmaz H;Boyali O;Atci Ib;Kocaman U
Institution: usak university education and research hospital, department of neurosugery, usak, turkey
Medical/Surgical History: suffered a doubtful head trauma one month ago; had undergone coronary bypass surgery and used regularly antiaggregation therapy (acetylsalicylic acid 100 mg/day) for 2 years
Signs and Symptoms: headache and debility complaints; we did not find any pathology on his neurologic examination; cranial computed tomography (ct) that revealed hypo-isodense collections of 2 cm thickness at bilateral frontotemporoparietal region suggestive of bilateral csdh; cranial magnetic resonance imaging (mri) at t1 and t2 axial and coronal sequence revealed bilateral frontotemporoparietal hyperintense lesion defined as csdh; there was no midline shift and compression of the ventricules; bilateral hematoma which was larger than 1cm
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: cranial computed tomography (ct); cranial magnetic resonance imaging (mri)
Diagnosis: spontaneously resolved post-traumatic bilateral chronic subdural hematoma
Laboratory Values: NA
Pathology: NA
Pharmacological Therapy: used regularly antiaggregation therapy (acetylsalicylic acid 100 mg/day) for 2 years; antiaggregation theraphy was stoped and enoxaparin sodium 20 mg/day was started; anti-edema treatment and antiepileptic drugs
Patient Outcome Assessment: patient and his relatives were not willing to undergo surgery and he was discharged with anti-edema treatment and antiepileptic drugs. one month later, he had visited to the cardiology policlinic and he had referred to our policlinic for control examination. the patient had no complaints and neurological examination revealed no pathological findings. control cranial mri revealed that almost all of bilateral csdh had resolved spontaneously (figure 3). he was symptomatically treated and discharged with suggestions.

Title: severe bilateral isolated coronary ostial lesions as a rare manifestation of radiation-induced cardiac disease a case report.
Authors: Acharya MN;El-Diasty M;Schmack B;Weymann A;Mansur A;Popov AF
Institution: department of cardiac surgery, university hospital frankfurt, frankfurt, germany; metesh nalin acharya, department of cardiothoracic surgery, harefield hospital, hill end road, harefield, middlesex, ub9 6jh, uk
Life Style: lack of conventional acquired cardiovascular risk factors such as hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, diabetes mellitus, or tobacco consumption
Medical/Surgical History: previous chest radiotherapy for breast cancer; without any pre-existing cardiovascular comorbidities; without other cardiovascular risk factors; significant for left breast carcinoma treated by mastectomy with lymph node dissection followed by mediastinal radiotherapy 30 years ago; lack of conventional acquired cardiovascular risk factors such as hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, diabetes mellitus, or tobacco consumption
Signs and Symptoms: isolated critical stenoses of the coronary ostia, and acute myocardial infarction; clinical examination was unremarkable except for a well-healed left mastectomy scar; electrocardiogram demonstrated inferior ischaemic changes; coronary angiography revealed 99 % –75 % stenoses of the left main stem, and right coronary ostia, respectively, with no additional downstream coronary lesions; trans-thoracic echocardiography demonstrated preserved left ventricular systolic function with ejection fraction 62 %, and no additional valvular abnormalities were detected; intra-operatively, both internal mammary arteries were very densely adherent to the chest wall, precluding their utilization as conduits
Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures: coronary angiography; electrocardiogram; trans-thoracic echocardiography
Diagnosis: severe, isolated bilateral coronary ostial lesions; intra-operative doppler probe scanning
Laboratory Values: NA
Pathology: NA
Interventional Therapy: underwent coronary artery bypass graft surgery for severe bilateral coronary ostial lesions; underwent urgent coronary artery bypass graft surgery to treat her critical coronary artery disease; intra-operatively, internal mammary arteries were not amenable to harvesting due to very dense mediastinal adhesions; therefore, saphenous vein grafts were performed to the left anterior descending, distal left circumflex, obtuse marginal and distal right coronary arteries; an intra-aortic balloon pump was inserted in the context of ongoing chest pain, and critical coronary anatomy; on-pump coronary artery bypass surgery was therefore performed with reversed long saphenous vein bypass grafts to the left anterior descending, obtuse marginal, distal left circumflex, and distal right coronary arteries
Patient Outcome Assessment: the patient made a satisfactory in-hospital recovery, and was subsequently discharged back to her local hospital for rehabilitation; intra-operative doppler probe scanning confirmed excellent graft flow. cardiopulmonary bypass was weaned with minimal inotropic support, and intra-aortic balloon counter-pulsation was discontinued 24 hours later. post-operatively, the patient required a tracheostomy to facilitate weaning from the mechanical ventilator. she was eventually discharged back to her local hospital for physical rehabilitation.
